Woltemade move underlines summer of change at Newcastle
- Published
It was rather telling that Matias Fernandez-Pardo was Newcastle United's final signing of a rollercoaster summer.
This was a pursuit which was anything but straightforward.
The Belgian had been Newcastle's top target before the window opened, but it was only in the final stages of the summer that the club were able to complete a complex deal following delicate negotiations with Lille.
It was ultimately a tale of two very different forwards on deadline day.
On the same afternoon Newcastle announced the rapid Fernandez-Pardo's arrival, towering club-record signing Nick Woltemade finalised his loan move to Juventus.
Woltemade only joined Newcastle last summer, but this has been a window of change on Tyneside.
Head coach Eddie Howe stepped down in July and was replaced by Matthias Jaissle just a few weeks before the start of the new campaign.
Captain Bruno Guimaraes was among a handful of key players to leave while eight new signings arrived as Newcastle's records for spending and sales in a single window were both smashed.
This was the summer which altered the face of the club.
Trippier's 'emotional' exit and unplanned setbacks
A shake-up had been signposted as far back as the spring.
It was in early April when Newcastle announced that defender Kieran Trippier would be leaving at the end of his contract.
The 34-year-old was approaching the twilight of his career, but his departure was still keenly felt as an influential figure behind the scenes.
"It was emotional for me, of course, because I loved the club so much and Newcastle gave me so much in return," the former England international said several months after moving on to Wolves.
"I'll always follow the club and want them to do well but, as a footballer, sometimes, you have to move on. With the utmost respect, I think it was the right time for both the club and myself.
"As I've always said, I wanted to leave in the right manner and show respect to my team-mates, the club and, most importantly, the supporters, who I have a great relationship with."
Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali's subsequent exits to Barcelona and Tottenham respectively did not necessarily come as a surprise, either, given they enabled Newcastle to comply and reinvest within the game's financial rules.
No-one internally had countenanced losing talisman Guimaraes, though.
However, having bailed Newcastle out so many times before, even the tireless midfielder dropped to the turf, untied his boots before the physio reached him and glared at the bench to come off during last season's final-day defeat at Fulham.
If ever an image summed up a bruising domestic campaign as Newcastle finished in 12th place - far below where the hierarchy had projected - and missed out on millions worth of European revenue.
The prospect of Guimaraes signing a new deal was unsurprisingly shot down by a figure involved in his subsequent £75m move to Arsenal a few weeks later.
After losing Alexander Isak to Liverpool against their wishes last summer, Newcastle ended up selling a fourth key player in less than a year.
They also missed out on top targets Victor Munoz and Johan Manzambi, who opted to move to Liverpool and Aston Villa respectively.
Yet those inside the club repeatedly stressed that the window could only be judged once it shut.
"Just because one element doesn't go the way you want doesn't mean you abandon the plan," a senior source said.
"We stayed on target, stayed focused, stayed calm and moved on. We didn't do a whole lot of mourning or crying when we had a setback.
"We pivoted to what's next."
'We always have hope and belief'
The final fortnight of the summer ultimately proved critical as defender Amar Dedic, midfielder Nico Gonzalez and forward Matias Fernandez-Pardo all joined the club.
Season ticket holder Adam Widdrington believes the trio's arrivals and Newcastle's performances in the 2-2 draw against Liverpool and the 2-0 win at Tottenham Hotspur changed the narrative.
"Plenty of pundits and other fans had Newcastle earmarked for relegation," he said.
"They said, 'Who's the manager? Never heard of him. Who are these young players? You have lost a load of players'.
"I still wouldn't class it as a great transfer window, but I think it's a good one, especially given the context of where it looked like Newcastle were heading in that Bruno dip.
"At that point, it didn't feel like there was so much to inspire the fans, but the last three signings shifted opinion a lot."
Fernandez-Pardo certainly feels more of a stylistic fit for a side who made the most sprints in the opening weekend (138) of the Premier League season.
Jaissle has already cited the forward's "explosiveness" which, for all his endeavour, was not part of Woltemade's game, even during an impressive start to his Newcastle career a year ago.
Fernandez-Pardo will have to quickly adapt and there will inevitably be ups and downs as the campaign progresses for the 21-year-old and a young side.
But they won't lack belief.
"We always have hope and belief," Jaissle said before a ball had even been kicked this season. "No one can take that away from us."

Acer's Predator Atlas 7 is the brand's smaller handheld gaming flagship model
It puts the Predator Atlas 8's features in a smaller form factor.
Acer has unveiled the Predator Atlas 7 as part of its announcements for this year's IFA conference in Berlin. It says the Atlas 7 offers the same flagship performance as the bigger Atlas 8 gaming handheld device, which it launched back in March, in a smaller form factor. While an inch in difference doesn't sound like much, Acer designed the Atlas 7 to be easier to hold. It has more contoured grips, an enlarged palm rest area, recessed keys and an anti-slip texture.
Like the Atlas 8, it's powered by up to an Intel Arc G3 Extreme processor, which supports up to Intel Arc B390 graphics. It has a 7-inch 16:9 FHD touchscreen display with a 120 Hz refresh rate and 500 nits of peak brightness, protected by Corning Gorilla Glass Victus to prevent scratches and cracks when dropped. Like the Atlas 8, it has an 80Wh battery capacity and can have up to 1TB in storage, as well as up to 24GB in memory. With an 80Wh battery, the Atlas 7 weighs under 750 grams. In September 2026, a rumor spread that a U.S. airman's widow was denied death benefits because he died in the context of the war in Iran, which Congress hadn't officially declared. 
The rumor appeared on Facebook, Reddit and X. 
The meme included two images: one of a young man smiling as he posed in front of a U.S. flag and another of a couple posing on a tarmac, in which the man wore Army fatigues and a woman with long blonde hair smiled in his arms. The meme read:
This is Major Alex Klinner, a U.S. Air Force airman from Alabama. He was killed in Iran on March 12 during Trump's ILLEGAL "Operation Epic Fury" war.
On Sunday, his widow exposed that Trump is REFUSING to give her death benefits, as Trump never actually formally declared war.
Let that sink in. Trump and Republicans are too weak to actually declare war as the Constitution demands, and they're leaving dead soldiers' families holding the bag.
BEYOND DEPLORABLE!
Several Snopes readers shared the meme via email, asking us to verify its claims.
The rumor stems from an Instagram post by a woman named Libby Klinner, whose bio says she is the "surviving spouse of Maj. Klinner," a former teacher and a mother to a toddler and twins. On Aug. 29, 2026, she posted a video of herself rocking a baby, with on-screen text that read "The Air Force recently told me that because we haven't officially declared war, my kids and I aren't eligible for some benefits."
A review of Klinner's Instagram feed indicated she lost her husband Alex Klinner, who had been deployed to the Middle East, on March 12, 2026. According to a March 14 announcement from the U.S. Department of Defense, Maj. John A. Klinner died two days earlier in a plane crash in Iraq, 12 days after the U.S. and Israel launched attacks on Iran. (A separate post by Klinner said her husband went by his middle name, Alex, though his first name was John.)
On Sept. 1, 2026, Under Secretary of Defense for Personnel and Readiness Anthony Tata said on X that someone had reached out to Klinner and her family "to confirm they have received all of the entitlements they are owed," though he did not specify if these included the alleged missing benefits Klinner referred to in her post.
Snopes found no reason to doubt Klinner's assertions. However, we were unable to independently verify details about the benefits in question without access to documentation or correspondence between Klinner and the Air Force. As a result, we also could not confirm whether Klinner was denied benefits because Congress hadn't declared war on Iran. For these reasons, we've left the claim unrated.
A spokesperson for the U.S. Air Force told Snopes via email that they had spoken with Klinner to ensure she is receiving the benefits she's entitled to and to answer her questions. We reached out to Klinner for further confirmation and await a response.
Klinner's claims about missing benefits
Klinner regularly posted on Instagram until March 11, talking about the difficulties of a loved one's deployment and sharing teaching tips. On March 14, she shared several photos of her husband, saying he had died. Her next post was dated May 9, asking her followers to support the families of other service members who died in the March 12 plane crash. The text in her images discussed grief and her husband's death.
On Aug. 29, Klinner posted on Instagram a video of her rocking a baby with the caption "Six months of a war we can't call a war..." (archived).
"The Air Force recently told me that because we haven't officially declared war, my kids and I aren't eligible for some benefits," the video's on-screen text read. "So not only was my husband killed in a war he never wanted to participate in, but now the benefits we're left with are being dictated by semantics and public perception."
"The missing benefits are combat pay-related and were missing from his final paycheck," the caption said.
On Aug. 31, Klinner posted again, saying the director of Air Force Mortuary Affairs Operations told her the agency was launching an audit into her benefits to ensure that she receives everything to which she is entitled, but provided no further details (archived).
We reached out to Air Force Mortuary Affairs Operations but did not receive a response by the time of publication.
Officials' response
In an email to Snopes on Sept. 2, the Air Force spokesperson said officials had talked to Klinner on Aug. 31:
We understand this matter has been difficult for Mrs. Klinner and her family, and we are committed to addressing her concerns with care and respect. Department of the Air Force officials spoke with Mrs. Klinner on Monday [Aug. 31] to ensure she is receiving all eligible benefits she and her family are entitled to, as well as ensure all her questions are fully addressed. We remain committed to providing clear information and continued support to Mrs. Klinner, as well as all the families of the Airmen who died in the KC-135 crash.
In his Sept. 1 post on X, Tata underscored the Department of Defense's commitment "to providing Major Klinner's wife and children with seamless, long-term support," but he did not reveal any details about possible missing benefits or whether Klinner may have received them (archived):
For further reading, Snopes has covered several claims about the war in Iran, including one rumor that said U.S. soldiers were "openly refusing" deployment orders.

'I've never been to Afghanistan': Six million deportees forced to start over under the Taliban
- Published
The elderly grimace, hobbling on crutches, and wide-eyed children stare, cradling chickens carried from homes they were forced to leave behind.
"It feels good to be in my own country," 35-year-old Nazia says, just minutes after she crosses from Pakistan, where she was born, into Afghanistan.
The Torkham crossing, known as "Zero Point", is where one hard life ends and another begins.
"But I've never been to Afghanistan before and many people here don't even have enough bread to eat," Nazia sighs as she heads, two of her children in tow, toward registration counters festooned with white and black Taliban flags.
Nearly her entire family, eight sisters and their offspring, were deported to Afghanistan this year from Pakistan or Iran.
They are part of the biggest cross-border movement of people anywhere in the world.
Millions of Afghans have fled across the borders to Pakistan and Iran for decades – seeking refuge or employment - and the number escaping Afghanistan has continued to rise since the Taliban takeover in August 2021.
Most are now being forced to return as these two neighbours crack down on undocumented migrants. Nazia and her family were undocumented but the UN and human rights groups say the security sweep is reaching far beyond that group to include registered Afghans too. Even Pakistan now publicly says that Afghans with Proof of Registration cards are not exempt.
The expulsions show no sign of stopping.
The number forced to return this year from Pakistan and Iran has already reached another million, according to the UN's Refugee Agency, the UNHCR.
"In a little under three years, we've seen six million people, a population that is itself the size of a small country, come back to Afghanistan," observes Charlie Goodlake, spokesperson for the UNHCR in Afghanistan.
"We've never seen in recent history a return movement on this scale," he underlines, standing in the baking heat in the tented village close to the border.
It's a desolate landscape of tarpaulin and plastic shelters, many now tattered and torn, erected by the UN and other aid agencies to provide refuge for a few nights for a people arriving with nowhere to go.
Many returnees have not set foot in Afghanistan for decades; many like Nazia have never been here at all.
"I left 45 years ago during the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and most of my brothers were born in Pakistan," explains Sarwar, who arrived a few days earlier with seven brothers and their families in a convoy of 40 people and the jumble of their worldly goods packed into a lumbering Pakistani lorry.
"We spent a long time there, so of course I felt heartbroken when they forced us out of our home," he says.
"But, despite all that pain, I am also happy because I am finally free of harassment by Pakistan's police."
Every family we met told us they had experienced prejudice and harassment by authorities in Pakistan.
The Pakistan government has not responded to the BBC's questions, but a foreign ministry spokesman told a briefing in Islamabad on Sunday that "the Government of Pakistan undertakes the necessary measures to prevent any instance of harassment or maltreatment of Afghan nationals in Pakistan. If such incidents have taken place, they are sporadic and are dealt with fully in accordance with the law".
Both Pakistan and Iran say it's past time for Afghans to go home, accusing some of posing a security risk, and others of being a financial burden.
The expulsions from Pakistan and alleged abuse intensified after a major escalation in fighting between Pakistan and Afghanistan last October. In February, Human Rights Watch highlighted "door-to-door raids, late-night home searches and arrests without warrants".
In Iran, which claimed last year to host more than four million undocumented Afghans, the mass deportations were accelerated after its 12-day war with Israel and the US in June 2025.
The New York based Centre for Human Rights in Iran accused the authorities of using the post-war climate to "cast suspicion on Afghan migrants - accusing them of espionage and branding them as potential spies for Israel".
The UN's refugee agency continues to underscore the humanitarian principle that any return should be "voluntary, safe and dignified".
But in Torkham, Sarwar's sister-in-law Zarina laments the precarious future they face: "We have no resources to start a business or earn a living, and we don't even own a tent to live in".
Inside the barren transit tent, which provides little escape from scorching 41C heat, Zarina sits alongside an anxious huddle of women and their children.
Are they worried about the future for women and girls in a country where the Taliban has barred women from much of public life, including secondary school and university?
Forty-year-old Zarina turns to make a sweeping gesture with her arm: "Look at them, they're all girls. Of course I'm worried."
Some returnees are not just worried; they're terrified.
"I don't leave this house," a former Afghan security guard, first deported from Iran and then Pakistan, nervously tells us when we meet him far from the border in what he hopes is a safe house.
"We are all living in fear including my wife and children who are also afraid to go outside."
He dismisses the Taliban government's amnesty, announced days after their return to power which declared that former government officials, security personnel and civil servants would not face retaliation and were encouraged to return to work.
"I have no trust in their amnesty because many of my colleagues have been killed." He says his case had been registered with the UN but was deported before he could be transferred to a safer country.
Financial hardship magnifies the pain. The steep cuts in foreign aid worldwide are especially sharp in Afghanistan where the Taliban are still stuck in sanctions linked to terrorism and human rights.
Pakistan confirmed on Sunday that 16,000 vulnerable Afghans have now been granted, on humanitarian grounds, a temporary exemption from being deported – a decision welcomed by the UN.
But sources estimate that the number of Afghans in Pakistan at risk of serious harm, including women and girls who would be denied education, could be as high as 250,000.
At the graceful foreign ministry compound in Kabul, Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi tries to put on a brave face.
"There's no doubt that we need some help," he admits. "There is pressure due to their return but in the long run, it will benefit them as well as Afghanistan."
In the first years after the Taliban swept to power in 2021, some of their ministers made light of humanitarian issues, saying God would provide.
The UN now estimates that 21.9 million people, nearly half the country, need assistance this year to survive. The UN's children agency, UNICEF, said last week that one million children faced "life-threatening" malnutrition.
"No country in the world could handle this kind of crisis on its own," UNHCR spokesperson Goodlake assesses, while acknowledging Taliban government efforts to help returnees as they arrive.
But, he adds, "We also know that many of the restrictions and edicts they put in place, particularly on women and girls, don't help us elicit international support".
Muttaqi reiterates his government's line that matters like girl's education are "internal issues" for Afghans to resolve.
The severe restrictions on the lives of girls and women is one of the major issues in the Taliban's international relationships and that has cost them. Five years on, only one country, Russia, has formally recognised their rule.
But when asked about this, Muttaqi points to the deepening diplomatic and economic ties with neighbours such as China and India, as well as Central Asian states.
As for Kabul's relative isolation from western nations, he asks, "those who didn't have relationships with us over the past five years, what have they achieved?"
He answers his own question: "Nothing."
We heard that word - "nothing" - from every family we met at Zero Point, but in a much different sense.
All were embarking on the hardest of homecomings, beginning all over again - with almost nothing.

Whatever happened to ... children infected with HIV due to failures in healthcare?
Seven years ago, Pakistan faced a startling medical tragedy. In the city of Larkana, in Sindh province, 494 children were diagnosed with HIV. Authorities were puzzled but eventually determined a leading cause. As NPR reported at the time: "the tragedy is … being linked to major failures in the health care system, including reuse of syringes and lack of standards for blood transfusions." The public was in an uproar. "There was panic, hue and cry," Masood Bangash, a district police officer, told NPR. Parents gathered outside clinics in Larkana to express their anger. The government pledged action, including a crackdown on unauthorized medical providers, to prevent more such infections.
Over the next week, we'll be looking back at some of our global health and development stories to see "whatever happened to ..."
This year, HIV cases among children are again being linked to unsafe medical practices. Here is a report from journalist Betsy Joles in Pakistan on the families affected –- and why the number of infections continues to rise in a country with an estimated 350,000 active HIV cases, according to the World Health Organization, and a surge among youngsters. This story is the first in our annual series, "Whatever happened to ..."
KARACHI — In August 2025, Ayesha Aftab took two of her four children to Kulsoom Bai Valika Hospital in Karachi for treatment for what she suspected was typhoid or malaria — diseases most common during Pakistan's muggy monsoon season in late summer. She brought along her youngest, Muhammad Rehan, as well. The toddler sat on her lap while her other kids received treatment and spiked a fever while they waited. The doctor on duty suggested an antibiotic injection to knock out his symptoms faster than a pill or over-the-counter syrup. "I thought, okay, the doctor knows better," Aftab said.
In the crowded ward, she saw hospital staff giving injections to child after child. Their methods were common practice, they insisted to Aftab, even in well-known hospitals in the city. "We had never been to these hospitals," she said, "so we thought maybe things happened this way."
But Rehan's health did not improve after the injection and Aftab's other two children remained ill even after weeks of treatment.
Laboratory tests provided a startling explanation: All three had contracted HIV, the bloodborne infection that causes AIDS and can be deadly if not treated quickly with the right mix of medicines.
Dozens of other parents who brought their children to government-run Valika Hospital say their kids got HIV after being treated there too. At least six later died. They blame the reuse of syringes and IV needles at the hospital — echoing some findings from the 2019 outbreak.
Multiple government-ordered inquiries since last November have noted safety issues at Valika Hospital, including improper handling of syringes. The department that manages the hospital suspended some staff, and the provincial government promised families financial compensation.
This outbreak came closely on the heels of another one in Taunsa, a district in Punjab province around 600 miles from Karachi, linked to medical care: 331 children infected with HIV between November 2024 and October 2025, prompting more government pledges to control the spread of the virus.
Why does this keep happening?
So why does the issue of unsafe medical practices leading to pediatric HIV keep resurfacing?
Doctors interviewed for this story say past measures have been stopgap solutions -– for example, cracking down on unregistered clinics in Taunsa and suspending a local hospital superintendent. But they note that the government has not addressed deeper systemic shortcomings when it comes to medical safety in Pakistan.
Fatima Mir, pediatric infectious disease specialist at the Aga Khan University Hospital in Karachi, says there remain significant "chinks in the armor" of Pakistan's healthcare system that create the conditions for more cases of pediatric HIV to occur.
They include persistently poor injection practices, along with unregulated blood donation services and reliance on informally trained providers in some areas, particularly rural ones where other options for care can be limited.
Mir says recurring outbreaks flagged among children are actually "bridging events" where the virus moves from high-risk populations (including injectable drug users, sex workers, transgender people and men who have sex with men) to low-risk groups. Healthcare facilities act as the conduit because of poor standards for safe care. "Infection prevention and control is actually the emergency right now," she says.
These problems are part of a larger issue: Pakistan has one of the lowest rates of healthcare spending per capita in the region and many of its public sector hospitals suffer from short-staffing (which could mean leaning on employees without sufficient training) and inadequate supervision to ensure safe practices.
Through the years, pediatric HIV cases have been linked to both public and private healthcare providers, where quality varies widely and government oversight is inconsistent, says Syed Faisal Mahmood, who specializes in infection prevention, also at AKUH in Karachi. "Healthcare in general is now driven not by quality but by convenience and by cost," Mahmood says, making it a "perfect storm" for unsafe medical practices.
During a speech to parliament in June, health minister Mustafa Kamal acknowledged "the wrong use of syringes" and IV drips as contributing factors in incidents of HIV.
The pediatric outbreaks that get flagged don't reflect the true gravity of the HIV crisis, public health experts warn.
"Since our disease surveillance system is also very weak, we will never know what exactly the prevalence is," says Zafar Mirza, Pakistan's former special assistant to the prime minister on health. He says this makes the spread of HIV "much larger than what we know."
What the children face
For kids who have contracted the disease, there's a lifetime of daily pills ahead –- and deep societal prejudice. In many people's minds, HIV and AIDS carry "back-breaking shame," says Zulfikar Ali Bhutto Jr., a prominent activist who launched an awareness campaign about HIV in Pakistan this year. That's because many associate them with sex — one way the virus can spread — and other socially frowned-upon activities like drug use.
His campaign is trying to stamp out the stigma that surrounds an HIV diagnosis and educate people about the basics, such as how the virus can't be spread through touching or sharing food.
For now, families say their children have to manage the judgement that comes with HIV, which can translate to discrimination against them and their siblings.
Muhammad Asif, a factory worker in Karachi, says his daughter Manahil was refused admission to school because of her HIV diagnosis. Three of his other daughters were also denied admission despite being HIV free. The cost of books and school supplies for a new school is another thing to manage on his $140 monthly salary.
"We have to spend money on our sick children and take them to hospitals far away. We either have to pay for transport or spend money on their schooling," Asif says.
Umaima Ansari, a teacher in Hyderabad, has experienced how the stigma that comes with HIV feels since her 3-year-old son Hussain tested positive.
His family suspects an operation soon after birth to treat hydrocephalus, which causes swelling in the brain, or a blood transfusion just over a year later may have carried the virus.
Following Hussain's diagnosis, Ansari says both public and private hospitals started turning him away, saying they would not be able to treat him for his other medical conditions because of the risk.
Even physiotherapists for management of his cerebral palsy, a diagnosis he also received shortly after birth, became wary. Ansari was advised early on by other medical providers to keep Hussain's diagnosis private. "Don't tell anyone he has HIV. People will stop meeting you. People will stop coming over to your house," she recalls being told.
What does the future hold?
The looming question: Will the government's new safety measures reduce the risk of medical HIV transmission?
So far, these measures include nationwide HIV screenings before surgeries to flag undetected infections, and a complete ban on certain types of syringes from January, a move that first started after the Larkana outbreak 7 years ago. The ban aims to replace conventional syringes with ones that lock, making them harder to reuse.
As for kids who've already been diagnosed, the activist Bhutto says grace from society is key.
"These children will have to live with this disease for the rest of their life as far as we know. So they need to live in a world that is kind to them."
Betsy Joles is a journalist based in Pakistan.

The liver is a large, forgiving organ, but tumours can grow deep within it, spread across both its halves, or take root in a liver already scarred by disease. Up until recently, cutting out the cancer was often impossible without leaving too little healthy liver behind to keep a person alive. Today, however, a growing field known as transplant oncology is changing that.
What happens
Instead of trying to cut the cancer out of the liver, doctors remove the entire diseased liver and replace it with a healthy one. The most common type of liver cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), is frequently multifocal, meaning it appears in several places at once. A transplant solves both problems in a single operation: it removes every tumour, eliminates the scarred field that keeps producing them, and restores completely normal liver function.
The central challenge of transplant oncology has always been selection. Donor livers are precious and scarce, and a transplant only makes sense if the cancer is unlikely to return. What increasingly matters is a tumour’s biology: how aggressive it is, how it behaves, and how it responds to treatment. This shift is the heart of modern transplant oncology. Teams now weigh blood markers such as AFP (alpha-fetoprotein) and PIVKA-II, patterns seen on PET scans, and the tumour’s grade under the microscope.
One of the most powerful tools in this field is downstaging, which means deliberately shrinking tumours until a patient who was previously ineligible becomes a candidate for transplant. A cancer that shrinks and stays quiet is showing favourable biology. One that keeps growing despite treatment reveals itself as too aggressive for a transplant to help. Roughly half of appropriately selected patients can be successfully downstaged, and those who are then transplanted after a mandatory observation window do strikingly well.
Expanding limits
While HCC remains the main indication, transplant oncology is expanding into cancers that were, until recently, considered off-limits. Bile duct cancers (cholangiocarcinoma) are a prime example. For certain patients with tumours at the junction of the bile ducts that cannot be removed surgically, a rigorous protocol combining chemotherapy, radiation, and careful staging before transplant has produced survival rates far beyond what surgery alone could achieve.
Beyond HCC and bile duct cancers, this treatment modality is also relevant to several other complex liver tumours, including intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and cancers that metastasise to the liver, such as colorectal liver metastases and neuroendocrine liver metastases. In children, it also plays an important role in the treatment of paediatric liver cancers, including hepatoblastoma, HCC, and hepatic epithelioid hemangioendothelioma.
Two lives, one principle
A 54-year-old man with chronic liver disease arrived with two hepatocellular carcinomas involving the right lobe of the liver. Owing to the underlying chronic liver disease, he was not a suitable candidate for bridging therapy. As his tumour markers were within normal limits, and a PET-CT showed no evidence of extrahepatic disease, his 45-year-old wife came forward as a living donor and donated her right lobe. He then underwent a successful living donor liver transplant, made an uneventful recovery, and is now five months post-transplant with excellent graft function and no evidence of disease recurrence. This case highlights another important indication for liver transplantation, where it offers a curative treatment for patients with both decompensated chronic liver disease and underlying liver cancer.
Another patient, a man in his fifties, had liver cancer that had grown into a major blood vessel. Rather than turning him away, his team treated the tumour with targeted local therapies and precision radiation, watched his tumour markers fall steadily to normal, and confirmed the cancer had responded before proceeding. Nearly two years after his transplant, he remains cancer-free.
Transplant oncology has therefore shifted the question from “can this tumour be removed?” to “does its biology make a new liver worth giving?” As selection grows more precise, more patients who were once told nothing could be done, are finding a real path to cure.
(Dr. Jayanth Reddy is lead consultant - HPB & liver and pancreatic transplants at Manipal Hospital, Old Airport Road, Bengaluru. jayanth.reddy@manipalhospitals.com)

The Trump administration is considering a new round of sweeping tariffs on semiconductors, a move that could extend beyond chips to products including laptops, gaming consoles and data-centre servers, POLITICO reported, citing eight people familiar with the discussions.
The proposed tariffs are being considered despite warnings from technology companies that higher costs and tighter access to advanced chips could undermine US ambitions to dominate the global artificial intelligence race.
According to POLITICO, one proposal under consideration would significantly expand the number of technology products subject to tariffs. Rather than targeting only semiconductors, the duties could also cover products that contain the chips, including laptops, gaming consoles and servers used in data centres.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick supports a structure that would link tariff relief for foreign companies to investments in US semiconductor manufacturing, four people familiar with the discussions told the news outlet.
The administration is also considering phasing in the tariffs, although the proposal remains fluid and could undergo significant changes in the coming weeks or months.
The potential tariffs have alarmed the US technology industry, which is already facing shortages of high-end semiconductors as demand surges because of the rapid construction of AI data centres.
Technology companies broadly support President Donald Trump’s push to expand semiconductor manufacturing in the US. However, industry representatives argue that advanced chip factories require billions of dollars and can take years to build.
Until domestic capacity expands, US companies will remain heavily dependent on imported chips from Asian suppliers, including Malaysia, South Korea and Taiwan. Taiwan alone produces more than 90% of the world’s most advanced semiconductors, according to the report.
The debate exposes a potential conflict between two major Trump administration priorities: bringing semiconductor manufacturing back to the US and winning the global AI race.
POLITICO reported that technology companies fear tariffs could raise the cost of the imported chips needed to power the AI boom and make it harder for US companies to obtain sufficient supplies.
The industry has warned that the measures could ultimately force some companies to delay or cancel planned data-centre projects.
The White House defended the administration’s semiconductor policy.
“Reshoring semiconductor manufacturing is a top priority for President Trump,” White House spokesperson Kush Desai said, according to the news outlet.
Desai said Trump administration policies had already secured hundreds of billions of dollars in investments in the semiconductor sector. The administration, he added, remains focused on attracting more investment, providing economic relief and protecting US national security.
Technology companies and industry lobbyists have stepped up efforts to persuade the administration to scale back the proposed tariffs, POLITICO reported.
The companies want the new duties to more closely resemble tariffs announced earlier this year, which included broad exemptions for data centres and other domestic uses.
Tech representatives and lobbyists have increasingly met with Lutnick and other senior Commerce Department officials, including Undersecretary Jeffrey Kessler, who heads the Bureau of Industry and Security, according to people cited by the media outlet.
Lobbyists argue that tariffs could slow the expansion of US data centres by making it more difficult for technology companies to secure the huge volumes of advanced semiconductors required for AI.
The concerns come as major US technology companies are embarking on a record AI spending spree, committing hundreds of billions of dollars to large data-centre projects and advanced chips.
One technology official from a major industry group said that the proposal could seriously undermine US efforts to establish AI leadership, describing it as “kneecapping yourself at the starting line.”

'Ghana was the crime scene': The country leading the demand for slavery reparations
- Published
This year has seen a dramatic change in tone in the global conversation about the transatlantic slave trade.
The demand for formal apologies, debt relief and financial compensation from nations and institutions that benefited from slavery has become increasingly forceful.
In March, a resolution was passed at the United Nations recognising slavery as "the greatest crime against humanity" - though the United States voted against the resolution and every European nation abstained from the vote.
The UK, which alongside Portugal dominated the transatlantic slave trade, has consistently rejected the idea of paying reparations, which is perhaps unsurprising given estimates of what Britain "owes" in damages to nations affected run into many trillions of pounds.
This resistance has not deterred the country that has become the leading voice on reparations: Ghana.
Ghana cannot afford to be silent on ensuring that we hold perpetrators accountable"
It was Ghana that tabled the UN resolution, and in June, a summit on reparations was held in its capital, Accra, with delegates from around 80 countries, who concluded that recompense was long overdue.
"Ghana has always been a pan-African leader. We're the first country to attain independence in sub-Saharan Africa and to prove that it is possible to fight imperial might, and win," Foreign Minister Samuel Okuzeto Ablakwa tells me.
Ghana has been given special responsibility by the African Union to be "champion for reparatory justice" and it is clearly a role the country's political leadership is taking seriously.
In part that is because about 10-15% of the estimated 12 million Africans who were forcibly removed from their homes, torn from their villages, and dehumanised on a scale never before seen, were from what is now Ghana. Even more were shipped from its shores.
"Ghana was the crime scene where these atrocities took place, so Ghana cannot afford to be silent on ensuring that we hold perpetrators accountable," Ablakwa says.
The minister has called for a system of reparatory justice that funds educational grants, venture capital for young African entrepreneurs and research into enduring health issues that some argue may trace their roots back to the severe malnutrition and inhumane conditions of enslavement.
And though he insists that this is not about direct financial gain for African leaders, one of the demands laid out at the recent summit on reparations clearly talked of debt relief and debt cancellation.
He also wants individual institutions that benefited from the slave trade to be held accountable and pay compensation. Among these is the Church of England.
In the 18th Century, the Church's missionary wing ran plantations and owned hundreds of slaves, which helped fund its work across the Americas and beyond.
Many Church of England clergy independently owned slaves, and a recent report by the Church's endowment fund reported the institution made large investments in the slave trade from which it made huge sums of money.
In July, the leader of the Church, the Archbishop of Canterbury Dame Sarah Mullally, visited Ghana in one of her first international visits in the role.
She travelled to Cape Coast Castle, one of the many coastal fortresses that had been run by the British, and where enslaved people were held before enduring the brutal "Middle Passage" to the Americas.
As she toured the dungeons where slaves were held and walked through "the door of no return" through which they were forced before being loaded on to ships, Dame Sarah looked emotional and stopped to pray.
"I felt the weight of the depth of evil that the transatlantic slave trade was. You can't help but be deeply moved by the horrific conditions that people were kept in," the Archbishop said.
She also prayed in a 17th Century chapel that was positioned directly above the dungeons.
"For me that is such a stark illustration of the way the Church was involved in the slave trade," she says. "How can the church have sat above the horrors that were going on below?".
"The Church of England has apologised for the part that we played in the transatlantic slave trade but we've also said there needs to be action that relates to that," Archbishop Sarah said.
The Church has set up a £100m ($135m) social impact fund designed to benefit communities thought to continue to feel the enduring legacy of the slave trade today.
But within the Church, the establishment of the fund has encountered resistance, just as the global push for nations to pay reparations has done.
One of the key counter-arguments centres on the fact that some Africans were themselves complicit in the capture and sale of their fellow people.
But Foreign Minister Ablakwa emphatically rejects this narrative. "I think that there's a strategy to divide and conquer and to create a very contrived confusion," he argues.
He stresses that the entire architecture of chattel enslavement was curated by Western slave-owning powers, who simply utilised local actors to help carry out their plans.
The foreign minister points out that when the laws, insurance policies, and financial architectures of the trade were being drafted, "there was no African at the table".
"We denounce and totally reject those claims that Africans are as guilty and complicit as those who masterminded this whole atrocity," he says.
Yet, within Ghana itself, the conversation around African complicity is far more nuanced, and for some traditional leaders, acknowledging the past is a vital prerequisite part of healing.
King Tackie Teiko Tsuru II, the Ga Mantse, leader of Ghana's Ga people, recently took the step of publicly apologising for his ancestors' involvement in the slave trade.
"I think that the transatlantic slave trade was the greatest crime against humanity, and ancestors also took part as players in that trade," says the king.
The Ga people became middlemen who traded with Europeans. They sold gold, ivory and ultimately enslaved Africans, often those captured in local conflicts, in exchange for the manufactured goods brought mainly by the British and Dutch, including textiles, alcohol and guns.
But the king felt he needed to say sorry not just for his own people's complicity, but the complicity of other Africans too.
"I stand on the same point of apologising on behalf of all traditional authorities and my ancestors and forebears for the part they also played in the slavery of our brothers and sisters.
"It has affected lives and societies up to now, and to be able to go forward, you have to look at your past. It dawns on us to admit our fault and correct it," he says.
The king believes strongly in the need for those who benefited from the slave trade to pay reparations and acknowledges that he, too, needs to commit to making financial amends.
"I believe that it underpins a state of moral courage and credibility."
For the Ga Mantse, admitting fault does not dilute the guilt of European empires; rather, it solidifies Africa's moral standing and sets an example as to how to move forward.
But Ghana is leading the way in another aspect of trying to heal the damage done by the slave trade. The country has run a high-profile campaign inviting the African diaspora - particularly African-Americans - to visit the continent.
It has been promoted as a means of bringing people together in the shared story of their traumatic past, with "reparations" quite literally focussing on "repair" at a very human level.
Yaw Asare, now a Ghanaian PhD student at Howard University, previously worked within the President of Ghana's Diaspora Office, which ran the campaign.
Initially, the gathering of black people from across the globe was, he felt, "a beautiful, profound experience devoid of capitalist motives". But he says in some respects the initiative soon morphed.
"The Ghana Tourism Authority also latched on to it and then used it to enhance their tourism project," Asare explains, saying the initiative started to become less about "repair" and more about hitting tourism quotas.
Asare says the campaign has often viewed the returning diaspora simply as a means of foreign cash flow, raising prices and negatively altering local economies.
"Now (local) people are finding that they cannot afford basic things," Asare says, describing how local Ghanaians were economically sidelined.
More devastatingly, he feels the commercialisation of the initiative overshadowed the deep, psychological work that is desperately needed for locals as well as "returning" members of the diaspora.
"We are dealing with humans, we are dealing with people. We cannot reduce them to, 'come see this site, pay this entrance fee'," Asare says.
He also questions - in an initiative that was partly supposed to be about addressing the trauma of Africans in the diaspora - why they were required to pay entrance fees at the same rates as European tourists at, for example, the coastal castles where slaves were trafficked.
He says all of this means a missed opportunity to address deep-rooted trauma some of which he feels is etched into the very geography and psychology of modern Ghana.
"Go to Jamestown (in Accra), people are huddled together because there is the fear of 'if I live far away, I could be taken'," Asare says, pointing to how centuries-old concerns dictated why people built their houses so closely together.
Jamestown is one of the oldest districts in the city, a community originally built around a British coastal fort where slaves were brought, traded and then sent on ships to the Americas.
For Asare, true reparatory justice must prioritise human connection and healing over financial transactions.
"We have to remove the band-aid and then look at the sore, the gaping wound that's present," Asare says about what he sees as real "reparations". "And see how we can dress it and nurse it and heal".

US aircraft carrier docks near Thai beach resort Pattaya after record 250 days at sea
- Published
After a record 250 days at sea without a port stop, the nuclear-powered aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln has docked in Thailand, giving its nearly 5,000 crew members a much-needed break.
The ship is docking close to the beach resort of Pattaya, known for its raucous nightlife and for sex tourism. For the US it also carries strong historical echoes.
When the weary sailors walk into the city's bars and restaurants, they will literally be treading in the footsteps of the hundreds of thousands of US troops who came here for R&R – rest and relaxation - during the Vietnam War.
They transformed it from a sleepy fishing village to one of the world's most famous and frenetic party towns.
Today the neon-lit alleys running down to the beach are much quieter than usual. The bars in the city's famous Walking Street still screen videos on their walls of pole-dancing women, trying to lure customers inside.
But there are not many of those customers, and most seem to be family groups from the Middle East more interested in the Turkish ice-cream vendor than the go-go bars.
The Iran War, which has affected tourism and consumer spending, has hit businesses hard here. The prospect of thousands of American sailors, with nine months of salary unspent while at sea, offers a rare opportunity to local businesses.
The US carrier left San Diego last November on what was supposed to be a six-month assignment in the Pacific and South China Sea.
However, the ship was diverted to the Gulf after the US and Israel began military operations against Iran in late February.
Recently some members of Congress raised concern about reports of food shortages, broken toilets and mental stress among the crew. The US Navy acknowledged that working conditions have been tough, but said the crew were sufficiently well-supported. It would not, however, comment to the BBC on the carrier docking at Pattaya, citing operational security.
Despite its close relationship with China, Thailand is a treaty ally of the US, and port visits by US Navy ships are a familiar occurrence.
But this is probably the largest number of US military personnel coming straight from a war zone to Pattaya since the fall of Saigon in 1975.
"This visit could be our best hope," said Anon Saiteer, who sells gems in a shop near Walking Street, which has put up a large sign welcoming the US sailors and marines and offering them a special discount. "We have nothing to lose – we just hope they will spend some money here."
But US and Thai officials are trying to ensure this happens without any of the salacious headlines for which Pattaya has become known.
The Thai authorities have said there are a few places where the US servicemen and women will not be allowed to go. One of them is Soi 6, which runs down to the main beach, and is known for its concentration of racy go-go bars.
While the Thai police have reminded their US visitors that prostitution is technically illegal in Thailand, there are actually thought to be 25,000 to 50,000 sex workers in the city. Many of them work in Soi 6, where they stand outside the bars imploring men to come inside.
The many cannabis shops in Pattaya are also off-limits to US crew members, along with sea-sports like paragliding and jet-skis.
"It is their decision," Mayor Poramase Ngampiches told the BBC. "The US military have done their homework."
The US Navy has organised shuttle buses from the port into Pattaya running from 5am to 2am every day the carrier is here in Thailand. Two hotels have been designated suitable for those US crew members who want to splash out on a night onshore.
The Thai authorities have deployed hundreds of police officers to keep an eye on the city's entertainment zones, and warned local businesses not to overcharge their American guests.
"The visits of US military men 50-60 years ago introduced Pattaya to the world and turned it into a tourist attraction," says Mayor Poramase.
"We have to be frank, the city has a reputation for bar girls. We understand the stereotypes. We can't stop that.
"What we can do is to show that Pattaya has changed, that we now have other things, such as sports, seminars, wellness and family-friendly activities. It's a mixture of everything."
Both countries hope that by the time the USS Abraham Lincoln begins the long journey home across the Pacific on 6 September, it will be with a refreshed and rested crew.

Commuters have expressed concern over safety concerns, overloading and overcharging by e-rickshaws in the summer capital.
Battery-operated rickshaws have rapidly emerged as the backbone of short-distance public transport across Srinagar, connecting commuters through the city centre, Downtown and Uptown localities. However, while commuters acknowledge the convenience of the service, they say rising instances of overloading, safety lapses, inconsistent fares and underage driving are increasingly putting lives at risk.
Passengers said overloading remains one of the most common violations, particularly during peak morning and evening hours, when some e-rickshaws carry far more passengers than their permitted capacity.
"E-rickshaw are meant for four passengers, but we often see five or even six people squeezed inside. Sometimes another passenger is made to sit beside the driver in the front, leaving hardly any space. Since these are three-wheelers, it becomes risky, especially while negotiating turns," said Nusrat Jan, a college student who frequently.
Another commuter, Mudasir Ahmad, said the problem is visible across several busy routes in the city.
"Many operators overload to earn a few extra fares in one trip. Passengers also agree because they don't want to wait. But the practice puts everyone at risk. A slight imbalance or sudden brake can lead to an accident," he said.
Commuters said the risk becomes even greater on roads riddled with potholes, particularly in several Downtown and uptown localities where uneven road surfaces frequently destabilise the vehicles.
"There have been several incidents in recent weeks where overloaded e-rickshaws were tilted or overturned after hitting potholes. Videos and photographs of such accidents keep surfacing on social media. Thankfully, many passengers escaped with minor injuries, but next time the consequences could be much worse," said Shabir Hussain, a resident of Downtown Srinagar.
Students said they continue to depend heavily on e-rickshaws because they are faster and more accessible than minibuses for short-distance travel.
"We rely on them daily because they save time and reach areas where larger vehicles don't. But there should be strict checks against overloading. Safety cannot be compromised for convenience," said Sana Jan, a university student.
Besides safety concerns, commuters also pointed to the absence of a transparent fare mechanism after conventional fuel-run autorickshaws were largely replaced by battery-operated vehicles.
"There is no standard fare system. Charges often vary depending on the driver's mood, rush hours or the urgency of passengers. Since these e-rickshaws have become the primary mode of short-distance transport, authorities should fix route-wise fares and ensure they are displayed prominently," said Mohammad Yousuf, an office employee.
Residents also expressed concern over reports of minors operating e-rickshaws in some areas, calling it a serious threat to passenger safety.
"Driving without a valid licence is dangerous not only for passengers but also for pedestrians and other motorists. Such violations should invite strict action," said Bashir Ahmad, a resident of Bemina.
Traffic Police said enforcement against violations has been intensified across the city. A Traffic Police official said that regular enforcement drives are being conducted to curb overloading, underage driving and other traffic violations involving e-rickshaws.
"Our teams have been carrying out sustained drives over the past several days across different parts of the city. We are checking overloading, documentation in these vehicles. Action is also being taken wherever minors are found operating vehicles. These drives will continue, and violators will be dealt with strictly," the official said.
The official said e-rickshaws have significantly improved last-mile connectivity in Srinagar and are an important component of the city's transport system. "The objective is not to discourage this mode of transport but to ensure that it operates safely and within the prescribed rules," officials said.

Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.
The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.
It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"
Of course he did.
Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.
"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.
"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.
"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.
"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"
Now a 19-year-old Kimi is dominating this year's F1 championship in only his second season.
This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".
"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.
It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.
"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.
Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.
"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.
"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"
Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.
"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.
In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.
He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.
"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."
Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.
The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.
Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.
But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he got into, he was quick, and won.
By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.
It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.
"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."
Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.
Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.
"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.
At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.
This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.
1 of 4
By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.
So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.
Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.
Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".
"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'
"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"
Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.
"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.
"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."
Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.
Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.
"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.
"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.
"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.
"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.
"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."
Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.
It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.
Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.
"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."
Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.
Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.
"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.
There were stand-out moments - Antonelli out-qualified Russell at the second race of the season on the high-speed Jeddah street circuit and stuck it on pole for the sprint in Miami.
But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.
"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.
Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.
"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."
Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".
"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."
A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.
"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"
Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".
"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."
Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.
"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.
"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."
Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He has taken the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.
In the best car in the field, Antonelli has taken six poles and six wins in 11 races and heads into the second half of the season, starting at the Dutch Grand Prix this weekend, with a 50-point lead in the championship, and well on course for his first world title. If it had not been for dodgy reliability, he could be even further ahead.
The extent of this turnaround has shocked almost everyone.
"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.
"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."
Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.
"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.
"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."
Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.
"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."
Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".
"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."

Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.
Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"
The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.
Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'
"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."
Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.
"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.
"About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."
Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son.
"In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says. "We have to live every day our best day. You work hard every day to arrive at the end of the project you have."
Back in February 2024, Wolff followed up his phone call to Marco with a meeting in Milan.
"Toto said: "Of course it will be difficult, but I think after one year of experience, we can do very well with Kimi in F1," Marco says.
"The project was 2025 experience, 2026 start to achieve results. I think we overachieved."

Could the man who murdered a Christian missionary and his sons walk free in India?
- Published
Warning: This article contains details of violent death that some readers may find distressing
One of India's most shocking incidents of anti-Christian violence is back in the news more than a quarter of a century after it drew condemnation from around the world.
The Supreme Court is hearing a petition seeking release from prison by a man who is convicted of killing Australian Christian missionary Graham Staines and his two young sons in 1999.
Dara Singh - whose real name is Rabindra Kumar Pal - has been in jail since his arrest in 2000, serving a life sentence for burning alive the Australian missionary and his six and 10-year-old sons in a village in the eastern state of Odisha (formerly Orissa).
Staines had spent 30 years working with leprosy patients, but Singh and his associates from Hindu hardline groups had accused him of forcibly converting poor Hindus from disadvantaged castes and tribals to Christianity.
The viciousness of the crime sent shockwaves through India's minority Christian community and caused global outrage. Now reports that Singh may be set free have brought alive memories of the heinous crime.
Staines lived in Baripada in Mayurbhanj district, where he worked among the local tribal community.
On the night of their murder on 22 January 1999, Staines and his sons had attended a Christian gathering in Manoharpur, a remote village in the neighbouring district of Keonjhar. They were sleeping in their jeep when a mob of 60 to 70 people led by Singh surrounded their vehicle, set fire to it and prevented them from escaping.
As Singh went on the run after the crime, police put up posters all over the state, offering an 800,000-rupee (approximately $18,000 then) reward for information leading to his capture. Reports at the time said he was helped by villagers and tribals who eulogised him as "a modern-day Tarzan who plays with elephants and rides tigers". He was arrested a year later during an overnight raid on a jungle hideout.
In a sensational interview, external with the India Today magazine's Ruben Banerjee from prison a few months later, he denied killing Staines and his children but said he "did not like Graham Staines" and had "spearheaded the movement against missionaries".
"Missionaries have been targeting our religion. They have been converting Hindus by deceit and inducements. Our religion is under siege. As a true Hindu, it was my responsibility to oppose them," he said. "Since I was possibly the most famous name in the region, the police implicated me in the killings."
Singh added that he was "prepared to be a martyr for the cause of Hindus" but believed that he would never get convicted.
His optimism was misplaced - in 2003, a trial court sentenced Singh to death and 12 others to life imprisonment. Two years later, the high court commuted his death sentence. It confirmed the life term of his accomplice Mahendra Hembram but freed 11 others, saying there was not enough evidence to support their convictions.
In January 2011, the Supreme Court upheld Singh's life sentence, refusing the prosecutors' plea to reinstate the death penalty.
The Staines murder was not the only crime Singh was guilty of. In 2007, he was convicted for two other heinous crimes he committed against religious minorities in 1999 - the same year he murdered the Australian missionary and his children.
He received life sentences, external for leading a mob that set fire to a church and killed Catholic priest Arul Das with an arrow as he tried to flee the burning building and, in the second instance, for beating and burning to death a Muslim garment trader Shaikh Rahaman.
Police had registered 10 cases accusing Singh of involvement in hijacking trucks of Muslim traders transporting cows - an animal many Hindus consider sacred - and setting them free. In his interview, Singh denied being "involved personally", saying "my supporters might have done it". But he admitted that he was "actively involved in the movement against illegal trade in cows and cowslaughter" which "had to be stopped at any cost".
Church leaders had alleged the attacks were carried out at the behest of hardline Hindu organisation Bajrang Dal but Singh denied he was a member and an enquiry commission, led by retired top court judge DP Wadhwa, later ruled that he had worked alone.
Graham Staines' widow, Gladys, who stayed on in India with her daughter Esther until July 2004, said she had "forgiven" Dara Singh in the Christian spirit. "Forgiveness opens up the path of healing," she said.
In July 2024, Singh filed a plea for remission in the top court, saying he was entitled to be released because he had spent more than 25 years in prison. He said his conduct had been good in jail and expressed remorse for his actions.
The 62-year-old blamed the crime on "the fervour of youth" in his petition, external seeking early release.
"The petitioner acknowledges and deeply regrets the transgressions committed more than two decades ago.
"In the fervour of youth, fuelled by impassioned reactions to the brutal history of India, the petitioner's psyche momentarily lost restraint and it is imperative for the court to scrutinise not merely the actions but the underlying intent, noting that there was no personal animosity harboured towards any victim," he wrote.
Last year, the top court asked the state government to take a call on his plea, but the authorities have so far not told the court what they intend to do.
At the last hearing on 19 August, authorities told the court that the Sentence Review Board (SRB), which is examining Singh's plea, was waiting for some more paperwork and sought an adjournment.
The two-judge bench of Justices Manoj Misra and Vijay Bishnoi expressed their annoyance at the several adjournments the state had sought in the case and said if the SRB failed to decide Singh's plea by 2 September, the court would. "You take a decision, whichever way you want. If you do not take a decision, then we will."
On Wednesday, though, the court did not hear the case. The date for the next hearing is yet to be announced.
Reports that Singh may walk free if the state government or the court accept his remission petition have led to some disquiet in India's 30-million Christian community - some of it because of unease over his earlier statements.
In his 2000 India Today interview, he said he had "no regrets" and "will never regret" killing Staines' children. "When Hindus die, others don't cry. Why should we weep when others die? Whatever has happened is right. Whatever will happen will also be right."
If released from prison, he said, he would "go back to what I have been doing - oppose cow slaughter and conversions".
"The government must stop them. If they are not stopped, more people might get killed. Anything can happen," he added.
In an article on the Union of Catholic News (UCN) website, human rights and Christian political activist John Dayal wrote recently that remission after decades in jail is "not unusual" in India and "the principle behind it - that punishment should allow for reform and eventual return to society - is humane".
But the anxiety among religious minorities in Odisha "is not abstract given the state's history of anti-Christian violence", Dayal points out, citing the Kandhamal riots of 2008, in which dozens were killed and tens of thousands were displaced.
"The Staines murders were not an ordinary homicide but a public, theatrical act of terror, intended to be seen and understood as a warning. The killings of Father Arul Doss and Sheikh Rehman extended that same message," he writes.
"What remains to be seen is not whether Singh will eventually walk free, but how the government conducts itself around that decision...and whether minority communities are given any reassurance," Dayal adds.

Norris sets up junior team to help drivers to F1
- Published
World champion Lando Norris is setting up his own junior team to support young drivers on their route to Formula 1.
LN4 Fusion, launched near Monza on the eve of the Italian Grand Prix weekend, will run teams across multiple feeder categories starting from next year.
It will be run by Rene Rosin, the founder and former boss of Prema, one of the most successful teams in the junior categories over the past two decades.
In parallel, Norris is setting up what is described as "an independent, fully funded driver development" scheme, to be called the LN4 Legacy Programme.
"I've been really lucky to have some amazing people around me throughout my career, and I know that getting to Formula 1 takes so much more than just talent," Norris said.

"That's what these two projects are all about. LN4 Fusion is about building a race team that can compete with the best in junior motorsport, with great people and a great environment for drivers to develop.
"The LN4 Legacy Programme is about helping talented young drivers get opportunities they might not otherwise have."
Norris' programme will run teams in the Italian F4 Championship, FIA Formula Regional European Championship and FIA Formula 3 Championship in 2027.
The aim is also to compete in Formula 2 next year, but the application process for that has not yet been completed.
Norris will be co-owner of the project along with an investment group run by businessman Dan Richards, who has a background in technology, particularly in healthcare and data security.

Richards said: "What we have created is far more than simply the acquisition of a racing team.
