Prashanth Fertility launched ‘Prashanth Fertility at Home’, an initiative to provide select IVF-related support services at patients’ homes across Chennai.
The service is aimed at helping patients maintain continuity during fertility treatment, particularly those who may find it difficult to make frequent visits to the fertility centre because of work and other commitments.
Under the initiative, a dedicated team will provide services such as injection administration, eligible monitoring, follow-ups and treatment coordination at home, while patients continue to remain under the supervision of their treating fertility specialists.
A dedicated vehicle and team will operate across Chennai. Patients can schedule eligible services through the Prashanth Fertility app, which also allows them to manage appointments, follow-ups and treatment-related medical records.
Speaking at the launch, actor Khushbu Sundar, the chief guest, highlighted the stigma and emotional challenges associated with infertility and fertility treatment. She said couples often have to navigate not only the physical and financial demands of treatment, but also social expectations and questions around parenthood.
Samhitha Moturi, Director, Prashanth Group of Hospitals, said fertility treatment involves multiple appointments, medication schedules, monitoring and follow-ups, and repeated travel to a fertility centre can be an additional challenge for couples. “The initiative has been conceived to take appropriate, clinically supervised aspects of care closer to the patient,” she said, adding that reducing practical barriers could help patients stay on track with treatment.
Geetha Haripriya, Chairman, Prashanth Group of Hospitals, said the initiative was intended to make fertility care “more accessible, more personalised, and more connected to the patient”.
The service is currently available across Chennai. Patients can contact the 24x7 helpline 044-2888-2888 for details about eligibility and scheduling.

Why Nigeria's one-time political giant may face extinction
- Published
Once the undisputed giant of Nigerian politics, the Peoples Democratic Party now finds itself on the brink of extinction.
A question hanging over the campaign for January's general election, which officially kicked off this week, is whether the PDP can survive.
A factional struggle that has ended up in the courts over who exactly is in charge could end up rendering it irrelevant at the ballot box.
It is a remarkable fall for the party, founded in 1998, which appeared impregnable after the end of military rule a year later - so much so that its chairman boasted in 2008 that it would govern for six decades.
For 16 years, it controlled the presidency - in the shape of Olusegun Obasanjo, Umaru Musa Yar'Adua and then Goodluck Jonathan - and the vast majority of the country's 36 states.
But the 2015 federal election was a seismic shock.
The PDP lost the presidential vote to Muhammadu Buhari and the newly formed All Progressives Congress (APC) - a coalition of opposition parties and disgruntled former members.
Thrust into the political wilderness the party's national leaders were bewildered - familiar with the trappings of federal power they had to work out what to do in opposition.
This was the beginning of the end, according to political analyst Ishaq Buhari.
"They were a party that was so used to power, being in opposition was a new challenge they struggled with from the start," he told the BBC.
If 2015 was a major blow, 2025 was the year the party's foundations were left in ruins.
It was marked by a dizzying wave of defections and bitter internal conflicts.
A group of state governors switched party allegiance, which had a particularly devastating effect.
At the start of that year, the PDP still held eight states. But by December, five state governors - from Delta, Akwa Ibom, Enugu, Bayelsa and Rivers - had gone over to the ruling APC.
They cited the PDP's declining viability and a desire for better co-operation with the federal government as reasons for their departure.
Early this year, the PDP held three states but that is now down to zero - with the Oyo governorship slipping from the party's hands just last month.
Internal power struggles, factionalism, insistence that power rotates through the regions and disciplinary measures have all added to the sense of disillusionment within the party.
The PDP has been robbed of high-profile figures and talent, including the loss of former Vice-President Atiku Aubakar last year.
The crisis was intensified by a debilitating leadership tussle.
In November 2025, a faction of the party, which observers say represented the majority of members, held a contentious national convention in Ibadan, Oyo state, despite court orders attempting to stop it.
The convention expelled Nyesom Wike, a prominent PDP member who is serving in President Bola Tinubu's APC-led government.
Wike, who helped found the party, heads a rival faction creating a political stand-off that has paralysed the PDP.
He had controversially helped the APC win Rivers state in the last presidential election leading to accusations that he had betrayed the PDP.
But in the eyes of the law the faction that he heads is the legitimate party.
This means that it has been able to submit its slate of presidential and parliamentary candidates to the electoral commission leaving the rival faction without any representatives on the ballot.
Despite the chaos, some die-hard loyalists remain optimistic.
Politician and staunch PDP member Aminu Adamu, part of the anti-Wike faction, believes a return to its former glory is possible.
He cites examples from Thailand and Argentina, where parties have bounced back after years in the wilderness.
"We have seen it happen before," he tells the BBC. "All we need to do is put our house in order and start to build from there.
"If we make all the necessary corrections, by 2032 I really think PDP can be a major force again."
Others point out that the party still has a grassroots network - essential to win and sustain power - with offices, activists, supporters and local leaders. But by 2032 it may be too late.
With the party in such disarray and candidates backed by Wike on the ballot - voters are unlikely to trust them.
Analyst Deji Olarenwaju believes the only thing that could save the once-mighty party is an alliance with the African Democratic Congress - now seen as the biggest opposition group or Peter Obi's Nigeria Democratic Congress.
"Because on their own they are going nowhere," he says.

Every morning, many of us drink one or two cups of coffee and feel good, refreshed, and ready for the day. Some of us drink one or two more cups at work before lunchtime. Some use pure coffee while others add chicory to it. We prepare the powder using a filter, add milk and sugar, and take a swig.
While many Indians have a fondness for coffee, almost everyone in the U.S. and Europe drinks coffee, and more of it, every day.
Now, what are the effects of drinking coffee? How many cups per day? Should it be black coffee or can it include milk and sugar? And how does this affect our health? These are some questions that have been on our minds — and for which research has offered contradictory answers in the past. Fortunately, a new publication, titled ‘Caffeine and Cardiovascular Disease: A Scientific Statement from the American Heart Association’, may clear some doubts. The authors of the statement analysed several studies that examined the effects of caffeine, the active molecule in coffee that stimulates the brain and the central nervous system and encourages the body to produce and use more energy.
The statement reported that moderate caffeine intake, especially through coffee, may lower the risks of type-2 diabetes, stroke, heart failure, and atrial fibrillation. However, high doses, especially from energy drinks, may harm cardiovascular health, and unfiltered coffee can also raise LDL cholesterol levels.
Data from the Nurses Health Study at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and Harvard Medical School and an analysis of 3 lakh people from the U.K. Biobank and Health Canada have indicated that drinking four cups a day may lower the risk of developing cancer, type-2 diabetes, heart diseases, and age-related disorders like dementia and Alzheimer’s disease. However, analyses also suggest that it would be prudent for pregnant and lactating women to limit their coffee intake to three cups a day.
Drinking hot black coffee is recommended, with little or no additives like sugar or milk. However, a group from Copenhagen, Denmark, pointed out in the Journal of Agricultural and Food Science in 2023 that adding milk to black coffee can be good as milk contains antioxidants, minerals, and vitamins and allays the bitter taste.
Chicory-blended coffee
Many people in South India prefer to have pure coffee, i.e. with no additives like chicory, which comes from a perennial herbal plant with coloured flowers. This herb contains no caffeine but a polysaccharide called inulin, which supports digestion and can help control blood sugar.
The benefits of a coffee and chicory blend and their implications for nutrition and health implications were discussed in a recent review paper by a group led by Pushpa S. Murthy at the Central Food Technology and Research Institute, Mysuru, published in the Journal of Food Science and Technology. Chicory contains several compounds that help protect the liver from inflammation, shield the stomach from damage, and may help defend against cancer. Adding chicory to coffee also improves coffee’s fragrance and taste.
The optimal blend of coffee and chicory was suggested to be 70:30 or 60:40, coffee to chicory, to strike a balance between taste and benefits. In fact, most coffee sellers across India have these ratios, unless of course a customer asks for ‘pure’ coffee. This writer himself used to prefer pure coffee until he read the review article by the Mysuru group!

World's youngest reigning traditional monarch dies aged 34
- Published
A traditional Ugandan ruler named as the world's youngest monarch has died aged 34, his prime minster announced.
Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV became king of Tooro in western Uganda at just three years old in 1995 after the death of his father.
The Tooro kingdom did not disclose the cause of King Oyo's death, but a Ugandan government minister was quoted in local media saying that he had been critically ill and was seeking treatment in the US.
Though Uganda is governed by an elected president and parliament, it has several traditional kingdoms which continue to have significant cultural influence despite not having political power.
Oyo, who Guinness World Records listed as the world's youngest reigning monarch, external, ruled over more than two million people. He was the 13th monarch of a kingdom that was founded in the early 19th Century.
Announcing his death, Tooro's Prime Minister Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki called his passing on Thursday an "immeasurable loss" to the royal family and the people of Tooro.
"I call upon all the people of Tooro to remain united, calm and prayerful during this profoundly difficult time," Akiiki said on Friday. "May His Majesty the King rest in eternal peace."
The Tooro Kingdom follows a hereditary system in selecting its monarch.
Oyo was not officially married, but Akiiki said "the continuity of the Crown is assured".
"His Majesty leaves behind a Prince as his heir, whose identity will be formally revealed at the appropriate time, in accordance with the traditions and customs of Tooro Kingdom," he explained.
When he became king in 1995 a regency, which included the queen mother, was established until Oyo turned 18 when there was an official coronation.
The young king was well respected by his people and according to a report in the Daily Monitor newspaper he promoted causes such as youth empowerment, education and climate conservation, as well as HIV/Aids awareness.
The country's largest and most influential traditional institution, the Buganda Kingdom, said it mourned with the people of Tooro following the death of their monarch, labelling him a valuable figure to Uganda.
Similarly, the Rwenzururu Kingdom also extended its condolences to "all those mourning this great loss", according to local media reports.
Others have also paid their respects to the late king.
The Federation of Uganda Football Associations, honoured King Oyo as a "true friend of the beautiful game", and announced a moment of silence before the kick-off of all matches until 4 September in memory of his "legacy, love, passion and contribution" to the sport.
Government minister Margaret Muhanga described the mood in the kingdom as "sombre... you can't see anyone smiling".
The king was "at the prime of his life", she said in a video shared on social media, "as young as he was, he had an impact on his kingdom".
Muhanga said they would be planting a million trees in his honour during the mourning period, and wants to ask the neighbouring districts in Tooro to do the same.
Uganadan musician Juliana Kanyomozi called it a "very dark day for Tooro", in an Instagram post. "Gone too soon. What a loss!!!!"
Meanwhile, pop star-turned-politician Bobi Wine, called for King Oyo's "soul to rest in eternal peace".

The Federal Trade Commission and 22 states sued Amazon yesterday, alleging that it has conducted a secret scheme to overcharge advertisers for seven years.
“Since 2019, Amazon.com, Inc. has secretly and systematically overcharged its approximately 1.2 million advertising customers by manipulating the ‘auctions’ that it uses to set the price of ads on its platform,” the lawsuit said. “Amazon represents, and advertisers believe, that competitive auctions set the prices for advertising on its leading e-commerce website. But, in reality, Amazon overrides and replaces the actual auction results with higher prices set by Amazon to increase its profits.”
The FTC said it obtained internal documents and messages that reveal how Amazon secretly inflated auction prices for Sponsored Products, Sponsored Brands, and Sponsored Display advertisements that appear alongside results seen by consumers when they search for a product. The FTC investigation began in 2024.
“Based on numerous internal documents describing its ‘hidden’ ‘surcharges,’ Amazon’s scheme has likely illegally extracted over $20 billion from its unwitting advertising customers,” according to the lawsuit filed in US District Court for the Western District of Washington.
The FTC lawsuit was joined by a bipartisan group of 22 state attorneys general from Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Nebraska, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, Vermont, and Washington.
The lawsuit said Amazon has conducted “billions of rigged auctions,” imposing “hidden surcharges on advertisers almost every time a shopper clicks on an advertisement on the Amazon website. Amazon’s deception continues to this day” and deprives customers “of the benefits of competition and fair and transparent dealing,” the FTC said.

రక్షా బంధన్ సందర్భంగా కాంగ్రెస్ నేత రాహుల్ గాంధీకి ఆయన సోదరి ప్రియాంక గాంధీ మణికట్టు వద్ద కాకుండా భుజం దగ్గర రాఖీ కట్టారంటూ ఒక వీడియో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. దీంట్లో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: రక్షా బంధన్ సందర్భంగా రాహుల్ గాంధీకి ఆయన సోదరి ప్రియాంక గాంధీ భుజం దగ్గర రాఖీ కడుతున్నప్పటి వీడియో.
ఫాక్ట్: వైరల్ వీడియోలో ఉన్నది రాఖీ కాదు. ఇది 22 జూలై 2026న ఢిల్లీలో జరిగిన ఒక ప్రెస్ మీట్కు సంబంధించిన పాత వీడియో. CJP ర్యాలీలో నిరసనకారులపై జరిగిన దాడిని ఖండిస్తూ, వారికి సంఘీభావంగా నిరసన తెలిపేందుకు ప్రియాంక గాంధీ తన సోదరుడు రాహుల్ గాంధీ భుజానికి నల్ల పట్టీ కట్టారు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పు.
ముందుగా వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఇదే వీడియో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) కనీసం 22 జూలై 2026 నుంచే ఇంటర్నెట్లో అందుబాటులో ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. ఈ వీడియోలో ప్రియాంక గాంధీ, రాహుల్ గాంధీ భుజానికి నల్ల పట్టీ కట్టడం చూడవచ్చు. ఈ వీడియోని వివిధ మీడియా సంస్థలు (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) కూడా ప్రసారం చేశాయి.
మీడియా కథనాల (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) ప్రకారం, 22 జూలై 2026న ఢిల్లీలో రాహుల్ గాంధీ ప్రెస్ మీట్కు ముందు ప్రియాంక గాంధీ ఆయనకు నల్ల పట్టీ కట్టారు. 21 జూలై 2026న ఢిల్లీలో జరిగిన CJP నిరసనలో విద్యార్థులపై జరిగిన దాడిని ఖండిస్తూ, వారికి సంఘీభావంగా ఆయన నల్ల పట్టీ కట్టుకున్నారు. దీన్ని బట్టి, ఈ వైరల్ వీడియో 28 ఆగస్టు 2026 నాటి రక్షా బంధన్కు సంబంధించినది కాదని స్పష్టమవుతోంది. అలాగే, రాహుల్ గాంధీ, ప్రియాంక గాంధీ సోషల్ మీడియా వేదికగా రక్షా బంధన్ శుభాకాంక్షలు తెలిపారు.
చివరిగా, రాహుల్ గాంధీ భుజంపై ప్రియాంక గాంధీ రాఖీ కట్టారంటూ వైరల్ అవుతున్న వీడియో రక్షా బంధన్కు సంబంధించినది కాదు.

Ireland is becoming a global leader in the field of innovation in harnessing digital technologies as a tool to address various barriers for access to care. In alignment with WHO, Ireland recognizes the importance of mobilizing assistive technology to help the 2.5 billion people in need globally, including older persons, people with disabilities, and those living with health conditions. This includes ensuring equitable access to assistive products such as glasses, hearing aids, walking aids, wheelchairs, prosthetics, and communication and memory devices.
In March 2024, Anne Rabbitte, T.D., Ireland’s Minister of State with special responsibility for disabilities at the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth, agreed to a €12.5 million donor agreement between the Government of Ireland and WHO, aimed at accelerating affordability and availability of assistive technology for those in need.
The cooperation has been building throughout the years. Back in 2022, Taoiseach Micheál Martin, TD, launched the Global report on assistive technology, along with the Director-General of WHO and the Executive Director of UNICEF. The Taoiseach highlighted the importance of international cooperation to ensure more equitable access to assistive technology, in order to achieve a society where everyone is included and enabled to live their best life.
Minister Rabbitte stated that: “Ireland has identified the serious need to invest in public health systems alongside the WHO. The present risk of rising health needs coupled with a decreasing pool of health and social care professionals globally reveals an urgent need for all of us to act now. Ireland’s contribution aligns with the recommendations of the Global Report on Assistive Technology and supports a five-year initiative towards achieving national health system models that include assistive technology. The programme will explore and demonstrate how digital technology can facilitate people-centred services, assistive technology policy, improve the affordability and appropriateness of assistive products, enable effective provision systems, and boost the capacity of health personnel to identify, screen, refer and provide assistive technology for all those in need.”
Health personnel in Tanzania participating in on-line training on assistive products, as part of an overall program aimed at provision of simple assistive products through community and primary health care facilities - making products such as walking aids and reading glasses more readily available for people within their local area. Digital technology was instrumental in facilitating efficient learning through the platform, and enabling support for health workers from their mentors through communication apps after the training. Credit: WHO/Kylie Shae
With an ageing global population and a rise in noncommunicable diseases, an estimated 3.5 billion people will need assistive technology by 2050. Dr Yukiko Nakatani, WHO Assistant Director-General, Access to Medicines and Health Products, welcomes this important contribution from Ireland and their leadership in the digital initiative. She said: “The 2018 World Health Assembly resolution on assistive technology calls upon WHO to take the necessary steps to promote equitable access to assistive technology in our endeavour to build a more inclusive world. Our partnership with the Government of Ireland will support WHO in achieving our mission to ensure health for all, everywhere, with assistive technologies as an important enabler of well-being, inclusion, and participation.”
Through Ireland’s contribution, and in collaboration with its broad network of partners, WHO will develop evidence-based guidance for Member States on strengthening access to assistive technology through understanding, prioritising and stimulating increased innovation and use of digital solutions. The work will also involve national, regional, and global projects that test digital solutions designed to address persistent access barriers such as: digital platforms that empower users with information about assistive technology and how to access it; digital tracking of products to manage supply; and online training and support for health workers. The results and lessons learned will help countries expand their knowledge, skills, and capacities in the provision of assistive technology as an integral component of Universal Health Care.
‘Leaving no one behind’ means ensuring that people with disabilities, the older population, those affected by chronic diseases and everyone who needs assistive technology are included in society and able to live healthy and dignified lives.
* * * *
Click below to find out what is assistive technology, who needs it, and how it improves lives
Assistive technology is an umbrella term for external products used by individuals to help maintain or improve their bodily functions. Common examples are wheelchairs, glasses, prosthetic limbs, white canes, and hearing aids as well as digital solutions such as speech recognition or time management software. Assistive technology helps people in all aspects of their lives, including in education, employment, fitness, leisure and other everyday activities such as self-care, cooking and reading.
Most people will need assistive technology at some point in their lives, especially as they age. While some may require assistive technology temporarily, such as after an accident or illness, others may require it for a longer period or throughout their lifespan. It is commonly needed by older people, children and adults with disabilities, people who have been injured or who have a health condition such as diabetes, stroke and dementia.
Equitable access is key
Improving access to assistive technology enables the inclusion and participation of users in their family, community and all areas of society, including the political, economic and social spheres. Assistive technology positively impacts a person, their family and friends, and has broader socioeconomic benefits. For example:
- early provision of hearing aids for young children supports their development of language and communication skills, limiting negative impacts on their education, future employment and community participation;
- provision of appropriate wheelchairs facilitates mobility, improving individuals’ access to education and employment while reducing healthcare costs due to a reduction in secondary complications such as pressure sores and contractures;
- therapeutic footwear for diabetes reduces the incidence of foot ulcers, preventing amputations and the associated impact on individuals and burden on health-care systems; and
- timely provision of assistive technology for older people can improve their independence and safety as well as enable them to live at home for as long as possible.

For many years now, activists in India have been fighting an uphill battle: getting healthy foods on the plates of people, both adults and children. What are they up against? A steady stream of ultraprocessed food, food that is high in fat, sugar and sodium, labels that either do not warn consumers or do so in text that is not displayed prominently, misleading claims about the ‘health’ benefits of certain food, unfettered advertisements, and worst of all, food sold in India that is unhealthier compared to the same items sold abroad.
What is at stake? The metabolic health of millions of Indians. We know that bad diets can contribute to obesity, which in turn can contribute to hypertension, diabetes and a host of other issues. This week, we look at developments in the diet and health sector, spurred by the Supreme Court’s criticism of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), the country’s food regulator, and what has followed.
Battle against Big Food
The FSSAI, long lambasted for allowing big food brands to get away with misleading advertisements, and for taking no action on warning labels on unhealthy foods, has now submitted a proposal in the Supreme Court for a front-of-pack pictorial warning label for food products high in any two or more “nutrients of concern”, reports Krishnadas Rajagopal. And while this a definite step forward, Bindu Shajan Perappadan interviews an activist who points out that the ‘two or more’ condition still leaves critical gaps in the framework.
In recent weeks, the FSSAI has also begun a crackdown on claims: it has issued more than 150 notices to food companies over misleading advertisements, false claims and labelling violations. Nestlé India, PepsiCo, Coca-Cola India, Abbott India, Red Bull India, Danone India, Monster Energy India, Ferrero India and Kenvue are among companies named by the regulator. Bournvita maker Mondelez India Foods has now withdrawn health and nutrient-comparison claims, along with related advertisements from e-commerce platforms.
Is Big Food taking this lying down? Not if you go by this Reuters report. Not only are they fighting against warning labels, they are selling products in India that are far more unhealthy than products sold elsewhere. Rishita Khanna discusses this in a podcast. Do give it a listen.
And finally, dive into Dr. C. Aravinda and Dr. T.B. Pritish Basakaran’s story on FSSAI looking into liquor labels as well.
Developments in cancer
Cancer is never quite out of the news is it? There’s good news and news that requires some reflection this week. In the good news, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved a groundbreaking new drug for advanced pancreatic cancer. The daily pills will be sold by Revolution Medicines under the brand name Rasonque. Also, following on last week’s news of an mRNA tumour vaccine that showed promising results in a melanoma trial, Dr. Harish P. delves into how tumour vaccines work, and if they could herald a revolution in cancer treatment.
In other news, R. Sujatha, examines a new study on childhood cancer in India and speaks to experts about why, when many cancers in children have high cure rates, children in India still face barriers in accessing and adhering to treatment.
For a quick explainer of what Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia or CLL is, do read Shrabana Chatterjee’s piece.
The Meta settlement
On August 26, social media giant, Meta, reached a settlement of up to $17.1 billion with at least 47 U.S. States, with certain conditions on how Meta should change its safety features on Instagram and Facebook. The lawsuit alleged that Meta regularly collected data on children under the age of 13 without parental consent, and that the company deliberately designed platforms to be addictive. Joan Sony Cherian writes a detailed explainer on the suit and the settlement, while Sahana Venugopal explains the new safety features to be rolled out, and asks the crucial question of how effectively they can be enforced. We’ll have to wait and watch to see how this pans out.
Mental health concerns
Students have been at the forefront of the news in India for weeks now. After decades of being told what to do and when to do it, students have now said enough: they want their concerns prioritised, and rightly so. India’s injury concerns have followed the team into the new season, with Jasprit Bumrah, Nitish Kumar Reddy, Harshit Rana and Washington Sundar named in the squad for the three-match T20I series against Afghanistan later this month, subject to fitness clearance from the BCCI’s Centre of Excellence (CoE) in Bengaluru.
The quartet’s inclusion comes after a frustrating run of injuries that disrupted India’s plans during their recent assignments. By the conclusion of the three-match One-Day International series in England in late July, the problem had snowballed to the point that even captain Shubman Gill could not hold back his frustration.
Bumrah and Washington suffered injuries during the series and were ruled out of the third ODI. Harshit and Varun Chakaravarthy had already been sidelined by hamstring problems during the preceding T20I series, while Nitish was still in rehabilitation following a quadriceps injury sustained midway through the home series against Afghanistan in June.
The most frustrating case, however, was that of Hardik Pandya. At the BCCI’s Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru recovering from back spasms suffered during the Indian Premier League, the all-rounder was ruled out of the Afghanistan games after the board revealed he had suffered a low-grade quadriceps sprain.
All six players had been expected to play against England, a tour viewed as an important part of India’s preparations for the 2027 ODI World Cup.
“If you keep the World Cup as the goal where we have to play 11 matches in a row, and here we have players not being able to finish a two-to-three-match series. There is some limitation where our players are not able to play continuously; they play one or two matches, they suffer a niggle, and then we are forced to play a different combination which we originally did not plan to play.
“So keeping all this in mind, it becomes a little difficult when you come to the ground on the morning [of the game], and you come to know a player has a niggle, then it’s almost like, do you want to take a chance? Some player is 80 per cent fit, you are playing with five bowlers and if this player comes out after bowling five overs, then who will bowl? This is difficult. So, as a group we need improved fitness and all those things,” Gill said after the third ODI at Lord’s.
There are more names on the list. Upcoming pacers Prince Yadav, Yudhvir Singh and Ashok Sharma, Test regular Akash Deep, and spinner Suyash Sharma have all needed interventions in Bengaluru in 2026 alone.
Naturally, the scopes have been aimed at the CoE for accountability. That the facility has had no head of sports science since Nitin Patel left 18 months ago does not help its case. It needed assurance from CoE head V.V.S. Laxman to allay concerns over the set-up’s functioning.
“The CoE is not merely a rehab centre. There are bigger roles to play for it in helping cricketers achieve excellence,” he said at a press conference in Bengaluru.
Indian players struggling with fitness is not a recent trend. Bumrah, the team’s undisputed pace phenom, has been a regular at the BCCI facility, especially since his back injury during the Border-Gavaskar Trophy in early 2025. Riyan Parag (shoulder) underwent his rehab at the CoE. Mohammed Shami’s return after knee surgery following the 2023 World Cup was handled at the CoE’s predecessor, the National Cricket Academy, also in Bengaluru.
But the recent troubles, especially with players like Pandya and Reddy getting reinjured, have put question marks over injury management in Indian cricket.
Why is workload so important?
Andrew Leipus, who has twice served as India’s head physiotherapist and was a candidate to replace Nitin, however, reasons that the present injury rut is merely a by-product of a rigorous cricket calendar and external factors that may lead to a player’s absence.
“I don’t think there’s a crisis. All teams go through periodic increases in injury prevalence. When things are going well, sports science or injury science all flies under the radar. It’s only when you start to lose that greater attention is paid to what’s going on,” Leipus tells Sportstar.
India is not alone in suffering from injuries. Take any major Test-playing nation with a rigorous calendar, and you’ll find names of players who have missed significant action. Australia, for example, was without its captain Pat Cummins and Josh Hazlewood for its blockbuster home Ashes earlier this year. England, too, has been marred by injury woes to its pacers Jofra Archer and Mark Wood.
“It is unpleasant when we get injuries occurring, and they do affect the performance. That’s not ideal. [But] you are looking at the definition of an injury as something that restricts a player from participating. Unfortunately, illness, fractures, those sort of things are categorised under one umbrella term of fitness. We, as medical professionals, see it as soft tissue injuries, which are perhaps more preventable through training, rehab and prehab protocols, whereas illness and the rest is just the nature of the beast.”
There are indeed cases where players were forced out due to either a bone injury or an illness. Rishabh Pant fractured his right foot during the Test series in England. Then, Abhishek Sharma was ruled out for one game during the T20 World Cup due to an illness.
In late 2025, Shreyas Iyer was ruled out for a lengthy stretch due to a rib injury while fielding during the Australia tour.
However, the muscle or tissue injuries in the Indian camp are hard to ignore, especially among the pace bowlers.
The quicks are the most common visitors at the CoE, and they invariably bear the worst of this short turnaround cycle in international cricket. None presents this better than Bumrah, who has been rested for several games across formats to manage his workload, another term used frequently in Indian cricket. Even Mohammed Siraj was rested for the tours to Ireland and England to manage his workload after a strenuous two months of IPL and a Test match against Afghanistan in the sapping heat of June.
“The load on bowlers’ bodies is much higher than the others. The ground reaction forces, the number of repetitions, the asymmetrical nature of what they are doing on the load — it’s a build-up of all those things. Most of the guys at the international levels are cemented into their actions; their bodies are hardened to the forces and stresses. So it is not the action as much as the workload.
“When you stress the body, there is some sort of a micro breakdown of the tissue. The body will repair itself, but that is if you give it enough time. But if you hit it again and again without proper time to recover from that load, then it is going to be a net breakdown of the tissue,” Leipus says.
But what exactly is workload and how do physios decide the ideal workload?
From a cricketing point of view, it is divided into two broad categories: chronic and acute, Leipus explains. Chronic workload is an indication of a player’s fitness level, while acute workload focuses on a player’s fatigue levels. To break it down further, the last four weeks of training are a player’s fitness levels, while the last week of training is fatigue level.
“If their fatigue level is higher than the baseline fitness levels, then there’s a high chance of injury. Suppose someone does not bowl a lot for a month and then suddenly goes to a camp and starts to bowl every day. There’s a sudden jump in their acute workload, and there’s a sudden jump in their fatigue, so the risk of injury goes up. The holy grail is to find that balance,” Leipus says.
It is precisely why national team set-ups obsess over workloads. For instance, Indian players’ workload, which includes their training, is recorded. Even their stints with their respective IPL franchises and State franchises are relayed back to the headquarters.
Straying away from the basics?
While Leipus stresses the need for workload management, there is another school of thought that points to a different underlying reason for recurring injuries in players, specifically bowlers.
Strength & Conditioning (S&C) work has trickled into every cricketer’s routine worldwide. It is the direct derivative of high performance. The CoE itself, besides its sprawling cricket grounds and net facilities, also boasts a state-of-the-art gym. Most international teams have a specialised S&C coach to make players stronger and fitter.
However, critics argue this is an approach borrowed from other sports and misinterpreted for cricket, which demands starkly varied physical exertion.
“There’s too much conditioning work going on in cricket that looks like doing fitness, but it does not translate to bowling fitness because it is a different energy system than what is needed. What bowlers need are multiple spells, three spells a day of three to four overs each with maximum intensity,” a bowling coach, who has trained multiple Indian pacers, tells Sportstar on the condition of anonymity.
India pacer Navdeep Saini echoed the point during an interview on the sidelines of the ongoing Delhi Premier League.
“If you want to stay fit, it is important to bowl for long. Nowadays, during normal training, you find bowlers training to bowl just four overs. That won’t help. If you have the ability to bowl just four overs in your body, then if you go to play a Test match, how will you bowl 10-15 overs in one day? So, I think the biggest concern among fast bowlers is that they bowl less and train a little more, like doing gym or running,” Saini said in a select media interaction.
This misinterpretation leads to mispreparation.
Adrian Le Roux, India’s current head of S&C, introduced the Bronco Test as a fitness standard for selection.
This test involves shuttle running over distances of 20, 40, and 60 metres. One run includes shuttling all three distances, which covers 240 metres. A player has to do them five times, totalling 1,200 metres, inside a set limit of around eight minutes to clear this test. The previous standard, the Yoyo Test, also involved shuttle running but was slightly different.
“These are both field tests for establishing basic aerobic conditioning. The Yoyo needs an audio player and has a break/recovery between efforts. It’s actually good for mimicking the demands of cricket to some extent. Bronco is continuous effort, change of direction multiple times and is timed. Both are a measure of slightly different parameters and aerobic capacities,” Leipus says.
But critics argue that the Bronco Test hardly checks for the kind of fitness needed in cricket and leaves players prone to injuries.
“The 2k time trial and the Bronco Test do not measure how fit the bowler or player is. It measures the general conditional fitness. It is a test taken from other sports (rugby). The stride pattern, the ground contact time and the speed (metres per second) for these tests are a lot lower, about four metres per second. They train for this level when, in cricket, they are required to only run at seven metres per second. The S&C, rightfully or wrongfully, is judged on whether the cricketers are clearing these tests. So it is misguided. That is why I feel there is a spike in injuries. Bowlers need to bowl and train with specificity. They need to bowl intensely and often. Skill requires frequency of practice,” the bowling coach says.
But this is just one branch of thinking. That the application of sports science to elevate player performance has permeated through global cricket itself hints at its feasibility.
Shanker Basu, former India S&C head, who held his post through one of India’s golden eras in Test cricket, opines that only a proper scientific approach can allow a player to survive all three formats.
“Today’s cricketers are extremely professional. If you give them a roadmap, they follow it to the T. I don’t think that is the case; maybe some people want to believe [that S&C is not ideal in cricket], but by and large the professionalism in cricket has only improved. We have professionals now who are guiding the cricketers.
“To play all three formats takes a toll on the player; you need a different kind of preparation. You need to account for so many factors that if you do not adhere to the plans, and are not scientific enough, you will get the raw end of the deal. It all depends on what you want out of the athlete.”
Time heals everything
But beyond workload and conditioning a player for the rigours of international cricket, the prevention of injuries depends on the most obvious factor: fixing the injury properly!
Leipus broadens it out into two aspects: fit to play and fit to perform. “You can get somebody fit to play; that could be you or me.”
But an international cricketer aspires to be fit to perform – where they are physically and mentally ready, and skill-prepared for performance in an actual match scenario. The biggest risk of reinjury is rushing the rehab and not meeting the functional parameters of fitness, he says.
“There’s always pressure. That’s what the coaches ask first: ‘How long is this injury going to take?’ But we try to get an objective measure; that’s where the MRIs and X-rays give us an idea of what is happening at the tissue level. Then we look at the context, the timeframe, whether there are any other psychological factors - the pressure on the player, is he in form or not.
“The ideal process of getting someone back is having no time pressure at all. Unfortunately, we live in a world where the guys are expected to play; that’s their job, and we are there to expedite that process. We understand the damage to the body or the perceived damage, then we look at the general return timeline for that type of injury, we look at the schedule and then work backwards from there whether the rehab to that kind of injury is going to be feasible or not. In an ideal world, we wish we had time and that we could meet the physiological milestone as the injury heals and we can build the load back up,” Leipus says.
Saini also emphasises the time factor in injury rehab. The 33-year-old has trained at the NCA and the CoE after multiple injuries, the most threatening being after the iconic Gabba Test in 2021, where he bowled a spell through a hamstring strain.
“When you go back after an injury, it’s not like you are bowling 140 or at the same level as before the injury. The first day after injury, you start from zero. And you have to push yourself so much to go back to your peak level. At that time, only your physio or trainer has the most important role. Because as a player, there is little doubt. You also fear getting injured again. So, at that time, only the trainer knows how to prepare the player,” Saini adds.
Given India’s busy schedule and the grand expectations of success placed on those who run the affairs, it is not hard to fathom that at some point, some player must have been rushed back into the team. Recently, news reports claimed that pacer Harshit was brought back before the completion of the stipulated recovery time.
Elsewhere, though, Australia’s decision not to field Cummins in four of the five 2025-26 Ashes Tests sets the right example here — keeping the player’s welfare before the team’s need, even for arguably the most-billed event in Australian sport.
Finding the right mix
Yet, the decision around the players’ workload and return falls on the players themselves too.
Saini adds that working towards one’s fitness does not stop outside the field. At a time when State T20 leagues have practically eaten into the off-season in Indian cricket, recovery during acute workload should be the priority for any player.
Take Saini, for example. After the domestic season with Delhi, he joined Kolkata Knight Riders for the IPL, then went to England for County cricket and finally came back to play in the DPL. Once the T20 tournament is done with, preparations start for the domestic season.
“If you want to take the off-season, then you have time to recover. But it is the player’s choice. You don’t want to miss matches either. If you have a mindset to play, then your body works accordingly. For me, the same routine is still going on. But now there is more focus on recovery, diet and sleep. If you start doing this at the age of 20 or 22 years old, you will be even better because you have been preparing your body for 10-12 years. Take Mitchell Starc, for example. We have seen that he still plays almost all Tests. He has been playing cricket all year. I think he is 37 now [36]. If he can do so much, why can’t we?” Saini says.
Saini pointed to the impressive fitness standards of India’s dominant pace trio, Bumrah, Shami, and Ishant Sharma, which managed a consistent run under Virat Kohli’s tenure despite facing their respective share of injury woes.
Basu, who looked after their training, revealed that a flexible programme, one which is tailored to specific needs, helped in bringing the best out of Indian players.
“We did not have anything fancy; we just took it case by case. Each person was different. Bumrah was one type, Ishant Sharma was another, Bhuvi was one type. Every player functions differently from the inside. Our plans were customised. We had a culture where I could advise freely. If someone had to be rested from training, if someone had to be given a break from gym work, it was done with a combined mindset. We all had a discussion on a daily basis. The injury rehab process was also similarly simple. Patrick Farhart was also there; he was a great help. We used to take every case day by day,” Basu says.
In a set-up as well established as the CoE, it is hard to imagine a drop in standard. The recent spate of injuries has brought questions to the CoE’s door, but Leipus might be right in granting the facility a little more leeway. “It’s about the use of fitness as a term. It’s a very generic term; it encompasses so many different variables, and it’s easy to point the finger at poor fitness? A broken finger is not poor fitness. Getting hit on the toe is not poor fitness. Managing a chronic knee or a chronic back in an important player is not fitness; it’s just injury management,” he says.
In the past, the team management has erred by wanting certain players’ rehab expedited, with Harshit being a case in point. While it is fair to expect accountability from the CoE, given the sheer scale of investment, it cannot be solely held responsible. Yes, it is one cog in the set-up, but the team is run by the management and the selectors too. The CoE trains and fixes the players, but it’s the other two that often dictate the pace of their recovery.
There are things the CoE needs to set in order, finding a head of sports science being one of them. But this demands more calibration than a crisis intervention.

In Chile, injured penguins sport copper vests to help them heal
Researchers in Chile have designed special vests for penguins to help them recover during El Nino
SANTIAGO, Chile -- Researchers in Chile have designed an unlikely new garment for injured penguins — snug red vests threaded with copper and zinc that they hope will help the aquatic birds heal faster.
Veterinarians have found success in the past using such suits to treat injured dogs and cats. Now they're trying out the technology on Humboldt penguins in Chile, home to the largest concentration of the vulnerable species.
“For years, vests with microfibers containing elements like copper and zinc have been tested on pets, particularly dogs and cats, and have greatly helped in the recovery of skin wounds,” said Ignacio Idalsoaga, director of the Buin Zoo, a wildlife park on the outskirts of Chile’s capital, Santiago, where researchers took measurements of penguins to develop the first bodysuits.
“We began to wonder — why can't this be used on penguins?" he told The Associated Press from the zoo on Wednesday.
The experiment comes as Chile's Humboldt penguin population declines sharply. Chilean and international researchers surveying the country's major breeding colonies in 2024 and 2025 found a 63% drop in active nests compared to the same sites three years earlier. The birds face mounting threats, including entanglement in fishing nets, plastic pollution, disease outbreaks and competition with fisheries for food.
Now Humboldt penguins also find themselves in the cross hairs of one of the world’s most disruptive weather patterns, El Nino, which brings unusually warm waters to parts of the Pacific Ocean, making the cold-water fish that they rely on harder to find. Hunger forces penguin parents to travel farther afield for food and leave their nests behind.
“Especially now, with all the problems caused by El Nino, we’re likely to see many abandoned chicks in the coming weeks, with injuries they suffer in the environment,” Idalsoaga said.
Wildlife clinics across Chile receive distressed penguins stranded along Chile's coast, some cut by fishing nets or boat propellers, others weakened by a lack of food, said Tomás Pino, a veterinarian who runs Conservación Humboldt, a nonprofit that rehabilitates injured marine animals in the country's north.
Treating those injuries can be tricky. Penguins often twist their long necks to peck at gashes and pull out their own stitches, Pino said. The vests prevent them from doing that while putting copper — of which Chile is the world’s top producer — to work as a salve. Copper and zinc woven into the fabric inhibit the growth of bacteria and fungi. Zinc also stimulates the formation of new blood vessels, helping damaged tissue heal faster.
“We’ve seen that the penguins tolerate it quite well,” Pino said. “We noticed that from one day to the next, the wounds were in better condition with the vest."

Summer off England duty took me by surprise - Itoje
- Published
England captain Maro Itoje says he was initially shocked when head coach Steve Borthwick raised the possibility of him taking the summer off.
Itoje missed England's matches against South Africa, Fiji and Argentina in July, holidaying in Mauritius and Nigeria as he took a first proper summer break from professional rugby in more than a decade.
The 31-year-old, whose mother died in the weeks before he led England through a deflating Six Nations campaign that featured just one win, says he is now feeling the benefits of his time away.
"I spoke to Steve Borthwick two weeks after the Six Nations and at the end of a long conversation he mentioned we would have to think about what to do in the summer," Itoje told Rugby Union Weekly.
"I was taken aback a bit - it wasn't something that was in my mind.
"At the end of the season it is just the done thing to go on tour.
"But once I had digested it and had thought about it, the more I thought about it, the more I thought it was the best thing for me.
"I'm not annoyed by it at all. It was a wise and prudent decision, it has given me the best opportunity to perform well over the next period of time."
Itoje made his England debut in 2016 and has won 102 caps, as well as touring three times with the British and Irish Lions.
He played more than 30 matches in each of the 2023-24 and 2024-25 campaigns, breaching the recommended limit of 2,400 match minutes in the former and narrowly avoiding doing so in the latter.
"I would argue that the mental recovery was far more significant than physically," he said.
"I feel like I'm in a good physical condition, but mentally it was a heavy, busy year, both personally and professionally. So, it was nice to have just a bit of time to take a breath."
Itoje bumped into the England squad at Heathrow Airport as their return from a defeat by the Springboks in Johannesburg coincided with his own from Nigeria.
"I was on the shuttle train back to baggage reclaim and looked to my right and there was [Saracens and England team-mate] Jamie George, I looked to my left and there was Steve Borthwick, and they both looked at me in disbelief," he added.
Apart from that coincidence, Itoje kept his distance from the England set-up over the summer, sending the squad the odd good luck message, but opting against watching their games live.
"It was difficult to do, but when you're supposed to take a break, then if you're living and breathing every moment of a game..." he said.
"I watched them back in retrospect [knowing the final score], partly because I wanted to remove some of the emotion from watching it.
"That's the beauty of live sport - when you watch a game, you're in every nook and cranny, every tackle.
"But that also probably has a hidden emotional weight. The whole purpose of the rest was to get back on the even keel, so that was my methodology."
Itoje's rest precedes another busy period in his life.
Saracens' Prem season begins away to Leicester on 27 September before England take on Australia, Japan, New Zealand and a final's weekend play-off opponent in November's conclusion to the Nations Championship.
And the start of the Rugby World Cup in Australia is a little over a year away.
Meanwhile, his wife Mimi is expecting the couple's first child - a boy - imminently.
"I am very excited," Itoje added
"I want a minimum of three children, I don't really have a maximum.
"My cousin's grandfather must have 60 kids, but that isn't a route I am going down!"

The goat is now a celebrity - how this graduation gift went viral
- Published
When Promise Okoro walked out of his final degree exams earlier this month, he fully expected the usual end-of-term celebrations.
His cheering friends were already outside blasting music and snapping and filming this much-loved Nigerian "signing-out" ritual.
Their white shirts filled up with messages scribbled by classmates and well-wishers – a colourful record of a shared journey through education.
But then, through the crowd, came Promise's mother, Chinyere, pulling a goat.
It turned an already joyful afternoon into a moment Promise and his friends would not soon forget.
The 23-year-old pharmaceutical technology student initially thought the screams meant someone was about to propose marriage.
Instead, he found his friends gathered around his mother, who was making her way towards him, gently coaxing the farm animal behind her.
"I was so happy," he told BBC Pidgin. "I felt so emotional."
He says he was not embarrassed at all. Instead, his classmates cheered.
The moment was captured on video and quickly spread online, drawing thousands of warm reactions.
For some people outside south-east Nigeria, a goat might seem like an unusual gift to mark the end of university. But among the Igbo people, the animals can carry deep cultural meaning.
They are valuable gifts, often given to show respect, appreciation and goodwill and are associated with important occasions such as traditional weddings, family celebrations and ceremonies honouring elders or special guests.
Promise has not yet hit on a fitting name for his prized possession.
Some have questioned what the graduand now plans to do with the animal - but he tells the BBC it is very much his companion so he would never eat it.
"It's now my pet, it's too precious to me, I have no intention of killing it."
In fact, the plan is to get a female goat and start breeding the pair.
Until then, Promise's goat will continue enjoying special status at the student halls where he roams freely and even has some human-like habits.
"I have noticed it loves fried rice a lot! The way he eats up my fried rice leftovers - very voracious," laughs Promise.
Now something of a local hero, the goat accompanied Promise to a nearby supermarket where fans clambered to take photos of the animal.
"It got on a car ride with me from my hostel to the mall... it was calm [even though] it's now a celebrity - more popular than me.
"I also take it around my street for some evening walks".
Promise gained not just a new friend but also high praise from his mother Chinyere - this gift was her way of saying "I am proud of you" and she wanted everybody to know.
She had travelled, goat in tow, for more than an hour from Ubaha-Eze, the small farming community where the family lives, to surprise her son at the Federal Polytechnic Nekede in Imo state.
Chinyere had once dreamed of buying her son something very different – a shiny new vehicle.
"I did not have money for a 4matic Jeep - I love that car - so I said let me buy this little gift," she said.
The 4Matic is a Mercedes-Benz SUV – a car she said was beyond what she could afford.
Chinyere is a trader who sells consumer goods, including food, drinks and local snacks.
Business has been difficult but even with the financial pressures she was determined to keep her promise to her son.
When he got into university she had said he would be rewarded if he stayed away from violent gangs and other bad influences and not to drop out. Promise had done exactly that.
And now his mother wanted to stick to the pledge. She bought the goat for 120,000 naira ($88; £66).
"People love my son, I want[ed] to prove that he is [loved]," she said
"As I walked in and met loud celebrating and shouting, it gladdened my heart knowing that my son will rejoice together with us all when he comes out," she said.
For Promise, the relationship with his mother goes far beyond the celebrations.
"My mom is very cool," he said. "There is nothing I can hide from her and whenever she is confused about something, she always calls me to ask of my opinion or idea."
As a student of pharmaceutical technology Promise said he has always wanted to help sick people in Nigeria.
He knows that many health professionals have left the country in search of better opportunities abroad, while those who remain often work in difficult conditions.
But he wants to stay and contribute to improving Nigeria's strained health system.
Even as he waits for his final results, he believes he performed well. "If there is a list of the top 50, I will say that I am one of them."
Nigeria's tertiary education completion rate is 11.3 out of every 100 people. That is slightly higher than the average of 10.5 out of 100 across sub-Saharan Africa, but below the 17.6 out of 100 average for lower middle-income countries.
For Promise, completing his studies is therefore not simply another line on a certificate.
It is a milestone his mother has been waiting to celebrate. And now, he says, it is his turn.
"The way she has shocked me, I will make sure I reciprocate."
Whatever surprise Promise eventually finds for his mother, it may be difficult to match the one she gave him: a brown goat, brought from their village with love and determination – a simple gift that has united thousands of people who have watched the moment unfold online.

Brighton sign winger Azeez from Millwall
- Published
Brighton have signed Nigeria winger Femi Azeez from Millwall in a deal worth £12.5m - potentially rising past £15m with add-ons.
Azeez arrives at the Amex Stadium on a four-year contract and becomes Brighton's 11th signing of the summer window, including their club record £45m move for Tottenham centre-back Luka Vuskovic.
Azeez, 25, scored 11 goals and provided eight assists in 37 games last season, earning a place in the PFA Championship team of the year.

If you've been shopping for an Amazon Kindle or smart speaker in the past week, you might've noticed some brand-new prices. That’s right: Amazon has hiked prices by $20 to $100 on its popular devices like the Echo, Eero, and Fire Stick.
It's not alone in this move. We've seen similar increases from other tech companies like Apple and Kobo, both of which raised prices this summer. Amazon declined to comment to WIRED as to why it made these price hikes, but one Amazon spokesperson commented to CNET that it was due to rising prices in memory and storage components.
It's still hard not to feel like companies are raising prices simply because they can—and as a way to make upcoming Prime Day and Black Friday sales look better than they really are. The new prices spread across all of Amazon's hardware categories, hitting its Kindle e-readers, Echo smart speakers, Eero routers, and Fire TV devices—especially the more affordable and popular products in those categories.
In fact, many devices are already “on sale,” but the sale prices are around what used to be the base price. That means discounts will look good this holiday season, but you'll just be paying what the item used to cost a couple of months ago.
Here are all of the price changes on Amazon's devices, and my run-down on which devices remain a good buy.
New Kindle Prices
If you're looking for a Kindle, all of these models have faced a price increase of at least $30, if not more.
- Amazon Kindle (2024, 11th Gen): $150 (up $40)
- Amazon Kindle Paperwhite (2024, 12th Gen): $200 (up $40)
- Amazon Kindle Paperwhite Signature (2024, 12th Gen): $250 (up $50)
- Amazon Kindle Colorsoft: $290 (up $40)
- Amazon Kindle Colorsoft Signature: $320 (up $40)
- Amazon Kindle Kids (2024, 2nd Gen): $180 (up $50)
- Amazon Kindle Colorsoft Kids: $300 (up $30)
The only category untouched is, interestingly enough, the more powerful of Amazon's e-reader and digital notebook devices: the Kindle Scribe line. All of the Kindle Scribe models currently available (both the second and third gen, and the color version) have remained the same price-wise. You'd think those would have risen too since the price hikes are supposedly due to storage and memory costs, but it's Amazon's e-reader-only devices that all increased in price instead.
New Echo Prices
Many Amazon Echo speakers also raised in price, going up by anywhere from $10 to $100. The larger price increases are for the Echo Show devices, which come with a screen.
- Echo Dot (5th Gen): $80 (up $30)
- Echo Spot (2nd Gen): $110 (up $30)
- Echo Dot Max: $120 (up $20)
- Echo Show 5 (3rd Gen): $100 (up $10)
- Echo Show 8 (4th Gen): $200 (up $20)
- Echo Show 11: $250 (up $30)
- Echo Show 15: $350 (up $50)
- Echo Show 21: $500 (up $100)
Interestingly enough, Amazon already has many of these speakers “on sale” for around their old sticker price; the Echo Dot is a “deal” for $55 right now when it was $50 as recently as August 20, and the Echo Dot Max is “on sale” for $95 after costing $100 on August 20 as well. These current prices are likely Labor Day sales, and might be the same pricing we see come fall sale events, too.
But not all Echo devices went up in price. The fairly new second-gen Echo Studio still has the same $220 price tag it did when it launched, and is also on sale already for Labor Day (catch it for $195 right now). You'll also find the older Echo Show 8 that I like stuck to its $150 price point. And even if some did go up in price, some are having better deals than others—the Echo Show 11 is currently on sale for $190, a fine discount on its old price and a good one on its new $250 price tag.
New Eero Prices
Amazon owns the Eero mesh router system, and there was a price increase in that category as well. It only hit the Eero 7 and Eero Pro 7, but unfortunately, we think those are the best models.
- Amazon Eero 7: $400 (up $50)
- Amazon Eero 7 Pro: $800 (up $100)
You can still get the Eero 6 on a budget, since that one has stayed the same in price, but there are plenty of other mesh Wi-Fi routers we prefer over Eero if you don't want to deal with the price hike.
New Fire TV Prices
I wouldn't call Fire TV my favorite streaming setup (and neither would our reviewers), but if you're an Amazon Prime lover, maybe you feel differently. Amazon's Fire TV sticks had a couple of increases. While only a couple of products were affected, it did hit our favored models.
- Fire TV Stick 4K Max: $85 (up $25)
- Fire TV Stick HD: $40 (up $5)
Fire TV is still one of the cheapest systems around, but it wasn't the one we'd recommend before the increases, and I doubt you'll see it rank any higher with these new prices in mind. Still, the deals might be worth shopping; the Fire TV Stick HD is already on sale for Labor Day for just $18, while the 4K Max is on sale for less than its old sticker price (but only by $10).
What’s Still Worth It?
Not everything is still worth buying with these prices in mind. Here are the devices I'd still shop. For the rest, I'd wait for a sale event or look to another brand to get a similar product.

The Roomba Max 875 and the Plus 678 Combo introduce iRobot’s new technology that seals the machines to your carpet.
iRobot has launched two new Roombas at IFA 2026 in Berlin, including what it calls its "most powerful robot ever." They also serve as the launching ground for iRobot's new SealForce Vacuuming Technology, which works by lowering a skirt hidden inside the machines' chassis and forming a tight seal against the carpets fibers. That gives the robots a suction force of 35,000 Pascals, iRobot's highest yet, enough to pull embedded dirt and debris in carpets.
The Max 875 Combo also features the company's ultrasonic ThermaMist Technology that sprays heated mist continuously while it's mopping in order to soften dried stains and dirt. Its PowerSpin Max Roller Mop uses the heated water to scrub the floor with a roller speed of 300RPM and 18 Newtons of downward pressure. This model can automatically detect carpet, raise its mop and then lower a protective shield to keep the rug dry. Meanwhile, the Roomba Plus 678 Combo comes with Roomba's SprayForce AI pre-treatment that uses high-pressure spray to break down dirt before mopping it up.
Both models are now available on iRobot's website, with shipping slated to begin in two weeks. Later this month, you'll also be able to buy them from retail stores across North America.

4 Madhya Pradesh boys from a family die within 10 days after waterfall visit
Four boys from the same family in Madhya Pradesh's Shivpuri died within 10 days after falling ill following a visit to a waterfall, with fever, abdominal pain, vomiting and diarrhoea reported.
Four boys from a same family in Madhya Pradesh's Shivpuri family died within 10 days after several relatives fell ill following a visit to a waterfall. Three of the deceased were brothers, while the fourth was reportedly the son of a relative.
The family members had gone to a waterfall on August 16 to bathe. After they returned, several members of the family began falling ill. However, the health department has not yet attributed the deaths to the waterfall water.
The family of Tanveer Ahmed had gone to the waterfall along with relatives. Around 16 people from the family and their relatives had reportedly gone there to bathe. After they returned, an illness suddenly spread among the family, and the condition of four children deteriorated one after another.
According to the family members, the children suffered from fever, abdominal pain, vomiting and diarrhoea. Despite treatment, all four children died.
The condition of the 14-year-old deteriorated first, and he died despite treatment. Subsequently, 19-year-old Ayaz and other children in the family also fell ill. The four deaths, one after another, left the family in mourning.
The deaths of four children from the same family within a short period alerted the health department and district administration. A health department team reached the family and collected samples from the family members as well as people living nearby. Officials are also examining the treatment received by the deceased children and the reasons behind their illness.
Additional District Magistrate Dinesh Chand Shukla said samples had been collected from around 62 people who had gone to the waterfall. He said a medical team was investigating the deaths, which occurred after the children developed fever. He also said the family had been provided financial assistance.
Officials have also collected samples of the waterfall water. Shukla said that during the sampling process, officials learnt that three girls were also unwell. They were subsequently sent to Gwalior for treatment.
The exact cause of the illness and the deaths will be known after the sample and investigation reports are received.

Good morning. The art for the Trump administration’s new publication, “The Magic Tablet,” has a very uncanny valley feel. Read Isa’s report below and let me know what you think.
ADA rejects claims of censorship, police involvement
Nearly three months after members of the American Diabetes Association were ejected from the group’s scientific sessions in New Orleans for handing out an editorial criticizing federal funding cuts, an internal review has denied allegations of censorship and of involving local police in the incident. The review also dismissed suggestions that the organization acted in response to the substance of the editorial, STAT’s Elizabeth Cooney reports.
Steven Kahn, editor-in-chief of Diabetes Care and one of the five who were escorted out of the meeting, has questioned the independence of the review. The findings are being sent to the ADA board for action, Liz reports, but it appears unlikely to quell the controversy that has burned on since the incident. Read more from Liz on the details of the ADA’s denials and how those involved have reacted. Separately, ADA CEO Charles Henderson wrote a First Opinion essay on his perspective of the events.
Stopgap spending bill passes House
The House voted yesterday to pass a stopgap government-funding bill that temporarily blocks the White House’s proposal to give political appointees more control over federal research grants. The bill passed 370-48, and now goes to the president for his signature.
The bill funds the government until Dec. 11 to get past the midterm elections without a government shutdown, and the ban on the research-funding policy expires at the same time. Read more on the details from STAT’s John Wilkerson and Anil Oza.
HHS wants kids to touch grass
The Department of Health and Human Services put on an event yesterday morning to promote its anti-screen-time message — “Live Real Life” — and promote its new children’s book, “The Magic Tablet.” The story follows a child who wants to become a content creator but, without a tablet of her own, decides to draw one and play make-believe. She then convinces her parents to get off of their devices.
That captured much of the vibe of the four-hour gathering. Researchers and policy wonks argued about the quality of data showing that social media harms mental health but also urged parents to offer kids enjoyable IRL experiences instead of setting strict limits on devices. Executives from Meta and Snap Inc. talked about new parental controls the companies are rolling out. HRSA director Thomas Engels said his agency is developing its own app for parents to better manage kids’ screen time and “productivity,” without offering details. Other speakers said lawmakers need to force tech giants to “de-engineer” features that promote longer sessions.
“These things were put in. They can be taken out,” said Dimitri Christakis, editor-in-chief of JAMA Pediatrics and a pediatrics professor at the University of Washington School of Medicine.
The one young person in these discussions was 21-year-old Adnan Alkhalili, who co-founded a university-based group called Touch Grass Together, which encourages students to get off their phones and out into the world. — Isabella Cueto
How will the next DSM address the algorithm?
The last time there was a new edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, in 2013, TikTok didn’t exist. ChatGPT was still nearly a decade away. Now, clinicians and researchers are set to discuss the next edition of the DSM, expected in 2030. A new First Opinion essay argues that the manual should include social media algorithms as a modern environmental influence on mental health, and particularly on eating disorders.
“The way algorithms now shape how people think about food, their bodies, and themselves would have seemed like science fiction in 2013,” two leaders at the National Eating Disorders Association write. Read more on why they believe the DSM should encourage clinicians to assess algorithmic exposure when performing eating disorder evaluations.
An unexpected discovery on alpha-gal syndrome
NIH researchers looking for a malaria prevention strategy may have instead discovered a way to fight alpha-gal syndrome, according to a paper published yesterday in the Journal of Clinical Investigation. The syndrome, induced by tick bites, can cause dangerous allergic reactions to red meat.
Alpha-gal syndrome occurs when a tick bite triggers an immune reaction to a molecule called galactose-α-1,3-galactose (long for alpha-gal) that’s found in food products like beef, pork, dairy, and, separately, tick saliva. The molecule also exists on malaria parasites; the researchers had been trying to identify allergen-specific monoclonal antibodies to neutralize infection, but none could bind well to the parasite. When the team tried the same approach in laboratory tests for alpha-gal syndrome, 13 out of 40 antibodies could bind to allergens, two blocked IgE from the immune system from attaching to allergens, and one interfered with the activation of immune cells called basophils, which are involved in the body’s allergic reaction.
It’s complicated, incremental research. But given the rising number of alpha-gal cases, it’s research worth watching.

3 women charged with fighting in Hong Kong mall granted bail, banned from venue
Trio make first appearance in court after confrontation over their children’s quarrel in shopping centre play area devolved into brawl
A Hong Kong court has granted three women bail after they were charged with fighting in the children’s play area of a shopping centre and barred them from returning to the venue.
Leung Lai-ha, 68, her 34-year-old daughter Ng Ka-wun and Xu Yang, 34, made their first appearance at Kwun Tong Court on Thursday to face charges after their altercation on August 26 at the atrium of APM shopping centre in Kwun Tong.
