Trump says Apple Maps has now changed Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’ for him: ‘Complete, ratified and binding’
Google Maps has also renamed the body of water for U.S. users
President Trump is celebrating that major tech companies have updated their mapping apps in line with his move to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America as part of the administration’s ongoing trade war with Canada.
“Apple Maps has just announced that it has changed the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America, so now that very important change of names, between Google Maps and Apple Maps, is complete, ratified, and binding,” the president wrote on Truth Social on Wednesday.
The change, first displayed on Tuesday, is visible for U.S. users.
“I know that the president reached out to Apple directly,” Interior Secretary Doug Burgum told Fox News on Monday.
The Independent has contacted Apple for comment.
Google began showing American users the new name on Saturday, two days after the president’s executive order renaming the Great Lake in the U.S. Geographic Names Information System.
“These updates follow our long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country, and are starting to roll out now,” the company wrote in a blog post, noting that users outside the U.S. and Canada would see the lake listed as “Lake Ontario (Lake America).”
MapQuest, meanwhile, has said it’s not changing the name of Lake Ontario.
The mapping service, which began falling out of fashion with the rise of Google and Apple Maps, saw a surge in downloads amid the naming controversy.
Canada, for its part, has strongly condemned the Trump administration’s actions.
“The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America,” Prime Minister Mark Carney wrote on X last month. “We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always.”
On Saturday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled a large billboard on the Canadian side of the lake reading "Lake Ontario. Now and Always.”
The mapping dustup is part of a larger trade war between the U.S. and Canada, after negotiations between the historic allies broke down in mid-August.
The U.S. has imposed 50 percent tariffs on billions of dollars worth of Canadian goods, and Canadian retaliatory measures of up to 50 percent will kick in next week.
Other U.S. officials have joined the president in trolling the Canadians. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth mocked Canada's military online.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has threatened that Canada isn’t strong enough to go "tit for tat" with the larger U.S. economy.
President Trump, meanwhile, has shared an AI-generated video on Truth Social where he kicks over a “Welcome to Lake Ontario” sign and replaces it with one reading “Welcome to Lake America.”
Canada has called on the Trump administration to “stop doing memes” and get back to the bargaining table.
"When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade and stop trying to be tough, and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions," Carney said Tuesday. "It’s not constructive, but that’s their democracy."
The U.S. and Canada have a trading relationship valued at nearly $900 billion per year.

Tugboat sinks off South Korea's southern coast, leaving 1 dead and 6 missing
A tugboat capsized and sank off South Korea's southeastern coast, leaving one crew member dead and six others missing
SEOUL, South Korea -- A tugboat capsized and sank off South Korea's southeastern coast on Wednesday, leaving one crew member dead and six others missing, the coast guard said.
The 286-ton tugboat was carrying eight crew members when it departed Wednesday morning to tow a merchant vessel in the waters off South Korea's southeastern city of Busan, the coast guard said in a statement.
After the tugboat overturned, one crew member, an Indonesian, was rescued by the merchant vessel. Another of the crew, a South Korean, was discovered unconscious by coast guard rescuers before being sent to a hospital on the mainland and declared dead there, the coast guard said.
The coast guard and the navy sent vessels, aircraft and other assets to rescue the six remaining crew members who are still missing, according to the coast guard. President Lee Jae Myung ordered authorities to mobilize all available resources.
The coast guard said the tugboat eventually sank at around 3:30 p.m. (0630 GMT) about two hours after the capsizing was reported. The cause of the capsizing wasn't immediately known.

Smelling a potential victory in the midterms, House Democrats are starting to think about oversight investigations next year and how to wield the power of the purse to make the Trump administration comply. In short, Trump’s West Wing renovations and DC arch could be on the chopping block, sources tell Inner Loop.
The nature of any investigations, and where Democrats will try to wrestle back power from the executive, are still to be determined, in part because taking back the House majority is not a foregone conclusion.
But House Democrats have a slew of investigations planned if they do end up controlling the chamber come November. Congressional committee aides have already been exploring how to force recalcitrant officials and family in Trump’s orbit to answer subpoenas.
With Trump uniquely focused on personal vanity projects this term, among the ideas is to more aggressively wield the power of congressional appropriations and threaten funding for Trump’s construction projects.
If Trump tries to block an investigation or ignores Congress and renames more buildings, House Democrats might cut off funding for any of Trump’s future West Wing renovations or perhaps block money for Trump’s triumphal arch.
The top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, Jamie Raskin, also suggested this week that cutting off funding could be used to rein in projects Trump has already started.
“We have the power of the purse, and we will make sure Donald Trump doesn’t destroy any other federal buildings or landmarks,” Raskin told reporters when asked what recourse Democrats have after a sharply divided Supreme Court permitted Trump to keep building his ballroom.
“Congress established the appropriation for the White House, and it's up to Congress to decide, and it's not up to the president to decide to bulldoze half of the White House because he wakes up that day thinking it's a good thing to do,” says Raskin.
Traditional enforcement of subpoenas through the courts can take years, as a case makes its way through the federal district court in Washington and then any inevitable appeals. In his first term, for instance, Trump asserted executive privilege for former White House counsel Don McGahn, who was subpoenaed but never testified while Trump was in office.
Democratic aides have also been weighing other ideas to make subpoena noncompliance unattractive, like adding cumulative monetary fines through an inherent contempt provision in the House rules, sources tell Inner Loop.
But legal experts have long believed the only way to give subpoenas teeth is for Congress to pass legislation that fast-tracks judicial review for contested subpoenas so they get resolved while the president is still in office.
The most viable idea kicked around in recent years has been a bill that sends a subpoena dispute to a federal district court panel, with an appeal that goes straight to the Supreme Court. Still, it is no panacea, given that the Justice Department prosecutes subpoena noncompliance, and it would never prosecute its own officials.
Trump might have to choose—subpoena or arch.

A pre-game stunt involving two passenger jets flying dramatically low over a stadium in South Africa drew huge cheers from the estimated crowd of around 56,000 people, but also sparked a major debate over safety risks.
The flyby by two Embraer jets, operated by local airline Airlink, happened on Saturday before the second rugby union Test between South Africa and New Zealand in Cape Town.
Flight tracking service Flightradar24 estimated that the lead jet passed just 41 to 46 feet (12 to 14 metres) above the roof of Cape Town Stadium, with the crowd and the world’s top-ranked rugby teams below. The second jet, which was very close behind, flew through a cloud of pink dust that shot up from the stadium roof as part of the show.
Airlink, a sponsor of the South African rugby union team, said that the flyby was conducted according to safety regulations. The airline said that it was carefully planned and rehearsed, with the aircraft travelling at around 150 knots (172 mph), when they went over the stadium. Each jet had three senior captains on board, Airlink said, operating in the roles of a commander, a co-pilot and a safety officer. The jets were not carrying any passengers.
“Airlink notes the concerns expressed in various social media and online forums regarding yesterday’s formation flyby over Cape Town’s DHL Stadium,” Airlink said on Sunday. “The flight demanded careful planning and rehearsal, as it required navigating at low altitude, at around 150 knots. The South African Civil Aviation Authority and Air Traffic Navigation Services provided valuable guidance, approval and support to ensure a safe flyby.”
South African rugby union has a tradition of stadium flybys at big games, starting when a Boeing 747 flew over another stadium in Johannesburg before the 1995 World Cup final between the same teams, who are fierce rivals. But this weekend’s flyby was especially low and dramatic, generating global interest after it was shown as part of the pre-game broadcast, and sparking a flurry of videos shot by witnesses.
Some aviation experts questioned whether the margin for error was too small. “Basically, that lead aircraft … was kind of like dodging over the roof and climbing over the one side and dipping below and then climbing over the other side. That was a little bit uncomfortable,” said Chris Martinus, president of Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association South Africa. “[If] something adverse happens, you just don’t have options at that kind of altitude.”
Keith Tonkin, an Australian aviation consultant and former military and commercial pilot, said on Monday that the Embraer passenger jets – which are small-to-medium jets designed for regional flights – were not designed or intended for that kind of low-level operation and warned against the precedent.
“The bigger picture is that a benchmark has been established and others may expect to do something similar, and that’s not going to end well,” Tonkin said. He added that turbulence or a bird strike at such a low altitude could leave the pilots with too little room to manoeuvre without hitting the stadium.
Airlink said that the flight data recorded by both aircraft confirmed that their flights were performed within civil aviation safety limits for speed and altitude.

On Saturday, Katie Taylor steps through the ropes at an 82,000-capacity Croke Park to face France's Flora Pili in her farewell fight.
Victory on the hallowed Dublin turf would write one final fairytale chapter - a chance to bow out as undisputed light-welterweight champion and put the seal on a career that has revolutionised women's sport.
There have been countless moments that have shaped the 40-year-old's journey.
From a childhood letter to a Twitter direct message, these are five sliding doors moments in the making of an Irish icon.
The letter to Deirdre Gogarty
Long before Taylor became Olympic champion, she was a 10-year-old girl in Bray who simply wanted to box.
There was nowhere for her to go though. Women's boxing was unsanctioned in Ireland, absent from the Olympic programme and devoid of any clear professional pathway.
But there was Deirdre Gogarty. Having relocated to the United States, she became Ireland's first female professional world champion in 1997 when she defeated Bonnie Canino for the WIBF featherweight title in Louisiana.
"How did you do it when everyone tried to stop you?" a 10-year-old Taylor asked in a letter sent to her hero.
"If you keep working at it and keep showing your skills, somebody's going to say 'we've got to let this girl box'," Gogarty replied.
Reflecting on the letter years later, Gogarty added: "It's mind-blowing. Especially when she wrote, 'maybe one day they'll let us box in the Olympics'."
Had that letter never been written, Taylor might still have found her way to the top, but Gogarty offered hope when none seemingly existed.
Heartbreak at Rio 2016 and the leap into the unknown
When the International Olympic Committee was undecided on including women's boxing at the Games, Taylor was brought in for showcase events in front of sceptical officials in Chicago. Her dazzling displays dismantled every argument.
"Katie won't say this, and I've been holding back from saying this, but single-handedly, Katie Taylor got women's boxing into the Olympics," her manager Brian Peters says.
Women's boxing made its Olympic debut at the London 2012 Games and Taylor claimed lightweight gold.
Four years later in Rio, however, that amateur journey ended when a split-decision quarter-final defeat shattered Taylor's title defence. She was at a crossroads - rebuild for another Olympic cycle or turn professional in an era where women's pro boxing was still neglected.
"It was probably the worst year of my career," Taylor later admitted. "I needed a change. I needed a new mindset."
Had she secured a second Olympic gold, the motivation to dive into the pro ranks might have evaporated. Instead, the sting of defeat forced reinvention.
Hearn's DMs & Taylor's loyalty
Turning professional was one thing, but securing both the right team and commercial backing was another challenge.
First came manager Peters, who initially stepped in out of concern for her future.
"I only took her on not to see her end up with people who didn't know what they were doing," Peters says.
On 4 October 2016, Taylor sent Matchroom's Eddie Hearn a direct message on Twitter, now known as X, asking if he would consider promoting her. Hearn replied 24 hours later, inviting Taylor, Peters, and her mother Bridget to a London restaurant. Hearn even borrowed his father's car to impress Taylor.
The charm offensive worked and Taylor made her debut at Wembley Arena a month later.
In a sport notorious for fractured relationships and bitter splits, Taylor's core team has remained the same from day one with Peters, Hearn and trainer Ross Enamait.
"In a business full of egos, she's stayed loyal to everyone around her and remained the most humble person you could ever meet," Peters says.
Had Hearn dismissed that DM - or had Taylor lacked the enduring loyalty that kept the same tight-knit team in her corner for a decade - the promotional engine that transformed women's boxing might never have started.
MSG & the Serrano test
By April 2022, Taylor was the undisputed lightweight champion. She had already survived a razor-thin majority decision against Delfine Persoon at Madison Square Garden (MSG) three years earlier to unify - a night when many felt her aura of invincibility was almost cracked.
Returning to MSG to face seven-division title winner Amanda Serrano presented a different magnitude of threat.
Their blockbuster marked the first time two women headlined the storied New York venue. In front of a sellout crowd of 19,187, Taylor claimed a split-decision victory in what was widely hailed as the fight of the year.
Had one scorecard leaned the other way or had the bout failed to deliver on its enormous hype, the momentum behind women's mega-fights would have stalled.
Instead, the victory spawned a record-breaking rivalry. Their 2024 rematch drew global viewing figures on Netflix on the undercard of Jake Paul v Mike Tyson, before Taylor sealed the trilogy at the Garden in 2025.

Cameron II: Legacy on the line
Taylor's first professional defeat came in May 2023 at Dublin's 3Arena when she was outpointed by Chantelle Cameron for the undisputed light-welterweight belts.
At 36, questions around retirement surfaced.
In the ring immediately following the defeat, Peters says he told his fighter to congratulate Cameron and ask for the rematch.
Six months later, Taylor delivered a masterclass in grit, claiming a majority decision to become a two-weight undisputed champion.
"The pressure was immense," Peters says.
"For all she had done, her legacy was suddenly questioned. Had Chantelle won the rematch, who knows what would have happened?"
The final pay-off - Croke Park
Croke Park is not really a sixth sliding door but rather the final pay-off.
After beating Serrano in last year's trilogy decider, Taylor quietly decided she was done.
"She actually retired that night," Peters says. "She said, 'We convincingly beat Serrano - where do we go from there?' I said I'll agree on one condition."
That condition was Croke Park or nothing.
"Croke Park - no disrespect to Wembley - is the greatest stadium in the world," Peters says. "You cut an Irish person and they'll bleed Croke Park."
Peters insists there will be no change of heart - no Cameron trilogy and no comebacks.
"When Katie gives her word, that is it," he says.
Regardless of Saturday's result, Taylor will be remembered as a pioneer who kicked open the door for women's boxing.

Canadian missing after Nepal flooding found safe, Anand says
Individual had been unreachable due to communication outages, foreign affairs minister says
Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand says one of the 30 Canadian citizens and permanent residents missing after catastrophic flooding in Nepal's border region with China has been found safe.
She says the individual was unreachable due to communication outages and was able to establish contact Tuesday.
The flash flooding struck one week ago after a glacier collapsed in the Himalayan border region between Nepal and China.
More than 1,100 people were killed and more than 3,900 are missing.
Nepal's Foreign Ministry says about 590 foreign nationals from 39 countries remain unaccounted for.
Anand says Canada will be sending more than 18,000 emergency items from Canadian Red Cross stockpiles to the area in addition to the $5 million Ottawa has already pledged in humanitarian aid.

Taapsee Pannu had often been associated with intense performances and hard-hitting stories, but the actor said she wanted to explore lighter genres, particularly romantic comedies. In a conversation with Hindustan Times, Taapsee said she had been waiting for filmmakers to look beyond the strong, intense characters she had frequently been offered.
Taapsee Pannu wanted to do a rom-com after intense roles; says, “There’s a certain creative bankruptcy”
While discussing her filmography ahead of Gandhari, Taapsee said she would love to take up a fun romantic comedy. “Please tell people, have mercy, give me something light. I would love to see you in a rom-com. I would love to do it too.”
The actor said the industry often became comfortable associating actors with a particular genre after they found success in it. “There’s a certain kind of creative imagination that our industry is not that good with,” she said. “When we see a certain actor good with a certain kind of roles and genres and worlds, we just want to play safe and keep casting that actor in the same world.”
Taapsee revealed that she had rejected several investigation dramas and action films after Baby and Naam Shabana because she did not want to repeat similar roles. “I can't begin to tell you the number of films I have turned down — investigation films that I have turned down, like a lot. Action films that I turned down after Naam Shabana and Baby until now,” she added. “Because it just felt like there’s a creative bankruptcy where you can’t imagine a person — if you're calling someone a good actor, not me, if anybody, a good actor — then please put the faith in that person to be able to perform range.”
She also said her filmography did not necessarily reflect her capabilities. “It’s not my fault if I am only offered 10 intense films,” she said. “I will choose the best out of it and present that, but it will still be a strong woman, intense film because that's the only genre that people have started imagining me [in].”
Taapsee cited Manmarziyaan as an example of her ability to carry a romantic story. “If today someone goes out to pitch a love story with me, people can't imagine it. They don't want to greenlight it because they feel like, ‘Taapsee in a love story? It's very difficult to imagine.’ I don't understand,” she asserted.
She also spoke about her experience with comedy in Khel Khel Mein. “I literally did Khel Khel Mein for me to have fun,” she revealed. “I knew there were seven of us on the table. I just get to have some fun is why I did that film.”
Taapsee credited director Mudassar Aziz for trusting her with comedy and said filmmakers needed to give her more opportunities to explore different genres.
Meanwhile, Gandhari, directed by Devashish Makhija and written and produced by Kanika Dhillon, featured Taapsee as Bani, a mother whose daughter was abducted. The film also starred Ishwak Singh, Jatin Sarna, Swastika Mukherjee, Mita Vashisht and Chhaya Kadam. Gandhari premiered on Netflix on September 3.

Matte gold, sloped, and steering-wheel-free, the Tesla Cybercab seems designed to catch the eyes of looky-loos. Now rubberneckers may have more opportunities: Tesla is set to host an event on Thursday at its Austin, Texas, headquarters to debut the Cybercab.
Tesla first rolled out a prototype Cybercab at a flashy event on the Warner Bros. lot in 2024. This week’s unveiling will likely mark the vehicle’s official introduction to the electric-auto maker’s small ride-hail service. It has operated a pilot program in Austin since last summer, and has since expanded to a handful of other cities in Texas and Florida, with permits to launch in Arizona and Nevada. (A “robotaxi” service in the San Francisco Bay Area is not legally permitted to operate without drivers behind the wheel.) Before the event, Tesla added 51 Cybercabs to its fleet of vehicles registered to operate in Texas (263 Model Ys are also registered).
“The streets won't be the same anymore,” Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla’s head of AI software, posted last month on X. When an X user asked whether the Cybercabs would “flood Austin,” Tesla CEO Elon Musk, with his characteristic moth-to-the-flame tendencies toward hyperbole, responded with a simple “Yes.”
Details on the event are still scant, and the basic business model for the Cybercab is in question—are the vehicles just for ride-hail operations, or meant to be sold to individual drivers? States regulate autonomous vehicles, and some tightly control permits and data collection. However, Musk still insisted this year that Tesla will sell Cybercabs directly to consumers before the end of 2026.
Either way, the physical Cybercab slated to be shown off in Austin on Thursday may be the easiest lift in Tesla’s deeply ambitious plan to shift from a company that builds cars to one entirely focused on autonomous vehicles and robotics. Manufacturing a car isn’t easy. But neither is running a functional autonomous vehicle service, nor building the software to power it. Tesla hasn’t yet proven that it can do either at scale.
“Longer term, the software is the most important piece,” says Seth Goldstein, a senior equity analyst for Morningstar who follows Tesla. “This is a very important step, to put the Cybercab in production, but ultimately, it only matters if the software can allow a car to navigate safely.”
Musk has promised for nearly a decade that the Teslas sold to everyday consumers are just a software update away from driverless capabilities, but that has yet to come true. (Musk admitted earlier this year that some vehicles will need a hardware upgrade to get the capability.) The company’s critical thesis is that a car can drive on complicated, chaotic public roads with only inexpensive cameras, which could allow it to deploy self-driving robots much more cheaply than the competition. Waymo, the US industry leader, took a direct swipe at Tesla last month, writing in a blog post that “cameras are incredible, but they aren’t enough.” Waymo’s more expensive setup uses lidar and radar along with cameras.
Tesla’s Full Self-Driving (Supervised) product, available to drivers for a $99 monthly fee, currently does many driving tasks, including changing lanes and stopping at red lights. But the company warns in its manuals that drivers must pay attention and be ready to intervene at all times. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), the US’s top auto safety regulator, opened an investigation into crashes involving FSD in 2024 following concerns that the system falters in situations with poor visibility. That probe is ongoing.
Tesla began testing its steering-wheel- and pedal-free Cybercab on Austin streets in late June 2026. Based on videos posted online, much of the testing occurs with a safety monitor in the front passenger seat, ready to intervene if something goes wrong.
Success in the robotaxi game also has a lot to do with balance sheets and spending. “These AV companies are spending so much money getting this technology in place, but in order to scale up the business, the economics come down to utilization," says J. D. Alexander, the founder of AVFleetTech, a consultancy focused on AV fleet operations.
Companies need to wring all they can out of their investments on wheels, making sure their vehicles are on the road and picking up passengers as much as possible. Efficiency comes down to how, when, and where the robots get charged, cleaned, and fixed—and making sure that the humans hired to do those things are well trained and motivated.
The nitty-gritty operations are complicated enough that other firms with robotaxi services and ambitions have partnered with several other companies to get it done. In Dallas, the rental company Avis manages fleet logistics, maintenance, charging, and depots for Waymo; Hertz is slated to do the same for Uber self-driving cars. Waymo also works with the fleet manager Moove in Arizona, Florida, and, soon, London, and with Lyft’s Flexdrive service in Nashville.
Tesla likes to do everything on its own, and it has clearly started to think about where and how it wants to stage its robotaxis. In new markets, Cybercabs might first operate out of Tesla service centers, where employees already repair and clean its electric cars. Tesla is tinkering with the cleaning part too. A Texas state architectural permit application the company filed in June 2025 indicated that the company’s main robotaxi hub would have a “cleaning robot” on the premises. However, Tesla hasn’t released details on that tech beyond a promotional video posted last year.
The physical Cybercab, then, is just a start. As more of the gilded cars “flood” the streets, it should be easy to watch them go.

Worms found crawling in khichuri served to children at West Bengal anganwadi
White worms were found in khichuri served to children at an anganwadi centre in Cooch Behar. The incident reportedly left two children ill and sparked a village protest.
White worms were found crawling in khichuri prepared for children at an anganwadi centre in the Kuthibari area of Dinhata in Cooch Behar, West Bengal. Two local children reportedly fell ill after eating the meal.
The incident came to light on Wednesday morning and led to anger among villagers in the area. Residents gathered at the anganwadi centre to protest over the food served to the children.
VILLAGERS LOCK ANGANWADI CENTRE
During the protest, villagers locked the door of the anganwadi centre. The action reflected their anger over the alleged presence of worms in the khichuri prepared for the children.
The incident was reported from Kuthibari under Putimari-2 Gram Panchayat in Dinhata. It has caused a stir among residents in the area.
SIMILAR INCIDENTS IN BIHAR
In a separate incident in Bihar's Nalanda district, at least 40 students fell ill after detergent powder was reportedly served instead of salt with their mid-day meal at Parasi Middle School. The students complained of stomach pain and vomiting and were taken to Hospital. Bihar Rural Development Minister Shravan Kumar visited the hospital and assured strict action against those responsible.
In another case in Arwal district, worms were reportedly found in a soybean dish supplied by an NGO to 75 schools in the Sadar block. Headmasters stopped the food from being served and informed the Education Department. District Education Officer Asgar Ali said the matter was being investigated and action would be taken against the NGO if negligence was established.

Souls-like is a genre that has lately been getting some amazing games, and more are yet to be released this year. Out of all the big names, one game that many Souls veterans would remember is Mortal Shell. A game that was released eons ago and, although it was rough around the edges, it held great promise.
Now, the developers have made a sequel, Mortal Shell II, and it is a complete reimagining of the gameplay while keeping the same philosophies intact. After spending well over 20 hours, here is my review of Mortal Shell II.
A Gorgeous Overworld That Keeps You Intrigued, but Gets Repetitive
Mortal Shell II’s greatest strength is how gorgeous the game’s overworld looks. From the very moment you jump into the game, the visual design of the world, lighting, and character designs keep you in awe. Even the monster designs are on point visually, with very distinct looks.
When compared to the old Mortal Shell, this visual upgrade leaves anyone who played the first version completely stunned. It has me excited for the upcoming games from Cold Symmetry. However, it’s not just the graphics that keep you hooked. The world of Mortal Shell II has a lot to offer.
Although the game is not an open world, the maps are fairly open and easy to explore. The game also keeps the exploration open-ended, making it feel more like an open-world game. Players are not tied to a set direction and are freely given the reins to explore anywhere they want.
What’s more is that every nook and cranny in Mortal Shell II has something to explore. From dungeons to hidden shells, weapons, and bosses, there is a lot to explore in the game. However, the reward for exploring does become repetitive after a while. Most of the dungeons only reward weapon upgrade materials or coins.
Very few places actually have unique weapons and sidearms. The dungeon designs also become repetitive after a while, although many still have very unique patterns. For example, one of the dungeons had a potion at the end, which, after drinking, would change the player’s direction key for some time.
While in that state, they would have to fight a boss and defeat it. Similarly, there was another dungeon that was filled with illusions, and players would have to figure out the secret paths to continue forward.
Such unique patterns definitely kept the ball rolling; however, the overbearing majority of the dungeons almost looked and felt the same after the first 5 hours. This was quite disheartening because the overworld areas looked drastically different based on where you were standing.
An Excellent Mix of Parrying, Dodging, and Shell Abilities
Mortal Shell II’s combat is truly unique. Like the first part, the game’s combat is heavily dependent on Shells, which are preset characters with unique abilities. Each Shell comes with a distinct characteristic, and you can also classify them into different classes. The Shells also have their personal story, similar to Elden Ring Nightreign‘s characters.
Proxima became my favorite pretty early on, as she is the female reinvention of the ‘Chad’ meme. There was an odd sense of pleasure I found in stomping enemies with my massive and perfectly toned figure. Her ability allowed her to dart into enemies or pull them to her, depending on their weight, and apply big lightning damage.
Similarly, other Shells had other abilities, like some that were very agile, while others dealt more break damage. Along with Shells, Mortal Shell II’s combat also perfectly mixed both parrying and dodging into its combat. They probably did it on the same level as Lies of P, which is quite a compliment.
What I liked most was Seals, which had different parrying abilities. Some allowed guarding, while others could mitigate damage. Other than them, players could also equip Tarstones, which were passive abilities that could be used in combat. One Tarstone imbued the Lightning property permanently on the weapon after leveling it to max.
Similarly, other Tarstones would also give very unique combat prowess, like allowing double attacks. Mixing that with the main weapon and sidearm players have, the combat becomes quite versatile.
The only qualms I had with the combat were how few Seals and weapons were in the game. I would have loved to see more options.
Bosses Are a Mixed Bag of Brilliant and Forgettable Fights
Mortal Shell II’s bosses are a topic that I still cannot make up my mind about entirely. While the game does have some outstanding boss designs, it also suffers greatly from reskinning normal enemies as bosses. Reskinned bosses were also common in Elden Ring, but Mortal Shell II does it a bit too shamelessly for my taste.
There are two types of bosses in Mortal Shell II. One is Ovum Thieves, found inside massive gates, and these are the main story bosses. Each of these bosses is unique, and they have some of the best fights in the game. On the other hand, the other type of bosses is found in dungeons or in the overworld. These bosses are reskinned versions of normal enemies.
Some of these bosses are a complete reimagining of the base enemy type, but the overwhelming number of them are just pure reskins. A huge reason for the repetitive feeling of Mortal Shell II is these reskinned bosses. Although I understand that making unique bosses requires a bigger budget, from a gameplay point of view, I personally cannot give it a free pass.
Still, the main story bosses are genuinely cool in the game. However, one more thing you should note is that the bosses can be a bit floaty. This is a problem for most enemy encounters in Mortal Shell II, but it is fairly easy to get used to.
Performance: Mostly Seamless, with a Few Noticeable Hiccups
I wanted to give Mortal Shell II a clean slate for performance because of how beautifully it runs for most of the game. However, I cannot do that, as the game often stutters greatly when entering a new area, or sometimes when fighting multiple enemies at the same time.
I have also had a couple of crashes, which were definitely not fun. Although the performance was fairly stable throughout most combat encounters, when the stutters do happen, it completely ruins the experience.
My Setup:
CPU: AMD Ryzen 9 7900x
CPU Cooler: CORSAIR H150 RGB
Motherboard: GIGABYTE B650M Gaming X AX
GPU: MSI Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB
RAM: 32GB (32GB x 1) ADATA XPG DDR5 5600FSB LANCER
SSD: 1TB AORUS Gen 4 5000E NVMe storage
Monitor: 1080p @165hz
When it comes to stats, I was getting over 200 FPS on average with DLSS and Frame Generation ON at Medium settings. The game is really good even at Medium settings, and cranking up the graphics didn’t improve the visuals in any significant way. What it did, however, was cause more frequent stutters, which is why I had to tone it down.
After turning off DLSS and Frame Gen, I was still getting well over 140 FPS on average, so the game’s performance was pretty good and stable. Hopefully, the crashes and other performance issues get fixed in upcoming patches.
Verdict: Mortal Shell II Is a Beautiful Promise That Falls Just Short of Greatness
Mortal Shell II is an outstanding upgrade to its first part, and one of the standout games in the Souls-like genre. It looks absolutely gorgeous, the sound design is amazing, and the combat is really unique while mixing the same things Souls players are familiar with.
However, the game suffers from repetitiveness, whether it be reskinned enemies, the same enemy types in multiple locations, or less variety in weapons. Stutters and crashes are another major issue holding back the full potential of the game.
Overall, I consider Mortal Shell II a great step forward in enhancing the Souls-like genre to the next level. With such massive improvement seen in the game’s sequel, I cannot wait to see what more the developers have planned with the game’s third installment, if there is one in consideration.

Man Utd and their calculated left-back gamble
- Published
As 23:00 BST ticked by on 1 September and the suspicion became reality, many Manchester United fans thought the same thing – what about a left-back?
Since the 2025-26 season ended, and United's summer transfer strategy started to be debated, it seemed obvious the club would move to address a perceived weakness in Michael Carrick's squad.
Luke Shaw is their only senior orthodox left-back. He started all 38 Premier League games last season, which given his previous injury record was phenomenal.
But as back-up Tyrell Malacia had unsurprisingly been allowed to leave when his contract expired at the end of June, and it is widely accepted 31-year-old Shaw will not be able to play repeatedly in a new campaign that could stretch beyond 60 games, a reinforcement was expected.
Various targets were identified, including Newcastle's Lewis Hall, Barcelona's Alejandro Balde and Racing Santander's Jorge Salinas. Finally, it came down to an attempt to get Rayan Ait-Nouri to cross the great Manchester divide by joining on loan, but City said no.
For that move to have progressed, United would have had to include an obligation to buy at a later date, but have instead chosen to bide their time for their first-choice targets.
Now the deadline has passed and, at least until the winter window opens in January, United and Carrick must stand or fall by what has to be viewed as a calculated gamble.
- Man Utd fail in attempt to sign Ait-Nouri from Man City 
  - Published15 hours ago
Will Man Utd try to sign Hall in 2027?
Firstly, it must be acknowledged Manchester United really like Lewis Hall.
Had they been able to do a deal with Newcastle for him, they would have done.
However, raided by Premier League rivals for their star men this summer, it became obvious in discussions around the highly-rated 22-year-old if Newcastle were to be persuaded to strike a deal, the transfer fee would be huge.
Manchester United's summer transfer budget was finite.
Faced with the reality of the situation, they opted to maintain their focus on the 'priority' midfield area and eventually committed £70m to bring in Carlos Baleba from Brighton.
Hall, it was concluded, is someone they are prepared to wait until next summer for.
United would have been prepared to take Balde on loan. Barcelona would only sell him. Salinas had a relatively low release clause, but Atletico Madrid were favourites to sign him. By the time they moved on to Argentina defender Nicolas Tagliafico, who they missed out on anyway, United had moved on themselves.
Their decision to belatedly act on an initial approach made by an agent around Ait-Nouri was an admission they are not totally certain of the path they have chosen.
Effectively that is Shaw as first-choice left-back, with Noussair Mazraoui as back-up, in a position he admittedly plays in for Morocco, supported by Diogo Dalot, who has switched flanks before, and Harry Amass.
Right-back role for Yoro and when does Amass play?
The Amass case is a strange one. A natural left-back in United's academy, who did well in a loan spell at Sheffield Wednesday last season, then got injured straight after switching to Norwich in the winter window, Amass, 19, impressed many observers with his performances during pre-season, when he shadowed Shaw.
Yet, for some reason, United were willing to let him leave.
In the summer of 2024, then manager Erik ten Hag opted not to pick the teenager in his squad for the Community Shield, even though Amass had given a creditable account of himself up against Mo Salah in a pre-season game in the United States just a week earlier.
Ten Hag felt, physically, Amass was not at the level required. In theory, the two years that have elapsed since then should have made the defender bigger and stronger.
There have been multiple expressions of interest in Amass. Even heading into deadline day, his omission from United's Premier League 2 game against Leicester on Monday reinforced a widespread belief he would leave, probably on loan.
But that has not happened and it is not clear what his role will be within the senior squad.
The willingness to view Mazraoui as a left-back option was helped by the performances of Leny Yoro in pre-season.
Signed from Lille for £52m in 2024 as a central defender, Carrick used Yoro mainly as a right-back this summer.
Against Ipswich on Sunday, that was the slot Yoro was introduced into as a replacement for Dalot, at the same time as Mazraoui was coming on for Shaw.
At just 20, Yoro has plenty to learn about the right-back role. However, he has pace, is strong and is good on the ball. United supporters only have to look at how Josko Gvardiol has adapted to the full-back role at Manchester City after signing as a central defender to realise switching positions can have a positive outcome.
That is the calculated risk United have taken.
What they absolutely did not want to do, having taken a hardline stance all summer on the fees they were willing to pay, and a refusal to spend more than they thought a player was worth, was end up making a signing like Alex Telles, or Matteo Darmian, or Sergio Reguilon, who all arrived in recent years but were evidently short of the standard required.
It makes sense. It is probably the right call.
But that is a view taken away from the emotion of matches and the rollercoaster of results. And the reality is they will be the deciding factor in whether it was a good decision or not.

- Instagram has announced a new feature for its app, called First Draft. Available only for iPhone users at the time of writing, it trims and blends selected videos, converting them into a reel within seconds.
- Although First Draft’s editing is on the basic side, it is nevertheless extremely useful for those newcomers (or even veterans) who are not comfortable with editing videos.
- Experts might find First Draft to be very basic, but its ease of use and speed make it perfect for content creators who feel held back by their lack of basic video editing ability.
Instagram has just rolled out a new feature, which it claims is going to make creating Reels easier. As its name suggests, First Draft basically gives users a quick “first draft” by turning all the video clips that they have selected into a quick Reel. The feature is an iPhone exclusive for now and only available on the main Instagram app, and not on Edits (the Reels editing app by Instagram), but an Android release is likely to follow soon.
Given all the AI hype and how much Meta is focusing on it, you might think First Draft is a new AI feature, but Instagram has confirmed that First Draft does not use Artificial Intelligence. Nevertheless, it has made people wonder if its ease of use could actually reduce the role of conventional, “manual” editing in the Reel world. Well, we have used the feature for a short while, and here is what we think.
How to use Instagram First Draft
Using First Draft is a pretty simple affair. Just follow these steps:
- Open the Instagram app on your iPhone (do remember to update it to the latest version), then tap on the “+” icon present on the top left side of the app to add new content.
- From there, swipe to Reels on the panel on the lower part of the app.
- Tap on the camera to record footage or select an existing video from your gallery, which will be displayed.
- Once you have selected all the clips you wish to add, look for the First Draft option, which will appear on the panel at the lower part of the app – it appears the moment you select a video. Tapping it will open a First Draft box, with a “Try it” button. Tap on this button.
- Hitting the button puts the selected videos into a processing phase where the app analyses the clips, identifies highlights, trims clips, and reduces the length.
- In a matter of ten seconds, the feature will present a pretty basic edited version of your videos, trimming them and cutting out awkward pauses, with preview frames beneath the result, which you can move back and forth to reorder.
- If you like the results, tap on the Next button in the bottom right corner of the app to go to the Instagram Reels posting page (you can also take your results to Edits), make more changes, if need be, and hit Publish.
How First Draft works
Instagram has stressed that the new editing feature is just a “starting point” on which creators can then build their final Reel. The social media platform says the feature can identify silences, awkward pauses, and other such moments. It then removes these moments, trims the video, and gives a first draft that highlights what it assumes are important parts of the video. It allows creators to select or record, edit, and share all without leaving Instagram.
Instagram has been ensuring that users know that all that is done by the feature is reversible, and does not come as an attempt to replace a creator’s creativity, but actually offers ‘early video trimming’ so users can move their focus from the technical part of editing to its creative part. Instead of using AI (which comes as a surprise), First Draft actually uses internal processing and audio detection to find moments of silence in selected videos. We have fiddled with the feature for a short while and can say that it actually works,serving up a very basic edit of videos (or of a single long video), even while leaving the “creative work” to the user.
Going by our first encounter with First Draft, it cannot really replace manual editing. It is not a very creative feature and only offers what can be termed as the ‘bare-bones’ of what your edited Reel might look like. We found the feature does eliminate pauses and silence, but when it trims videos, there seems to be no method to its madness, which basically means you can end up with some of the important bits removed from the video. In its current form, it might come in handy for people who create piece-to-camera video formats, but you would still need to revise and re-edit the whole thing on your own.
Also See: Instagram Edits vs CapCut: Best Video Editing App for You
First Draft: Who is it for (and who might not like it)
It is rather basic, but those who are new to creating videos and struggle with editing might find First Draft useful. It offers a very quick, hassle-free edit of videos. This can be helpful for creators who are not as skilled when it comes to editing their content, or are intimidated by the task. First Draft can be a very simple, quick-fix solution for them. But it is unlikely to appeal much to those creators who have been in the game for a while, are good at editing, and have their own style and flair in the editing field. We can already see them skipping this new feature.
But given that a large number of Instagram users do not really know much about video editing, First Draft seems to be an extremely handy tool, especially for those who do not want to get into the hassle of going through all their videos one by one and trimming out stutters and pauses. The fact that one can do so right from within Instagram, without having to open an additional app, is a huge bonus. As mentioned by the platform itself, First Draft is just a starting point and nothing more. Even in its current form (and we think it will get better in clip selection), it will help new creators start their content journey and feel more comfortable without getting knee-deep in editing hassles from the get-go.
Experts might shake their heads at how basic the feature is, but then remember how DSLR photographers shook their heads at 0.3 MP cellphone cameras? First Draft might be the first step to breaking down the editing barrier that holds back many content creators, and if it gets better (maybe with even options to automatically choose background audio or add subtitles in other languages, and so on), who knows, even experts might find it a handy tool to save them some time. But that’s in the future (and we bet AI will come into it at some stage). As for now, First Draft is mainly for Instagram newbies who want Reel creation with zero hassles. And that actually is a bigger deal than some of the pros might admit.

NEW DELHI: Russia remained the largest supplier of crude to India in Aug, while US supplied highest volumes of LPG and LNG, data from maritime intelligence and research firm Kpler shows.
India purchased 2.1 million barrels of crude per day from Russia this month, accounting for 45% of its total oil imports. The figure, however, was down from 2.8 mbd in July, which was the highest ever. The other top suppliers included the UAE (0.5 mbd), Saudi Arabia (0.5 mbd) and Venezuela (0.3 mbd).
India’s overall crude imports also declined in Aug compared with May, June and July, when refiners ramped up purchases to guard against any shortfall in a scenario of the conflict in West Asia escalating. Crude supplies in Aug were estimated at 4.6 mbd, nearly 8% lower than the over 5 mbd imported in July. Experts said the decline reflected some moderation after strong buying in recent months, scheduled maintenance at some refineries in India and lower availability of Russian crude.
India also emerged as a key supplier of gasoline (petrol) and diesel to Russia as refinery operations in the country were hit by Ukrainian attacks on its facilities. 
According to energy analytics firm Vortexa, Russia’s seaborne gasoline imports increased to 125,000 barrels per day in Aug, equivalent to a projected 470,000 tonnes for the month, with the supplies coming from countries such as India, Türkiye and Morocco.
US emerged as the largest supplier of LPG and LNG, accounting for nearly 51% and 38%, respectively, of India’s total imports during the month. Of the 1.1 million tonnes of LPG imported by India, about 0.6 MT of cooking and heating gas came from the US, compared with 0.9 MT in July. The UAE (0.1 MT) and Algeria (0.1 MT) were the other major suppliers.
US also supplied 0.8 MT of the 2.2 MT of LNG imported by India during the month, followed by Oman (0.5 MT) and Nigeria (0.4 MT). The diversification of energy imports, however, has led to higher commodity costs due to increased freight bills from longer voyages and insurance charges, experts added.

The MAGA Right Is Only Pretending to Be Censored
The conspiracy theory that persists even though no evidence supports it
For nearly a year and a half, the Trump administration prepared its case. Political appointees inside the State Department combed through old files and databases. Civil servants received notice that their personal emails would be examined. Darren Beattie—the founder of a far-right conspiracist website, then the undersecretary of state for public diplomacy—sent out a request for files on anyone who had communicated with or written about the Global Engagement Center, a now-dissolved agency that once worked to expose propaganda campaigns by Russia, China, Iran, and other countries around the world.
The request, seen last year by the MIT Technology Review, was far-reaching. Beattie was seeking information on Bill Gates; the commentator Bill Kristol; Chris Krebs, a former U.S. cybersecurity official; a German government minister; the analyst Renée DiResta, formerly at Stanford University, as well as others associated with a research project called the Election Integrity Partnership; and, as it happens, me.
This unprecedented investigation was meant to expose the Biden administration’s “censorship–industrial complex,” a shadowy network allegedly dedicated to the mass suppression of American free speech. Since 2020, internet trolls have accused Biden-administration officials, social-media companies, and university researchers of weaving a nefarious plot to censor conservatives. Since 2025, MAGA ideologues have been using this alleged plot as an excuse to dismantle government programs, stifle research, intimidate American citizens, and even distort American foreign policy.
And yet for the past year and half, neither Beattie nor anyone else has actually managed to prove that the plot ever existed. Like a soap bubble that vanishes with the touch of a hand, the “censorship–industrial complex” belongs to that mystical category of things that disappear when you examine them too closely.
The failure to produce evidence is not for lack of trying. During the Biden administration, MAGA allies and politicians filed multiple lawsuits with the goal of exposing alleged censorship. None has done so. One of them, brought by the Missouri attorney general, made it all the way to the Supreme Court before justices asked for underlying evidence that the government had censored anyone. The answer was no. Another, brought against the Stanford research project by America First Legal—Stephen Miller’s team—failed in July, when a judge found the suit had no standing, no jurisdiction, and, after a discovery process requested by the plaintiffs, no evidence. There was no proof, in other words, that the Stanford research had resulted in anyone being censored. Other cases against the Biden administration were simply settled by President Trump’s Department of Justice without finding any evidence of “censorship” either.
Now the Trump administration’s most dedicated ideologues have also failed, spectacularly, to prove the existence of a “censorship–industrial complex” inside the State Department. After months of searching, Beattie’s successor as undersecretary for public diplomacy, Sarah Rogers, recently decided to publicize the unimpressive results of the inquiry into the Global Engagement Center. But instead of writing a report admitting that the documents that surfaced contained nothing of interest, she leaked them, selectively, to an internet troll known as DataRepublican.
Here is where the story becomes especially convoluted, and I will simplify as best I can. “DataRepublican” is the X pseudonym of Jennica Pounds, who has a history of misreading data and connecting dots to describe nonexistent conspiracies. But the plan went wrong: Upon receipt of raw documents from Rogers, including screenshots without context, Pounds decided that Rogers was a “Deep State” operative and refused to release them. Subsequently, it emerged that Pounds herself has been secretly employed by the Pentagon, which presumably makes her a deep-state operative too. But that’s another story.
Because Pounds would not publish the documents, Rogers did so herself, in a long thread on X. As she must have known, they contained no evidence of conspiracy, no proof that anyone in the Biden administration censored millions or even dozens of social-media posts. Instead, Rogers, who is theoretically responsible for promoting good relations with people in foreign countries, went after a series of U.S. citizens. She found a GEC official who had about a dozen email exchanges with the Stanford project, almost all about Russian accounts. She posted a brief excerpt of the congressional testimony of Daniel Kimmage, a former State Department employee and GEC deputy coordinator, who truthfully explained that the center was set up to deal with foreign disinformation, not American media. Rogers wrote that “that was a lie,” without offering proof.
Rogers also included several misleading posts about the Stanford project, plucking a number from a table and implying that it meant the researchers had somehow targeted more than 400,000 tweets, when they in fact had merely noted their existence. More to the point, the Stanford team did so after the election, not in some kind of smoke-filled room but in an academic report that is still publicly available and that DiResta has cited repeatedly.
Rogers also criticized another very public, not remotely secret report, written jointly by the United States, Britain, Canada, Germany, Slovakia, and the European Union, investigating “gendered disinformation,” a subject that sounds very “woke” until you realize that deepfake porn videos and orchestrated misogyny are tactics regularly used against female politicians such as Annalena Baerbock, a former German foreign minister, or Giorgia Meloni, the Italian prime minister. The Iranian regime uses them to harass female dissidents around the world. Democratic governments would be negligent if they did not try to understand them. But even if you are not bothered by the online harassment of women in politics, it’s still impossible to argue that the publication of a report (and its translation into nine languages) proves the existence of a secret censorship–industrial complex stifling Americans’ views. “Watergate it was not,” Orna Blum, a former State Department official, wrote last week.
And if the scandal wasn’t Watergate, Rogers is not Bob Woodward. She is a public servant who dumped raw data online, seemingly without asking whether anyone would be damaged or which American foreign-policy interests could be served, all in the name of proving nothing.
In the normal course of things the saga of the GEC documents would be, and should be, dismissed as a storm in a teapot. But unfortunately, the administration’s pursuit of a nonexistent censorship–industrial complex has already had real consequences for real people. In April 2025, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that he was closing the Global Engagement Center because it had “spent millions of dollars to actively silence and censor the voices of Americans they were supposed to be serving.” This was untrue, and even at the time there was no evidence for such an extraordinary statement. On the contrary, the GEC was the only institution in the U.S. government that was publicly tracking hostile international information operations, including by exposing websites in Africa or Latin America that appeared local but were in fact run by Moscow or Beijing. Rubio’s statement maligned the people who worked on these reports. Will the secretary of state now apologize to them? Compensate them? Rehire them?
The closing of the center also means that no one is now doing that work. Thanks to Rogers, Beattie, and a handful of others, the U.S. decided to blind itself to the reality that Russia, China, and Iran, with its viral animated Lego videos, all run deceptive campaigns that reach millions of people around the world. And now Americans do nothing to halt, explain, or counter them.
But it is not only American foreign policy that has been damaged. Following a series of expensive lawsuits as well as public harassment, Stanford shut down its internet-monitoring projects too. DiResta, one of the most prominent scholars in the field, left the university and was subjected to years of online harassment, an experience she has previously described in The Atlantic. Other research projects across the country also suffered, as funders and university provosts were, paradoxically, scared away by the Trump administration’s threats to curtail their free speech in the name of halting “censorship.”
The study of foreign online campaigns and the proliferation of conspiracy theories has now become difficult and controversial, for people both inside and outside the government. That doesn’t mean that these campaigns don’t exist. It just means that Americans don’t know about them, don’t understand them, and cannot track them.
As if this same conspiracy theory had not done enough damage, Rogers and others at the State Department are also putting the nonexistent censorship–industrial complex at the center of American foreign policy toward Europe now too. At a conference at the Hudson Institute last spring, Rogers said that a “censorship class” had already “scuttled to Europe” to pursue a supposed vendetta against Americans from across the ocean. At the same event, Senator Eric Schmitt of Missouri—who, in his previous role as the state’s attorney general, had brought one of the failed lawsuits against Stanford and supported legal challenges to the 2020 election—declared that “we are witnessing a deeply troubling assault on free speech” in Europe.
These views, all of which derive from the same set of false stories, are actively shaping American policy in Europe. Late last month, the State Department put forth plans to spend $4 million to support right-wing media in Europe, including a consortium of “independent journalists” who would support the Trump administration’s view of the world. In recent months, the U.S. has imposed visa restrictions on Thierry Breton, a former EU commissioner who is now a private citizen, for his role in creating the Digital Services Act, a European law designed to protect minors, provide transparency around algorithms and targeted advertising, and ensure that behavior on the internet conforms to existing legislation. The U.S. also sanctioned four European researchers who campaigned for the digital-services law or against hate speech—essentially punishing them for their free speech, in the name of promoting free speech. Two of them, the leaders of a German organization called HateAid, called the visa ban “an act of repression by a government that is increasingly disregarding the rule of law and trying to silence its critics by any means necessary.”
Belatedly, even some part of the Trump administration appears to have quietly concluded that all of this has gone too far and that maybe, in fact, it would be useful for the U.S. government to understand how hostile governments seek to manipulate the internet. In May, the State Department put out a tender for software developers who could help analyze “foreign adversarial propaganda” and thus replicate the work once done by the Global Engagement Center. In August, a State Department contractor also posted a job opening for research analysts who can, among other things, “evaluate how foreign governments, state-sponsored organizations, terrorist groups, and other malign actors use social media and digital communications to influence public opinion and targeted audiences.”
As DiResta wrote this week, “they’re hiring people to do the very job they just spent 16 months claiming was a conspiracy.” So much time, energy, and money was wasted pursuing a fiction. Now more time, energy, and money will need to be spent to clean up the damage.

Olympic and world champion long jumper Tara Davis-Woodhall has cast doubt over her participation at next week’s inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship after a head-on car crash left her with severe concussion.
“Unfortunately, I’m in a down right now,” the American told journalists on Wednesday.
“I was just involved in a car accident and have not been able to practise. It was a head-on collision, so dealing with some things.
“I went through something that’s unfortunate and now I’m trying to figure out what I can do to get myself back on the horse.”
Davis-Woodhall revealed that she did not sustain any life-threatening injuries, with both cars travelling at an estimated 20mph (32km/h) and both written off.
“I have a severe concussion. I don’t know where my head’s at right now. I’m just making it day by day. I haven’t trained at all due to it.”
Davis-Woodhall confirmed that she was a doubt for the September 11-13 Ultimate Championship in Budapest.
“At this point I’m working with my team and doctors to get healthy, but I’m not sure if I will be ready to compete at Ultimate Championship next week,” she explained.
“It’s really unfortunate timing. I’m at the peak of my training right now. I’m as fast as I’ve ever been. I’m as strong as I’ve ever been, so this decision is very difficult for me.”
The 27-year-old clinched gold in women’s long jump at the 2024 Paris Olympics and at the 2025 World Championships.
