Ekomie started his professional career with Bordeaux but secured a switch to top-flight side Angers in the summer of 2024.
He made 21 appearances across all competitions in his debut season for the club, and his impact increased last term.
The 23-year-old featured in all but two of his side's Ligue 1 matches in 2025-26 - with 25 of his 32 league appearances being starts.
On Ekomie's signing, manager Parkinson said: "We're very pleased to sign Jacques. It's a transfer we worked very hard on.
"Jacques is a good young player and we're looking forward to integrating him into the group."
Ahead of his side's 1-1 draw with Watford, Wrexham manager Parkinson stated deals for various players to join the Red Dragons had fallen through in what had been a "difficult window".
But speaking in his post-match press conference after the Championship contest with the Hornets, the boss said there were "no guarantees" that Wrexham would further bolster their squad prior to the 23:00 BST transfer deadline on 1 September.
Midfielder George Thomason has operated as a makeshift wing-back in the absence of Cacace - who started just eight of Wrexham's 46 league games last season.
Cacace has missed all three of the Red Dragons' matches across all competitions so far this season and still has two years left to run on his contract at the Racecourse Ground.
Wrexham could yet add to their midfield and forward options in the final stages of the summer window.
Parkinson's men return to action against Birmingham City at the Racecourse Ground on Friday night (20:00 BST).

A six-year-old boy died from scurvy, the so‑called “sailor’s disease” common in the convict era, a coroner has found.
Brisbane boy Connor Dean died after a cardiac arrest under general anaesthetic at Queensland Children’s hospital in 2024.
Deputy state coroner Stephanie Gallagher released her findings last month, ruling his fatal brain damage was most likely triggered by vitamin C deficiency and scurvy.
“Although the precise mechanism leading to the cardiac arrest could not be definitively determined, the treating clinicians and forensic pathologist considered vitamin C deficiency to be the most likely underlying factor,” she determined.
Issues with an unnamed multivitamin were also canvassed in the inquest.
Scurvy was once common among sailors and convicts who went without fresh fruit and vegetables on long sea voyages.
However, it is now so rare in Australia that serious cases are almost always found and treated.
Connor had Down syndrome, was born with a serious heart defect that was repaired in 2018, and had delayed development, speaking mostly in single words and walking with a wide‑based gait.
In July 2024, he went to his GP, with his parents reporting he had knee pain and was limping.
He was admitted to Queensland Children’s hospital on 18 July, with X‑rays and MRIs failing to show a clear cause.
He then developed a bad cough and tested positive for parainfluenza as his oxygen levels and kidney function worsened.
He suffered a cardiac arrest after being given general anaesthetic and died on 10 August.
Scans of his skeleton later showed bone changes “in keeping with scurvy”.
Blood tests revealed a vitamin C level of less than 1 micromole a litre, compared with a normal range of 20 to 120 micromoles a litre.
He was also low in vitamins A and E, had borderline low vitamin D and blood‑clotting problems that suggested vitamin K (potassium) deficiency.
His paediatrician told the court he and dieticians had longstanding concerns about the boy’s growth, with his height and weight well below the usual range, even for children with Down syndrome.
“He was reported to have become very fussy with his intake and his diet was said to contain no fruit or vegetables at that time,” the paediatrician said.
“He had only gained 300 grams in the last 11 months.”
Connor was prescribed multivitamins.
However, during his final admission, doctors found the multivitamin the family was using, known in the findings only as “the Product”, did not contain vitamin C.
“I am concerned that a product such as (the Product) is available in Australia. I believe that it is misleading to call this product a multivitamin when it misses essential vitamins such as vitamin C,” the paediatrician said.
“It is my clinical opinion that Connor would not have had vitamin C deficiency, and the clinical features of scurvy that led to his death, if he had been taking a different multivitamin that contained vitamin C.”
The multivitamin’s manufacturer offered “sincere condolences” but rejected the paediatrician’s criticism and said there was “no basis on which to draw the conclusion that [its multivitamin] has contributed to Connor’s death”.
The coroner agreed there was not enough evidence to say the multivitamin caused or contributed to the death.
Instead, she focused on the failure to detect Connor’s severe vitamin C deficiency in time.

The EPA classified trifludimoxazin as having "suggestive evidence of carcinogenic potential," which essentially means that while there is evidence the chemical could potentially be one that causes cancer, there isn't enough data to say for sure. Additionally, the EPA does not consider trifludimoxazin a PFAS, though the intergovernmental Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development does.
In late summer 2026, some people on social media claimed that U.S. President Donald Trump's administration approved the use of a potentially carcinogenic pesticide that's a "forever chemical," also known as PFAS. PFAS, an abbreviation for perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances, are long-lasting chemicals that persistently remain in the environment, capable of accumulating in things like rivers, plants, animals and people's bodies, that often have harmful health effects on people, according to the Environmental Protection Agency.
For example, one Facebook post (archived) claimed that the EPA "just approved a carcinogenic herbicide called trifludimoxazin," to be used on crops including corn, wheat, oats, soybeans, peanuts, citrus fruits (including oranges), apples and tree nuts such as almonds. According to the post, environmental groups consider trifludimoxazin a PFAS pesticide and "forever chemical." 
The U.S. EPA just approved a carcinogenic herbicide called trifludimoxazin for agricultural use on a wide range of crops, including corn, wheat, oats, soybeans, peanuts, citrus fruits (including oranges), apples, and tree nuts such as almonds.
Trifludimoxazin is also considered by many environmental groups to be a PFAS pesticide because it contains highly fluorinated chemical structures and can break down into persistent fluorinated compounds - i.e. nature can't break it down properly as it's synthetic. Environmental organizations have described it as a "forever chemical" and have filed lawsuits challenging the EPA's approval.
Environmental groups have also pointed out that the company's own studies showed evidence suggesting cancer concerns and that the EPA downplayed those findings whe not was approved. The EPA claims the product is safe and that people shouldn't be concerned. Not a good look for MAHA.
Similar Facebook (archived) posts (archived) shared the same claims, which were also spread on X (archived) and Reddit (archived). Snopes readers searched the site and sent us emails asking if the rumor is true.
The Trump administration's EPA proposed approving trifludimoxazin in June 2025 and went through with the approval in June 2026. Researchers have found some evidence suggesting the chemical may be carcinogenic, but it's not a "known carcinogen" like some posts claim. Trifludimoxazin is a PFAS as defined by the intergovernmental Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, although not as defined by the more narrow EPA definition.
Trifludimoxazin is a pesticide, specifically an herbicide, that kills certain broad-leafed plants and grass weed species at agricultural sites farming "row crops (e.g., cereal grains, legumes, soybean) and tree orchards and groves (citrus, pome fruits, and tree nuts)," according to the EPA (PDF Page 6).
This wasn't the first time the EPA has tried to approve trifludimoxazin. In 2021, while Joe Biden was president, the EPA approved pesticide products containing trifludimoxazin, however; this approval was halted by lawsuits filed by environmental groups. The EPA then changed rules to require further EPA assessments before approving a new pesticide, and, ultimately, the makers of trifludimoxazin dropped their request for approval at the time.
The same environmental groups are attempting to halt the new approval for trifludimoxazin through lawsuits, as they did previously.
Potential carcinogen
The EPA did find evidence suggesting trifludimoxazin could possibly be carcinogenic, although it did not do enough research to confirm with certainty whether the chemical is carcinogenic.
In one study of rat carcinogenicity through chronic dietary exposure (PDF Page 8), the EPA found "suggestive evidence of carcinogenic potential." According to the EPA, such a classification means that the data raises a concern that the chemical has "potential carcinogenic effects in humans," but the EPA has determined the data is "not sufficient for a stronger conclusion."
Trifludimoxazin's entry on the pesticides properties database maintained by the U.K.-based University of Hertfordshire says that the chemical is "known not to cause a problem" as a carcinogen. The entry does report that trifludimoxazin is a potential liver toxicant, though. The database also notes "no serious health implications have been identified" with trifludimoxazin.
So while trifludimoxazin could potentially be a carcinogen, there currently isn't enough evidence to say with certainty that the chemical causes cancer.
Forever chemical
There are at least three definitions of PFAS, according to a 2022 paper in the peer-reviewed journal Digital Discovery: a broader definition from the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development that is widely used internationally, a narrower definition used by the EPA and a definition that is a compromise between the two other definitions.
The University of Hertfordshire's database also classifies trifludimoxazin as a PFAS.
Where else has it been approved?
According to the University of Hertfordshire's database, trifludimoxazin has not been approved for use in the United Kingdom or the European Union as a whole. However, each individual state within the European Union has approved the pesticide for use in their individual countries. It has also been approved for use in Canada.
For further reading, Snopes has previously fact-checked claims about potentially toxic chemicals, including a claim about the use of paraquat by the parent company of the pomegranate juice brand Pom Wonderful.

India has been named the host of the inaugural Women’s Champions Trophy, ICC announced on Wednesday.
The Brabourne Stadium in Mumbai and the Vadodara International Cricket Stadium will host the T20 tournament, from February 14 to 28.
Missing from the host roster is the D.Y. Patil Stadium in Navi Mumbai, a popular women’s cricket venue in the country, and even one that the players of the national side have deemed the spiritual home of the women’s game in India.
The D.Y. Patil, a privately-owned venue within the D.Y. Patil University campus, was also the venue of India’s famous triumph in the Women’s ODI World Cup in 2025, where India beat South Africa in a high-octane and well-attended final. It is also a popular host in the Women’s Premier League, India’s top flight women’s franchise tournament.
ALSO READ | From Motibaug to Kotambi: Vadodara’s cricket passion finds a new home
D.Y. Patil earns NGT ire
During the conduct of the Indian Premier League’s 2026 edition, the National Green Tribunal (NGT) issued notices to six mainstream cricket stadiums and their respective associations raising concerns about sustainable use of water to maintain grounds and facilities.
The NGT bench comprised of chairperson Justice Prakash Shrivastava and expert members A Senthil Vel and Afroz Ahmad who passed the order on April 16, directing cricket associations to regular groundwater extraction and put in place rainwater harvesting for maintaining pitches. Even installations of sewage treatment plants were taken into consideration at venues where rainwater harvesting might not entirely be feasible for operations as a primary way.
The six stadiums in the firing line were Arun Jaitley Stadium in New Delhi, Sawai Mansingh Stadium in Jaipur, Shaheed Veer Narayan Singh International Stadium in Raipur, Dr. DY Patil stadium in Navi Mumbai, Bharat Ratna Shri Atal Bihari Vajpayee Ekana Cricket Stadium in Lucknow, Rajiv Gandhi International Stadium in Hyderabad and Barabati Stadium in Cuttack.
“In such a background, the submission of counsel for the applicant is that all the activities in these six stadiums should be completely stopped and they should not be allowed to carry out any sports activity therein,” the NGT noted in its order.
The tribunal had also questioned why sporting activities shouldn’t be stopped for failing to furnish disclosures to the Central Ground Water Authority (CGWA).
It is unclear if this is why the venue has dropped off the radar for the prestigious Champions Trophy, but the stadium faces the question of receiving clearance for further sporting activity to happen at the premises.
Neither the ICC nor the BCCI has addressed reporters explaining the choice of venues or why D.Y. Patil Stadium has failed to make the cut.
The BCCI’s rotation policy for venues, which seeks to give more venues a chance to host marquee games, might have worked in favour of the Brabourne Stadium in Churchgate. This is also frequently used to stage WPL games across its four editions. CCI president Madhumati Lele Shrivastava was a member or the WPL Governing Council as well.
The Vadodara International Cricket Stadium, inaugurated in December 2024, has also found favour as a venue for women’s cricket fixtures in India from bilaterals to the WPL. Indian Olympic Association CEO Raghuram Iyer had even hinted at the city, 100km away from 2030 Commonwealth Games host city Ahmedabad, being considered to stage the cricket events of that edition.

Generative AI has been suspended by New York City's schools.
The city's Department of Education imposed a one-year moratorium on the use of AI by students in elementary and middle school classrooms, officials said on Wednesday.
High school students, meanwhile, will take two "AI literacy courses" each year and will have access to AI programs in specific educational contexts, said the city's schools chancellor, Kamar Samuels.
"The tech industry wants us to believe that AI in early education is not only inevitable, but that it is necessary," Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at a press conference in Brooklyn. "We do not see it that way."
Under the new guidelines, generative AI programs will be either blocked or deleted from school software. Ailish Brady, an education advisor in the mayor's office, said the city would disable AI features in 38 previously approved educational programs or stop using products whose AI features can't be turned off.
The policy also sets daily limits on personal device screen time for children — 30 minutes for kids in third through fifth grade, and 45 minutes for middle school students, Samuels said.
The AI ban will impact about 600,000 students, about two-thirds of the school system's student population, which is the largest in the country.
Mamdani said school officials will evaluate the policy's effectiveness and results after the 2026-2027 school year. He drew a distinction between younger students and high schoolers, who he said need to be prepared for a world increasingly shaped by AI.
"Whether we like it or not, our teenagers are growing up in an AI-saturated world. We cannot pretend that that world does not exist," he said. "It would be irresponsible not to prepare our children for the fast-evolving technological future that lies ahead."
The high school AI literacy courses are meant to help students "think critically about AI before they begin to rely on it," according to a press release announcing the policy.
"The two 45-minute modules will introduce students to what AI is and is not, as well as AI-related bias, risks, ethical considerations and impacts on careers and future skills."
AI modules permitted for high school use do not include chatbots, officials said. The modules are designed for specific subjects, and each has strict time limits.
Quill, for example, is a program designed for use in English classes to support text analysis. Students can use the program for only 15 minutes each week, according to the policy.
New York City's AI pause for schools comes amid a public reckoning over how best to expose children to generative AI, as educators across the country bemoan how students are using the technology to cheat on assignments and parents petition for more restrictions.
The AIM Coalition, a group of parents, teachers, and activists in New York, has called on the city to institute a two-year AI moratorium in public schools.
In a press release issued Wednesday, the group said the new restrictions are a "step in the right direction," but added that "broad exceptions leave students at risk."
"Teachers' use of AI and high school pilots will still leave parents with little ability to keep their child out of such programs," said Marina Marcou-O'Malley, a director of an educational reform group in New York.
In March, the city's school system released guidance for the use of AI in classrooms. Those guidelines permitted students to use AI for research, exploration, and creative projects, provided its use was age-appropriate and guided by educators.
Officials said on Wednesday that the new moratorium was informed by feedback from students and teachers. Mamdani said the ban is the most "comprehensive of its kind anywhere in the country."
Microsoft, which in 2023 announced a partnership with New York City Public Schools "to support their exploration of the development of generative AI tools," did not respond to a request for comment on Wednesday.
When reached by Business Insider on Wednesday, OpenAI did not comment directly on Mamdani's moratorium. The company said it works with educators and school districts to discern where guardrails are needed in its educational platforms.
Under the new policy, teachers are allowed to use AI for lesson planning and "operational tasks," officials said.
"This moratorium is a commitment to getting the future right," Mamdani said.

Long past his sexually explicit enfant terrible mumblecore origins, writer-director Joe Swanberg continues his ongoing experiments in honoring the romantic comedy’s conventional satisfactions while expanding its sexual parameters with “The Sun Never Sets.” Wendy (Dakota Fanning) has been dating sedate single dad Jack (Swanberg regular Jake Johnson) for two years. When he decides they should take a break so that Wendy can see other people and make absolutely sure she’s happy in their relationship, a love triangle is sparked. Both bizarre and boring, it’s definitely a signature Swanberg product: performance-driven, sexually (at least putatively) adventurous, full of craft beer.
In drone shots scored to generic indie-pop, Wendy (Dakota Fanning) drives into town, looking vaguely wistful under opening credits — so far, so romcom. But she’s not on the right heterosexual track to marriage and children, which particularly rankles after bestie Lindsay (Debby Ryan) announces she’s pregnant. With two kids and an ex-wife, Jack has no desire for more children or another marriage, but senses that Wendy might come to resent him for denying her both. So, he proposes she take six months off for her to see what else is out there; very reluctantly, she accepts.
Popular on Variety
Jack’s unnamed best friend (Lamorne Morris, popping in for a “New Girl” cameo reunion with his old castmate via Zoom) tells him the plan is half-baked, but Jack is unconcerned because he’s in Anchorage rather than his former base of New York City: “It’s a bunch of sweaty guys who smell like salmon. I’m not worried about it.” Mistake! Wendy immediately runs into old flame Chuck (Cory Michael Smith), who literally just got back to town the day before and, no longer a bad boy, begins by proposing marriage and seven children. The man who won’t change anything versus the man who’ll immediately change everything — descriptions that first apply to one character, then another, as Jack becomes desperate to win Wendy back while Chuck’s immature cracks emerge, leaving the lead with two theoretically equally red-flag choices at all times.
Scenery and single salmon joke aside, “Sun” doesn’t particularly show off its novel setting, unfolding in interiors proving Anchorage can be just as generic as any other American city: one of Swanberg’s beloved craft beer bars, a dive bar on trivia night, an art gallery for local painters, spacious suburban kitchens, less tony apartment complexes. Within these confines the main characters register as aliens; Wendy and Jack aren’t just flustered but people who seem to have never been inculcated with a rudimentary sense of social propriety. For example, Wendy is on a bar date she didn’t want to go on when she runs into Chuck, immediately sending the other guy packing; her decision is mirrored later when Jack also splits with his date Sara (Karley Sciortino) in a different bar after running into Wendy. Here, Sara finally raises her voice to express bafflement: “Is this a bit?”
The otherwise strangely becalmed register might make more sense if the protagonists were conceived as unflappable sociopaths, but the film’s theoretical naturalism heightens the inadvertent strangeness of watching people put other through so many stress positions while keeping their voices and mannerisms calm and level. That disjuncture could work if the film were stylized in some way to indicate that we’re operating in a realm of heightened emotional logic, rather than the familiar world of naturalism.
But despite shooting on 35mm, Swanberg continues to pursue a visually inconspicuous style that’s complementarily but counterproductively in line with the performance style. This is a film about difficult people in self-made traps — not unlike the willfully abrasive performers in the work of one of Swanberg’s admitted inspirations, Maurice Pialat, who understood the dramatic importance of externalized volatility to drive his emotionally bruising scenarios. Here, everyone both behind and in front of the camera seems a little too concerned with remaining likable and smooth on the surface. Like its protagonists, “The Sun Don’t Shine” wants to, but can’t, have it all.

Trump Meant It Literally When He Said He Was Taking the Oil
The Venezuela operation is the purest distillation of his amoral foreign policy.
“We’re going to be taking out a tremendous amount of wealth out of the ground,” Donald Trump said when he announced the capture of the Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro in January. And lo and behold, it has come to pass.
Trump announced last week that he had made a deal with Venezuela to develop its oil reserves. Well, not so much a “deal” as a payment by Venezuela of tribute at gunpoint. In a social-media post, Trump announced that the oil “is a Gift from Venezuela to the People of the United States.” This is a surprisingly generous offer from a country that is much poorer than the United States and, like most countries, disinclined to hand over its wealth to foreigners as a present.
Venezuela’s elected representatives did not approve this deal, because Venezuela’s representatives have not in fact been elected. The country also did not hold a referendum to approve it. Instead, after capturing Maduro, whom Trump had accurately denounced as a dictator, Trump installed one of Maduro’s cronies, Delcy Rodríguez, to govern in his place, in which capacity she has displayed roughly the same level of respect for democratic norms and civil society as her predecessor.
Trump’s Venezuelan-oil heist has received far less attention than either his ballyhooed promise to avoid foreign wars or his ongoing quagmire in the Persian Gulf. Yet this operation reflects Trump’s foreign-policy instincts in their most nakedly amoral—which is to say, quintessential—form.
The Trump administration laid the groundwork for its intervention by painting Maduro not only as a despot but also as the leader of a criminal syndicate. The Justice Department indicted Maduro and his allies for having “acted as leaders and managers of the Cartel de Los Soles,” a derisive nickname for the country’s kleptocratic rulers.
Trump, however, apparently viewed regime change as a way to exploit this arrangement rather than transform it. His invasion followed the logic not of an American president promoting democracy or regional security, but of a mobster angry to discover that a small-time crook is running a racket in his territory without giving him a taste.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, The New York Times reported in July, “has become the de facto viceroy of Venezuela, holding sway over a sovereign nation in a way that no American official has since L. Paul Bremer III arrived in Baghdad in 2003 to run U.S.-occupied Iraq.” A salient difference is that Bremer’s occupation was intended to establish the grounds for free and fair elections, which did eventually take place. Trump, in stark contrast, casually told the Times in January that he expects the United States to run Venezuela for years.
The new oil deal makes that outcome more necessary and therefore more likely. Rodríguez has tied herself to a policy that is toxic to both the left and the right sides of Venezuela’s political spectrum. Left-wing Chavismos despise foreign exploitation, and the opposition resents the Chavismos’ corruption. Exposing Rodríguez’s regime to free and fair elections creates a high risk of electing a government dedicated to unwinding Trump’s deal, which gives both her and Trump a strong motive to postpone such voting.
When Trump deposed Maduro, some right-of-center analysts credited him with taking the first step in what they imagined would be a democratization project. The Wall Street Journal’s editorial board celebrated the capture as “an act of hemispheric hygiene against a dictator who spread mayhem far and wide,” as did The Washington Post’s (headline: “Justice in Venezuela.”)
Both editorials mixed praise for the operation with caveats that the important work of transitioning to a legitimate government lay ahead, while fretting that Trump was confusing the issue with loose talk about running the country and extracting its oil. “The president often shoots from his hip in these press conferences and would be wise to reconsider,” the Post proposed. “Mr. Trump also talked about ‘the oil’ far too much,” the Journal cautioned, adding, “Sooner rather than later, Venezuela needs another election.”
It all sounded a bit like congratulating Michael Corleone for taking a stand against organized crime by murdering the heads of the Five Families, while urging him to clarify his intent to focus the family business on selling olive oil at market price.
Venezuela’s constitution expressly prohibits the sale of its untapped oil reserves to foreign interests. But Trump’s oil deal is designed to survive democratic scrutiny. Its “structure was deliberately intended to bind future Venezuelan governments to the agreement and make it difficult to unwind,” as The Wall Street Journal characterized the explanation given by a source involved in the deal. The Journal’s reporting suggests that Trump’s Venezuelan partners may not hold the highest regard for legal niceties. Alejandro Betancourt, the Venezuelan businessman who leads the private company partnering with the Trump administration, has been investigated for, though not charged with, money laundering. Diego Arria, a former Venezuelan ambassador now in exile in the U.S., told the Journal that the U.S. is working with Venezuelan government figures who are wanted in the U.S. for drug trafficking and other crimes.
They are, in other words, Trump’s kind of partners. The president seems to despise democratically elected leaders (witness his current tantrum against Canada’s prime minister, or his yearslong feuding with South Korea, the European Union, and other erstwhile U.S. allies). He has always gotten along swimmingly with criminals (since his early days engaging in social and business dealings with mobsters in New York) and dictators (such as Vladimir Putin, whom he simply cannot quit). Trump’s favorite brand of partner combines disdain for the law and democratic norms with an absolute dependence on Trump.
Trump has been saying for years that a vital objective in any foreign conflict is to seize the enemy’s oil. Indeed, he has been saying for years that he has been saying this for years. “I’ve been saying it for years. Take the oil,” he told The New York Times in 2016.
Trump has shown time and again that his obsessions, even his most childish and comically sinister-sounding ones, are often quite earnest. In Venezuela, he is finally fulfilling a lifelong scheme.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.
Read Press Release: WHO and King Salman Humanitarian Aid & Relief Centre expand life-saving health interventions with new agreements at Riyadh Humanitarian Forum
UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.
Read Press Release: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia confirms US$ 500 million commitment to global polio eradication effort
The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum 2025 was a significant event that underscored the continued partnership between WHO and KSrelief, as well as with other international partners to address critical humanitarian health crises. The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

Russian drones tore into central Kyiv on Wednesday, wounding 11 people on the seventh day running of attacks.

Germany blames Moscow for the attack.

Russia claims to hit ships supplying weapons for Ukrainian war effort
Russian forces struck two cargo vessels on Wednesday, one in Ukraine's port of Chornomorsk and another in the Black Sea, Russia's Defence Ministry said.
The ministry said the vessels were transporting weapons and ammunition for the Ukrainian military.
It also said Russian forces struck three logistics centres in the Kyiv region and port infrastructure in Odesa. Reuters could not independently verify the ministry's assertions.
On the ground: Russia attacks Kyiv for a seventh consecutive day
Russian drones tore into central Kyiv on Wednesday morning, wounding 11 people and damaging residential and university buildings on the seventh day of nearly round-the-clock attacks that have upended daily life in the city.
The attack on a downtown university took place while students were in class, forcing some 160 to seek shelter, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
Two people were also killed and eight wounded in Russian strikes on the southeastern city of Dnipro, the regional governor said, where food warehouses and educational buildings were damaged.
It came as Ukraine braces for a new season of Russian strikes on energy infrastructure, amid a critical shortage of US-designed missile interceptors needed to down Moscow's ballistic missiles.
Earlier on Wednesday, Russia struck power facilities in the southern Odesa region with missiles and drones, authorities said, knocking out power to more than 350,000 homes.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said late on Tuesday he had ordered his forces to prepare the new campaign of "massive" strikes.
"Unfortunately, there has been far too little response from the world and its most influential leaders to this latest Russian escalation of strikes," Zelensky wrote on X.
Ukraine is finalising drone deal with Germany, Zelenskiy says
Ukraine is finalising a drone deal with Germany, president Volodymyr Zelensky said on Wednesday after a call with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
The agreement — proposed by Ukraine several months ago — is expected to cover the joint development of various types of drones, missiles and related software.
“Our teams are already finalising the text of the drone deal, and this will, among other things, definitely provide both Germany and Ukraine with additional defence capabilities,” Zelensky said on the Telegram app.
The deal will build on existing German-Ukrainian defence cooperation, including a multi-million-euro programme to supply to Kyiv some 15,000 Strila interceptor drones designed to counter Shahed-type attack drones.
Russia vows to fend off disruption to civil aviation after Ukraine's threats
Russia vowed to head off any disruption to civil aviation on Wednesday after Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenksy said that Kyiv’s drones had made Russian airspace dangerous to use.
Zelensky warned airlines and insurance firms on Tuesday that the presence of Ukrainian drones as it responded to Russian attacks meant “the war started by Russia is closing its own skies”. He said he was not targeting civil aviation.
And Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said on Wednesday the country had also officially notified the International Civil Aviation Organization that Russian airspace was not safe.
While European and US carriers do not fly over Russia due to the war that erupted when Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, the airspace is used by other airlines from countries such as China, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates and other Gulf states.
"We are working in close contact with the Ministry of Defence and the Russian National Guard. And I believe that we will not allow any significant disruption to civil aviation,” said Russian transport minister Andrei Nikitin.
On Wednesday, Flightradar24 data showed disruptions at Moscow's main airport, while some airlines cancelled flights though they did not specify the reason for doing so.

Masked men ransack, loot TMC leader Abhishek Banerjee’s office in Kolkata
TMC lawmaker Abhishek Banerjee alleged that police did not respond for at least two hours and blamed the ruling BJP for the attack
A group of armed masked men ransacked and looted Trinamool Congress (TMC) lawmaker Abhishek Banerjee’s office on Kolkata’s Camac Street in the early hours of Thursday. Banerjee called the attack outrageous, unacceptable, and a disgraceful assault on the rule of law. He alleged that police did not respond to calls and emails for at least two hours and blamed the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) for the attack.
“At around 4.30 am, BJP hooligans, armed with weapons, stormed our party office in the heart of Kolkata. They attacked our people, snatched their phones, smashed furniture, ransacked the premises and destroyed electronic equipment,” Banerjee wrote on X.
Banerjee, nephew of former chief minister Mamata Banerjee, posted a video on X, purportedly showing men wearing masks and helmets fleeing with what appeared to be monitors and smart television sets. Some of the attackers could be seen carrying two smart televisions and other gadgets at a time. A second video showed the ransacked office, shattered glass, broken furniture, and damaged electronic gadgets.
“This is what the BJP has done to my party office in the early hours of this morning. Will the Governor of WB [West Bengal] act? Will the Union Home Minister act? Will the PMO [Prime Minister’s Office] act? Or will they continue to look the other way? It is high time the judiciary, particularly the Calcutta High Court, takes serious note of what is happening and acts to uphold the rule of law in West Bengal,” Banerjee wrote.
Police said an investigation has started and they have detained some people for questioning.
BJP legislator Sajal Ghosh denied the charges of the ruling party’s involvement in the attack, saying it was part of Abhishek Banerjee’s attempt to stay relevant.
“...the BJP is in no way associated with this attack. The people of Bengal have discarded the TMC and voted for the BJP with a huge mandate. He [Abhishek Banerjee] is trying to stay afloat and politically relevant. That is why he is making such allegations. What were his workers doing in the office at that time?” Ghosh asked.
On August 27, the Kolkata Municipal Corporation removed an allegedly unauthorised TMC billboard from the building where Abhishek Banerjee’s office is located. This week, a team from the fire department audited the office. A case was registered against Abhishek Banerjee, and police on Tuesday questioned him in connection with a clash between his supporters and government officials who removed the billboard.

Tiger Woods had his driver’s licence suspended for five years on Wednesday after reaching a plea agreement in a case stemming from a rollover car crash in Florida in March.
The 50-year-old golf superstar pleaded no contest to lesser charges of careless and reckless driving, while the more serious DUI charge he initially faced was dropped under the agreement.
During a brief livestreamed hearing at the Martin County Courthouse in Stuart, Florida, Judge Darren Steele warned Woods about the consequences of driving during the suspension.
“If you were to drive for any reason at all you would go immediately back to jail,” Steele told Woods.
Tiger Woods Florida crash
Woods was involved in a road accident on March 27 near his home on Jupiter Island, Florida. His SUV clipped a truck pulling a trailer and overturned while he was attempting to pass on a residential road.
Authorities determined that Woods had not been drinking alcohol but said he appeared to be impaired. Investigators found two pills containing hydrocodone, an opioid painkiller, in his possession.
Woods initially pleaded not guilty to charges of DUI with property damage and refusing to submit to a lawful test. He told authorities that he had been looking at his phone and changing radio channels when the crash occurred.
He was subsequently jailed and released on bond.
DUI charge dropped under plea agreement
The DUI allegation was ultimately dropped as part of the plea agreement, with Woods agreeing to plead no contest to the lesser driving charges.
The case comes after a series of serious health issues for the 15-time major champion. Woods has undergone multiple back operations and suffered severe leg injuries in a 2021 car crash in California.
Following the March accident, Woods said he was “stepping away” to seek treatment and focus on his health. He later travelled outside the United States for treatment at an inpatient facility, reportedly in Switzerland.
Woods returns to public spotlight
Woods made his first public appearance since his arrest at the PGA Tour’s Travelers Championship in June, where he introduced PGA Tour Chief Executive Brian Rolapp.
Rolapp announced a new competitive structure for the PGA Tour that is scheduled to take effect in 2028.

Britain's Matthew Brennan sprinted to his third win at the 2026 Vuelta a Espana on Wednesday has he powered to victory on stage 11.
The 21-year-old Visma-Lease a Bike rider easily held off Frenchman Bryan Coquard and Belgium's Jordi Meeus at the climax of the 153.8km route from Cartagena to Lorca.

Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) Chairman Mohsin Naqvi has defended the major changes made to 
Pakistan
’s Test squad during the ongoing England series, saying the decisions were "essential".
Pakistan made sweeping changes before the third and final Test against England, scheduled to begin on September 9.
The move came after Pakistan lost the first two Tests heavily, with England taking an unassailable 2-0 lead. Pakistan lost the first Test by an innings, while the second ended in a 194-run defeat.
Naqvi responds to criticism
The changes have drawn strong criticism from former Pakistan cricketers, fans and analysts. However, Naqvi said he was not concerned by the backlash and maintained that the decisions during the England tour were necessary.
He said he was also examining issues beyond the team's poor performances but believed it was not the right time to discuss matters unrelated to cricket. While acknowledging Pakistan’s disappointing Test results, Naqvi pointed to improvements in the team’s white-ball cricket during his tenure.
"I have never been afraid of criticism, and I never will be. Those who say cricket has been destroyed since I came - look at what the rankings were before," he said as quoted by Geo News.
Major changes to Test squad
Following the second loss, the PCB released seven players from the squad: Mohammad Rizwan, Imam-ul-Haq, Salman Agha, Ali Usman, Aamer Jamal, Awais Zafar and Khurram Shahzad.
The board replaced them with five uncapped players, along with Saim Ayub and Abdullah Fazal, who together have only 10 matches of experience. The new players include Arafat Minhas, Mohammad Imran Jnr, Saad Baig, Mohammad Imran Randhawa and Razaullah.
The PCB also made changes to the coaching staff, bringing in Mike Hesson as head coach and Ashley Noffke as bowling coach. Both are already part of Pakistan’s white-ball coaching set-up. Sarfaraz Ahmed and Umar Gul were released from their respective coaching roles.

Orangutans in danger as wildfires blaze through Borneo
A weak orangutan was found laying on the ground in Ketapang, West Kalimantan on Borneo island.
Indonesia has intensified efforts to contain haze from wildfires across six provinces in Borneo and Sumatra islands.
The wildfires have destroyed part of the habitat of hundreds of orangutans and risking the survival of the species.
"The situation is quite critical", said Karmele Llano Sanchez, CEO of the wildlife foundation Yayasan Inisiasi Alam Rehabilitasi Indonesia (YIARI).
Sanchez said the fires are "leaving [the orangutans] without any food or water".
The orangutan found will be moved to a rehabilitation centre to get more treatment and will be released back into the wild after recovery, according to YIARI.

Teams will race to navigate three of the planet’s most unforgiving landscapes — the jungle, the desert, and the Arctic — using Gemini to help them identify dangers, survive brutal weather changes, and stay one step ahead.
Google says Donaldson will also use a Fitbit Air in one of his upcoming challenges and appear in a Gemini campaign from Google. The deal comes a couple of months after Donaldson’s YouTube channel became the first to hit 500 million subscribers, and a recent Bloomberg report saying YouTube has been offering prominent creators deals to keep their content exclusive to its site as more creators strike deals with Netflix.

New Delhi: Former Chief Economic Adviser Krishnamurthy V Subramanian has defended India’s 7.8% GDP growth in the April-June 2026 quarter, rejecting questions over the credibility of the numbers and backing the methodology used to calculate them.
Subramanian said India had shifted to the “cutting edge methodology of the double deflator”, which separately adjusts the prices of inputs and outputs while calculating real economic growth.
Khichdi Example Explains GDP Method
Using khichdi as an example, Subramanian explained how the method works when the prices of the final product and its ingredients rise at different rates.
“So think about just a simple example. Let's say I make Khichdi and I sell Khichdi. To make Khichdi, I need to use rice and lentils,” he said.
Explaining further, he said, “So, you know, the double deflator is actually you deflate the output at the price level, change in the price level of the output, and you deflate the input at the price level of the input so that you get, arrive at real quantities, and then you do arithmetic with the real quantities.”
Investment Shows Momentum
Subramanian also rejected concerns that investment indicators were failing to keep pace with GDP growth.
“This year, if you see Q1, the gross fixed capital formation, which is basically technical jargon for investment in the economy, has grown by 12 per cent,” he said.
He added that private capital expenditure by listed companies grew 11%, bank credit expanded about 20%, while the IIP for capital goods increased more than 15%.
However, Subramanian acknowledged concerns around job creation.
“That said, though, and I think this is something which we have to acknowledge, that overall, you know, the rate of employment creation, especially in the formal sector, you know, is actually not as high as the GDP growth,” he said.

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) on Friday (August 28, 2026) submitted in the Supreme Court a proposal to provide information relating to added sugar, fat and salt in pictorial form on the front-of-pack (FOP) of food products, in line with international regulations.
“The proposal is intended to provide a simple, prominent and easily comprehensible warning to consumers regarding food products which are high in specified nutrients of concern,” an FSSAI affidavit filed in the Supreme Court said.
The affidavit proposes an FOP warning label in red hexagonal shape for food products which are high in any two or more “nutrients of concern” such as added saturated fat, added sugar and salt, based on thresholds specified under the Dietary Guidelines for Indians 2024.
The warning label would read ‘High Fat’, ‘High Sugar’, ‘High Salt’ or ‘Highly Sweetened Beverage’ and be displayed in a font one point larger than that used in the nutrition information table on the back of the pack to help customers readily identify at-risk foods.
The FSSAI said single-ingredient food products and those which are “inherently rich in fat, sugar or salt, like ghee, edible oil, jaggery, honey” are proposed to be exempted from FOP warning requirement.
Phased implementation
The affidavit said the FOP labelling mechanism is intended to be implemented in phases to “facilitate consumer acceptability and provide industry adequate time for reformulation”.
Phase I would cover products high in two or more specified nutrients and specified sweetened beverages. Phase II would extend the warning mechanism to products high in any one of these nutrients.
The affidavit in the Supreme Court came in a petition filed by NGO, 3S and Our Health Society, represented by advocate Rajiv Shankar Dvivedi. Mr. Dvivedi said the NGO would file a comprehensive rejoinder to the FSSAI’s compliance affidavit in the apex court after inviting public comments.
The compliance affidavit by the food regulator follows scathing comments on August 13 from a Bench headed by Justice J.B. Pardiwala on the state’s obligations to protect public health. The court had observed that not only developed but even developing countries were adopting international standards of packaging food products.
Bringing awareness
“A positive step in that direction would further accelerate our country’s endeavour to be fully developed, by bringing awareness to the public in general of the ill-effects, emanating even from indigenous foods, despite our conviction that indigenous foods coming from diverse cultures in this country were never intended to be packaged,” the court had recorded in its August 13 order.
The court had noted that the Economic Survey has already suggested FOP labelling, and the Union government would not have any impediments in implementing the changes.
“We are doing this in public interest. Keep it in mind,” Justice Pardiwala had addressed the government on August 13.

- The claim that U.S. President Donald Trump diverted 300 first responders to work on his Washington, D.C., beautification projects, thus making those workers unavailable for immediate rescue efforts in the aftermath of the Aug. 29, 2026, Grand Canyon National Park flash floods, is unproven.
- The rumor stemmed in part from users sharing a Sept. 1 article from the online publication The Lever, which reported, "Trump reassigned 300 National Park Service emergency responders to golf course and reflecting-pool renovations before the Grand Canyon flooded."
- The Lever cited a CNN article published days before the flooding reporting hundreds of NPS first responders were reassigned without saying exactly when the staffing shifts occurred. The CNN story cited its own review of internal communications and department data, as well as anonymous sources.
- Snopes has not been able to review the same internal CNN documentation, nor have we located information confirming or debunking the claim that Trump's reported diversion of first responders hampered flood rescue efforts.
- An Interior Department spokesperson said of the rumor that the reported diversion of workers hampered the flood response, "That is 100% false." We reached out to numerous other relevant parties and will update this article if we receive further details.
A rumor that U.S. President Donald Trump diverted 300 first responders to Washington, D.C., to work on his administration's beautification projects circulated online in early September 2026. People sharing the claim suggested they would have proved key in rescue efforts, possibly saving lives, had they been available immediately following the Aug. 29 flash floods inside Arizona's Grand Canyon National Park. We have not yet found evidence that would confirm or debunk this rumor.
The National Park Service, an agency under the Interior Department, announced closures to bridges, the Colorado River, lodging and trails, as well as confirming two deaths, one person missing and around 80 people rescued or evacuated.
An NPS news release said the two people who died, John Giusti, 46, and Brent Rosenkranz, 42, both of Granbury, Texas, were hiking in Bright Angel Canyon and were a part of the same group as the missing person. A key water pipeline sustained severe damage, as well.
In one example of the rumor, on Sept. 1, an X user posted (archived) a message appearing to place blame for the deaths on Trump.
(@factpostnews accessed via X)
Other posts featured the claim on Bluesky (archived), Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), TikTok (archived) and X (archived).
Some posts directly cited the online publication The Lever, which published an article on Sept. 1 with the headline "Before Deadly Floods, Trump Diverted Emergency Responders To Beautify D.C." The story's subheading reads: "Trump reassigned 300 National Park Service emergency responders to golf course and reflecting-pool renovations before the Grand Canyon flooded."
The Lever's article cited a CNN story published prior to the floods on Aug. 25, telling of Trump's administration sending 300 NPS incident management team workers — a division responding to wildfires and other incidents — to work on what CNN dubbed Trump's Washington, D.C., "pet projects," such as the past renovations for the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and the future overhaul of the East Potomac Park golf course. The CNN article does not say exactly when the purported staffing shifts occurred.
The CNN reporters cited their own review of internal communications and department data, as well as anonymous sources regarding other information.
Neither the Lever's article nor users' posts explicitly said the Trump administration's reported diversion of 300 workers hampered rescue efforts surrounding the flash floods. Either way, users inferred it, some believing Trump very recently diverted the workers, with one Snopes reader emailing, "Did tRump divert 300 specialized emergency first responders from American national parks to work on his Reflecting Pool, in the midst of needing them for Grand Canyon rescues?"
Snopes has not been able to review the same internal documentation CNN cited, nor have we located information that might allow us to conclusively rule on the veracity of the claim that Trump's reported diversion of first responders hindered Grand Canyon flood rescue efforts. This claim is therefore unproven and we have left it unrated.
Via email, the White House referred us to the Interior Department, where a department spokesperson said of the rumor that the reported diversion of workers to Washington harmed the flood response, "That is 100% false."
We requested documentation, information and/or comment from the Arizona Department of Public Safety, CNN, Coconino County Emergency Response, Grand Canyon National Park, The Lever and NPS, and will update this article if we receive further information.
A brief timeline of rescue efforts
Within three hours of the flooding on Aug. 29, NPS Grand Canyon shared details about officials evacuating 50 people by air. By the next morning, the division reported 62 total evacuations out of the roughly 80 rescues to date, and said it had gotten assistance from the Arizona Public Safety Department.
A Sept. 1 notice from NPS Grand Canyon announced the continuation of search-and-rescue operations, as well as that the "NPS Western Type 3 Incident Management Team" — the same as the incident management teams CNN and The Lever reported about — would be taking over command as of that morning. The Arizona Daily Sun published a photo reportedly showing a member of that same team observing an Aug. 31 news conference, two days following the flooding.
For further reading about Trump's beautification efforts in the nation's capital, we previously reported about an allegation that his administration chopped down dozens of beloved cherry trees to renovate a golf course, as well as that his motorcade ride inside the reflecting pool caused damage he later blamed on others.

Alanis Morissette sues former tour manager over alleged 'calculated blackmail campaign'
Lawsuit claims Keren Urinov threatened to frame Canadian singer-songwriter for drug trafficking
Alanis Morissette is suing her former tour manager for what she calls a "calculated blackmail campaign" to frame her for drug trafficking unless the Canadian singer-songwriter agreed to sign her to a lengthy contract.
Morissette filed a lawsuit in California on Tuesday, obtained by CBC News, alleging that Keren Urinov is threatening to report her to British authorities for drug trafficking unless Morissette agreed to employ her as a tour director for 15 years and pay her "massive compensation."
Morissette is suing Urinov for civil extortion, fraud and negligent misrepresentation, writing in the lawsuit that she "will not be coerced into delivering her blackmailer an extraordinary payday" and that she pursued legal action "to expose Urinov's scheme and hold her accountable."
What happened?
Urinov, who previously worked for Live Nation's Israeli operations, was hired in 2025 as a temporary tour manager for Morissette's world tour.
In July 2025, the singer and her team, including Urinov, were allegedly flying from the U.K. to Spain for a concert.
At the airport, the lawsuit claims a British Border Force official flagged a bag, asking who owned it. When Urinov said it was hers, she was arrested and issued a seizure notice alleging that the bag contained marijuana and xylazine — a non-opioid animal tranquilizer.
During questioning, Urinov allegedly admitted that the bag and the drugs were hers, showing the authorities her Israeli medical marijuana licence, the lawsuit says. It was returned to her and she was released.
The next day, Urinov was allegedly detained again at an airport for questioning about the bag they'd taken the previous day.
'A series of increasingly extortionate letters'
The suit claims Urinov told Morissette that — again — she admitted the bag and the drugs belonged to her.
But after the tour wrapped, Urinov and her lawyers allegedly sent "a series of increasingly extortionate letters to Morissette," threatening to sue her in the U.K. for "unspecified claims" if Morissette refused to tell British law enforcement that the drugs were hers.
According to the lawsuit, the letters said Morissette could "put an end to the matter" by giving Urinov a fixed 15-year contract that included "income equivalent to that of a tour director with annual increases and bonuses."
She also allegedly demanded Morissette arrange for an immigration lawyer to get a work visa that would allow Urinov to work in the United States — and that if the visa couldn't be obtained, she'd demand more pay.
'Reluctant' but 'no choice but to sue'
The lawsuit also details reasons Morissette felt Urinov "was a terrible manager of the 2025 tour."
This includes "unnecessarily" spending nearly $70,000 US after an "inexplicable error with a hotel booking that no competent tour manager would have made," the court filing states.
Morissette also alleges that while on tour, Urinov told the singer's team that she and a friend were arrested in Latin America "years ago" for smuggling drugs in a surfboard and that Urinov illegally fled the country after being released on bail.
"This was an astounding revelation, given that Urinov had told Morissette's team during her interview for the tour manager position that nothing in her past would cause any complications with obtaining visas or travelling, and she never mentioned her arrest or crimes in Latin America," the lawsuit states.
The lawsuit also says Morissette was "reluctant" to file, but that she had "no choice but to sue."
"Morissette will not agree to work with an incompetent blackmailer for the next 15 years or pay her a ransom under the gun," it reads.
Morissette is seeking a trial by jury. CBC News has reached out to Urinov and representatives for Morissette but has not yet heard back.

The US Navy's top admiral sees laser weapons as a strategic answer to the cost challenge of combating cheap drones.
The Navy has been looking to laser and directed-energy weapons as a potentially cheaper means of neutralizing uncrewed systems, preserving limited and much more expensive interceptor missiles for higher-end threats. Laser weaponry, however, has been tricky to develop, as its effectiveness in combat depends heavily on power, cooling, and other shipboard systems.
In a Wednesday op-ed for The Washington Post, Adm. Daryl Caudle, chief of naval operations, identified the cost imbalance of using multimillion-dollar interceptors to take out low-cost drones as a "defining challenge for the US Navy."
"Recent conflicts have demonstrated how quickly low-cost drones, one-way attack aircraft and other relatively inexpensive weapons can pressure even advanced air and missile defenses," the admiral explained, cautioning that "a defender who fires multimillion-dollar interceptors against inexpensive drones may win the immediate engagement while losing the larger campaign of endurance."
"This is why directed energy weapons — especially high-powered lasers — matter strategically," Caudle said.
As the sea service battled the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen from October 2023 to May 2025, Navy warships routinely relied on missiles to eliminate drone threats. The Navy also regularly used top interceptors to combat ballistic missiles, straining stocks.
Last year, Adm. James Kilby, the acting chief of naval operations at that time, told Business Insider that the way the service had been heavily leaning on its interceptors in the Middle East would not be sustainable in a high-tempo fight.
During his July 2025 confirmation hearing for the CNO position, Caudle told the Senate Committee on Armed Services that the Navy faced a "learning curve" choosing the right weapons.
He said that lessons from the Red Sea led the Navy to look to cheaper air-to-air weapons and electronic warfare when possible, but further consideration is necessary.
The war with Iran this year, which has seen the US military face both drone and missile threats, has also demonstrated how quickly American forces can expend key stockpiles of high-value defensive munitions. The fighting added to concerns already sharpened by the Red Sea campaign over how long US interceptor stockpiles might last in a lengthy conflict.
While the defense industry is expediting and expanding the production of critical munitions, recent conflicts have turned up the pressure on the military to find more cost-effective, more sustainable solutions for defending against large numbers of drones.
Laser weapons are a promising capability to meet that threat and preserve those stockpiles, Caudle wrote, arguing that "lasers offer the possibility of shifting part of naval defense away from finite stored munitions toward shipboard electrical power."
That said, "lasers are not magic weapons," he wrote.
Lasers are line-of-sight weapons bound by combat realities like the atmosphere, ocean environment, beam strength and accuracy, and power and cooling requirements. To properly support laser weaponry, warships need enough power and the correct coolants to keep it from overheating. That means ship design has to be considered alongside weapon design.
Caudle stressed that laser weapons are not a replacement for high-end interceptor missiles. Instead, he added, directed-energy capabilities should be deployed as part of a larger, layered defense, employed against certain lower-cost threats.
The admiral said that the Navy needs to start incrementally readying the sea service for laser weaponry with more manageable, self-contained systems on ships rather than waiting for "perfect megawatt-class systems."
He said that such systems would not represent a "final answer," but rather "a practical bridge between promising technology and an operational capability the fleet can learn from, improve, and scale."
The Navy has been working on laser weapons for years, evaluating them for maritime missions at its Directed Energy Systems Integration Laboratory in California.
The sea service installed an early operational laser demonstrator, the Laser Weapon System, on the Austin-class amphibious transport dock USS Ponce in the 2010s, and then it installed a 150kW Solid State Laser Technology Maturation demonstrator, or SSL-TM, on the San Antonio-class amphibious transport dock USS Portland in 2019, using it to successfully destroy a drone target in May 2020 before it was uninstalled in 2023.
Additionally, the Arleigh Burke-class destroyer USS Preble is equipped with Lockheed Martin's High Energy Laser with Integrated Optical-dazzler and Surveillance, or HELIOS. Lockheed Martin said earlier this year that HELIOS eliminated four drones during a Navy-operated demonstration last year. Some other destroyers are equipped with the lower-powered Optical Dazzling Interdictor, Navy, or ODIN, which is used mainly to disrupt the optical sensors on drones and other threats.
Other services have explored the use of lasers as well. Last week, the US Army saw a laser weapons win, using the Army Multipurpose High Energy Laser to eliminate three drug cartel-linked drones at the southern US border.
