You might've noticed we're in something of a "Dancing with the Stars" renaissance.
The season 34 finale scored the show's highest ratings since 2016, Deadline reported, and the cast of lovable pros have taken over TikTok and venues near you, since the "DWTS" tour also draws in huge crowds of increasingly younger fans.
"We joke about how 10 years ago, we had to make sure the tour was safe for walkers. Now, we have college students lining up — thousands of them buying merch," Ryan O'Dowd, president of unscripted at BBC Studios LA, which produces the show, told Variety in November 2025.
After a hugely successful 34th season, the stakes are high for season 35. The judging team from last season — Derek Hough, Carrie Ann Inaba, and Bruno Tonioli — is back, as well as co-hosts Julianne Hough and Alfonso Ribeiro.
After months of speculation, the full cast was announced on September 2 on "Good Morning America." Among them are reality stars, athletes, child stars, and a couple of people with dance experience. The cast appeals to millennials, who will be sure to appreciate Julia Stiles, Taylor Hanson, and the "Fresh Prince" reunion between Ribeiro and Tatyana Ali, as well as Gen Z viewers who are "Love Island" and "Secret Lives of Mormon Wives" fans.
Here's the full cast of season 35 and their pro partners.
Ciara Miller
Miller, 30, was one of the first two stars to be announced for season 35 back in April.
Miller is best known for her tenure on the long-running Bravo reality series "Summer House," which she joined during filming in 2020, and for appearing on season three of "The Traitors" in 2024.
She joined "DWTS" when her name was in the headlines for the biggest scandal of her reality TV career: Her good friend and castmate Amanda Batula broke girl code and secretly began dating Miller's ex, West Wilson, all while Batula still wasn't legally divorced from her estranged husband, Kyle Cooke. Messy.
Miller's dance partner will be Brandon Armstrong.
Maura Higgins
Higgins, 35, was the other star announced alongside Miller in April. The Irish TV personality was introduced to audiences on season five of "Love Island UK" in 2019.
Since then, she's been a contestant on "Dancing on Ice," "I'm a Celebrity…Get Me Out of Here!," and the US version of "The Traitors" earlier this year. She also hosted the "Love Island" aftershow, "Aftersun," for both the US version and "Love Island Games" from 2023 to 2025.
Her partner is Mark Ballas.
Jackson Olson
Olson, 28, is the second baseman for the Savannah Bananas, a barnstorming baseball exhibition team that's popular on social media. Olson himself has 2.2 million followers on TikTok.
Banana Ball has a singing-and-dancing component, so he has some experience breaking it down.
He was announced as part of the cast on May 12 during the Disney Upfronts panel. On the same day, Disney announced that it had acquired the rights to the Banana Bowl, the Banana Ball championship, which will stream live on Disney+ on October 10.
His pro partner will be Emma Slater.
Guillermo Rodriguez
Rodriguez, 55, has been Jimmy Kimmel's trusty sidekick on "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" since 2003. TMZ first reported he was cast on season 35 on June 17 before Kimmel confirmed it that night on his show.
Rodriguez will be dancing with reigning champ Witney Carson, who, at the time of publication, is about four months pregnant, making her the first pro to compete this far along in a pregnancy.
Tyler Cameron
Us Weekly reported that a source close to "DWTS" confirmed Cameron's addition to the cast on August 19.
Cameron, 33, is best known for his appearances on "The Bachelorette" (he came in second on Hannah Brown's season in 2019) and "The Bachelor Mansion Takeover," a home makeover show set at the long-running series' iconic home base.
He's also competed on "Special Forces: World's Toughest Test" and "The Real Dirty Dancing" — so yes, he also has dancing experience.
His partner will be Sharna Burgess.
Jenna Dewan
That same Us Weekly report confirmed Dewan's addition to the cast. The 45-year-old has an extensive background in dance, beginning her career as a backup dancer for Janet Jackson, and later starring in the early-aughts classic film "Step Up," which showcased her dancing. It's also where she met her first husband, Channing Tatum.
Besides "Step Up," Dewan has appeared in "American Horror Story," "Supergirl," and "The Rookie."
Dewan has also hosted two separate dance competition shows: "World of Dance" and "Flirty Dancing."
Her pro partner is Val Chmerkovskiy.
Tatyana Ali
TMZ reported on August 20 that Ali, 47, had been cast on season 35. Ali has been working in Hollywood for decades, but she's best known for her six-season role on "The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air" as Will's younger cousin, Ashley Banks.
She will be dancing with Jan Ravnik.
Julia Stiles
The same TMZ report said that Stiles, 45, had been added to the cast as well. Stiles is another '90/2000s icon, best known for her roles in "10 Things I Hate About You" and "The Prince and Me," as well as the "Bourne" franchise.
Of course, she also memorably played a dancer in "Save the Last Dance," a film that lives on 25 years later.
She is officially partnered with Ezra Sosa.
Conner Leavitt
On August 20, Us Weekly reported that Conner Leavitt, 32, was part of season 35, a year after his wife and fellow "Secret Lives of Mormon Wives" cast member, Whitney Leavitt, came in fifth on season 34.
Her relatively early exit was controversial — so much so that, after fan demand, Whitney Leavitt and her dance partner, Mark Ballas, appeared on "Call Her Daddy" to perform what would've been their final freestyle dance.
Conner Leavitt's partner will be Adele Zaikman, the recently crowned winner of "Dancing with the Stars: The Next Pro."
Sarah Jane Nader
Leavitt's not the only person following in a family member's footsteps. Nader, 23, was cast for season 35, per Us Weekly. Her older sister, Brooks, competed on season 33 and very publicly had an on-and-off relationship with her pro partner, Gleb Savchenko.
The Nader sisters both star on the reality series "Love Thy Nader."
Per an August 20 TMZ report, the younger Nader will be paired with a female pro, marking the third same-sex pairing on "DWTS," after JoJo Siwa and Jenna Johnson in 2021 and Savchenko and Shangela in 2022.
This was confirmed on "Good Morning America," where it was revealed that she will be dancing with Hailey Bills, who's making her pro debut this season after competing on "Dancing with the Stars: Juniors" in 2018.
Taylor Hanson
Taylor Hanson, 43, along with two of his brothers, make up the band Hanson, best known for their '90s hit "MMMBop."
He was announced as part of the cast on "Good Morning America" on September 2. His partner will be Britt Stewart.
Ezra Frech
Frech, 21, is a track-and-field athlete and two-time gold medalist at the Paralympics. He was born without his left knee and left fibula, making him the fourth celebrity with a prosthetic limb to compete on the show after Amy Purdy, Noah Galloway, and Heather Mills.
He was announced on "GMA."
Frech will be dancing with Daniella Karagach.
Giada De Laurentiis
De Laurentiis, 56, is one of the best-known chefs out there. She starred on her own Food Network shows ("Everyday Italian" from 2003 to 2008, "Giada at Home" from 2008 to 2015, and "Giada Entertains" from 2016 to 2021), has published multiple cookbooks, and created her own line of cookware.
She will be dancing with Alan Bersten.
Connor Wood
Comedian, social media personality, and podcast host Wood, who also goes by Fibula, was announced on "GMA." The 30-year-old will be partnered with Rylee Arnold.
Harry Shum Jr.
Shum, 44, is the second celebrity this season to have extensive dance experience — he starred on all six seasons of "Glee" as Mike Chang, who was known for his dancing ability.
Shum also danced in films such as "Step Up 2: The Streets," "Step Up 3D," and "Center Stage: Turn It Up" in the early 2000s. More recently, though, he's been focused on acting, appearing in "Grey's Anatomy," "Crazy Rich Asians," "Voicemails for Isabelle," and "Blue Eye Samurai."
He will be dancing with Jenna Johnson, per "GMA."
Amber Glenn
The final star of "DWTS" season 35 is Glenn, the 26-year-old Olympic figure skater who won everyone's hearts when she rallied and completed a nearly perfect free skate after a mistake in her short program left her in 13th place.
However, she's still a gold medalist on the powerhouse women's figure skating team, making her the first openly LGBTQ+ US women's figure skating champ.
Her partner will be Pasha Pashkov.

Celtic sign five in one day after Van den Berg & Lotomba arrive
- Published
Celtic have recruited five players in one day to bolster their squad before Wednesday's Europa League signing deadline.
The arrivals of teenage Dutch midfielder Joel van den Berg on a four-year deal from PSV Eindhoven and the loan signing of Swiss right-back Jordan Lotomba from Feyenoord were announced after the Scottish Premiership win over Aberdeen.
Earlier in the day, Celtic confirmed loan deals for former England goalkeeper Sam Johnstone and teenage Chelsea duo Shumaira Mheuka and Landon Emenalo.
The Scottish transfer window closes on Thursday (17:00 BST) but for players to be eligible for continental competition, they needed to be registered on Wednesday.
Lotomba, who made 28 appearances for Feyenoord last term, joins on a temporary deal until the end of the season.
Van den Berg signed a four-year deal with the option of a further year and was at Celtic Park for the 3-0 win over Aberdeen.
Johnstone, 33, arrives from Wolverhampton Wanderers and will provide competition for Finland international Viljami Sinisalo.
Striker Mheuka, 18, has extended his contract at Chelsea until 2031, having made nine outings for the London club.
Four of those came in the 2024-25 Conference League, including his only start. Last season, he captained the Chelsea Under-21 side, scoring 18 goals in 19 games.
Emenalo, 18, also joins on loan from the London club and will offer cover for Kieran Tierney at left-back.
He made 14 Premier League two appearances for Chelsea's Under-21 team last season and set up three goals in those outings.
Johnstone ready to embrace Celtic pressure
Johnstone, who won the last of his four England caps in 2023, made 17 appearances last season but lost his starting place at relegated Wolves in December and has not played since an FA Cup loss to Liverpool in early March.
"I'm buzzing to be here and I'm excited to get going," said the goalkeeper, who began his career at Manchester United and has had spells at Aston Villa, West Bromwich Albion and Crystal Palace.
"I didn't need convincing by anyone, but Joe Hart rang me the other day just to reiterate what a place this is, what a great group of lads and how the fans are unbelievable.
"You hear about the size of the club, but just being here for a day, you notice how big the club is. And the pressure to win, which is what I like - pressure to win, pressure to perform and we all want to win trophies."
Kasper Schmeichel had been first choice at Celtic since the summer of 2024, but played his last game in February and subsequently retired because of a shoulder injury.
Manager Martin O'Neill said Johnstone would be "a very good addition" and that Mheuka has "great quality".
O'Neill also said new left-back Emenalo "has many attributes which I think can benefit us", adding he is "very quick on the ball and, while he can defend, he certainly gets up the pitch into attacking positions too."

A rumor that the CEO of a popular chain of convenience stores in the southern United States said the the company would no longer pursue locations in so-called "blue states" circulated online in August 2026.
Users on Facebook and a popular thread on Reddit suggested Buc-ee's CEO Arch "Beaver" Aplin III said the company was focused on building in "conservative, business-friendly states."
The quote was correctly attributed to Aplin.
The Buc-ee's CEO said it during public remarks on Aug. 17, celebrating the opening of a Buc-ees location in Benton, Arkansas, after being introduced by Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders.
Aplin's full remarks are viewable on YouTube.
The quote in question began at the 2:11 mark, when Aplin revealed Sanders had asked him to build a Buc-ee's in Arkansas. He said:
We're building in a lot of places but when you find a conservative, business-friendly state with a phenomenal workforce, it makes a difference. And I'm starting to realize life's too short to try and build in places that people don't appreciate what you're bringing. Versus a place like this, where people do appreciate what you're building.
So that leadership, that concept, that idea of conservative, business-friendly, family-oriented concept, works so much better if it trickles down from the very leadership from the very top at the governor's office.
A Buc-ee's news release said the Benton location was the company's 58th store and would create more than 200 jobs for the community. Buc-ee's was founded in 1982 and operates primarily in the South.
Local media covered the store opening, including NBC affiliate KARK, CBS affiliate KTHV and the Arkansas Democrat Gazette. The local reports didn't mention Aplin's specific comments nor did they report anything about the chain avoiding blue states.
On Aug. 18, Sanders posted a clip of Aplin's remarks to her Facebook page and wrote, "That's why red states like Arkansas are surging and people and businesses are fleeing blue states."
Later reporting from The Comeback and Fox Business homed in on Aplin's comments, as well as Sanders' takeaway that the chain intended to stop pursuing locations in so-called blue states. It was these reports that started circulating wider online and got increased media pickup, resulting in the claim gaining popularity.
While we found this to be a reasonable interpretation of Aplin's comments, it's crucial to note that Aplin himself didn't explicitly say the company would be "avoiding blue states" during his remarks on Aug. 17. We reached out to Buc-ee's for clarification on the company's plan's for development in red vs. blue states and will update this article if we hear back.

Hundreds of candidates seeking recruitment to 3,284 junior assistant typist posts staged a protest outside the official residence of Deputy Chief Minister Brajesh Pathak on Wednesday demanding completion of the recruitment and appointment process by the Uttar Pradesh Subordinate Services Selection Commission (UPSSSC).
The job aspirants held placards and accused the State government of neglecting their grievances and delaying the process.
Following the protest, Mr. Pathak met the aspirants and said he has instructed officials to resolve the issue immediately. “I met the candidates and spoke to the UPSSSC Chairman. I have instructed that their issues be resolved immediately. Our government stands firmly with students and the youth. We are working on meeting their demands,” he said.
The Deputy Chief Minister added that all students desire a speedy resolution. “I have just directed the UPSSSC Chairman to ensure that the typing examination is held promptly in accordance with the students’ demands,” he said.
‘False assurances’
The aspirants said they have been waiting for the typing test for a long time.
“We met the Deputy Chief Minister regarding the delay in the recruitment drive. The typing test has not taken place yet. Now, they are suggesting to hold it in December. We want the test to be held as soon as possible. However, the commission keeps giving us false assurances,” said Abhinav Mishra, one of the protesting aspirants.
He said though the protesters appealed to the Deputy Chief Minister and he later facilitated a discussion, the UPSSSC officials only said the matter would be considered and that they are deliberating on it.
“We want them to issue an official notice confirming that the typing test for the 3,284 vacant posts will take place in October. It is already significantly delayed,” Mr. Mishra said.
Meanwhile, the Opposition Congress extended support to the aspirants’ demands and alleged that the Bharatiya Janata Party government in the State has “failed” in providing employment to the youth.
“The government made tall promises about employment generation, but it has completely failed. Aspirants were forced to reach the Deputy CM’s residence for regular and time-bound recruitment. The recruitment calendar is not being followed. Our leader Rahul Gandhiji was in Prayagraj holding a dialogue with the youth. We will support them in every way possible,” Congress national secretary Shahnawaz Alam said.

55km Indo-Myanmar border fencing completed, says Manipur home minister
The home minister clarified that the government has been putting its effort to identify the unsettled area of the Indo-Myanmar stretch
Manipur home minister Govindas Konthoujam informed the Manipur legislative assembly floor on Wednesday that around 55km Indo-Myanmar border fencing out of 398km has been completed.
He was responding to the calling attention motion raised by Congress MLA Konthoujam Ranjit Singh to the growing apprehension and concern amongst the people of Manipur on the reported proposal for a land swap deal between India and Myanmar.
The home minister clarified that the government has been putting its effort to identify the unsettled area of the Indo-Myanmar stretch bordering Manipur and Myanmar. Adding that “border pillar numbers 75 to 79 remain one of the most sensitive stretches in the Moreh sector”.
“The government acknowledged the necessity of border fencing and we are targeting to complete the fencing work by 2028”, said Konthoujam.
“Out of the 398km from border pillar number 32 to 130, 55km has been fenced in the state,” adding, “there has been a delay in progress due to issues related to transportation of materials,” he added.
On reports of a “land swap” with Myanmar, the minister said, “There has been no information from the Ministry of External Affairs to the state government on the matter.”
Konthoujam said the people of Manipur are always against on any matter if it questioned on the territorial boundary which the government acknowledge.
“Also, before any decision is taken, the affected people will be informed by the central government,” he said.
The minister said the government acknowledged the problems caused by arms, drugs and illegal immigration due to the porous border. “Due to porous borders, the state has suffered from arms, drugs and illegal immigration proliferation,” he said.
The Opposition also sought clarification on account of the atrocities committed in the past two years particularly the abduction and subsequent killing of women and children in Jiribam, the bomb attack at Tronglaobi claiming the lives of two children, the killing of three Kuki church leaders at Saheibung and the ambush along the lmphal-Tamei road resulting in the death of four Naga civilians.
Konthoujam responding to the calling attention railed by Congress MLA Keisham Meghachandra Singh on “justice for victims”, said the government took necessary security measures to control law and order in Manipur despite harsh geographical terrain and additional security forces are deployed in the state.
Four have been arrested by the National investigation Agency (NIA) in connection with killing of six Nagas and the case has been progressing, he said.
“We handed over most of the cases to NIA so that the cases could be solve in a transparent manner as due to the ongoing crisis there is trust deficit among the communities of Meitei-Kuki and Kuki-Naga,” said Konthoujam.
Home minister also informed that a total of 9,647 case were registered since May 3, 2023 clash. Out of the total, 3,020 cases are undergoing investigation after formation of separate Special Investigating Team (SIT) and 312 cases have been charge sheeted while 29 cases have been handed over to NIA and 32 at Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI).
The government is trying hard for reconciliation of peace but cooperation is needed among community leaders to remove trust deficit among each other, he added.

World No 124 Bu completed the upset after an hour-long rain delay, securing his maiden Grand Slam main-draw victory on his seventh attempt.
"I'm a really lucky loser," Bu said.
"After I lost in qualifying, I took a day off but I saw a few guys pull out, so I took the decision to come back and tried to do some work in case I could play. Yesterday, they told me I could... when I heard that, I was super excited."
Jodar responds to question about his shoelaces
Jodar was asked about people discussing his shoelaces breaking during matches on social media and if he's more aware now of how he might be perceived online.

Jodar: "What's the question?"
Moderator: "It had to do with delays during matches."
Jodar: "The shoelaces didn't break today. So the question? What is the question? I don't know. I don't know the question."
Journalist: "Sorry, I'm sure like when your shoelaces were breaking… I'm sure you noticed a lot of people were talking about it online. I'm wondering, are you worried that if you talk about your physical condition… if people might think you're making excuses, basically?
Jodar: "Doesn't make sense." Moderator: "We can go to the next question."

In Summary
- As concerns around smart glasses and privacy grow, Meta has ensured that users cannot use the cameras on its smart glasses if they cover or tamper with the LED that lights up during recording.
- While Meta’s move is a step in the right direction, it still does not go far enough to address the privacy issues posed by smart glasses.
- Smart glasses brands need to do more to prevent misuse. This includes informing and educating not just users, but also the public, who could unknowingly end up in footage shot on these devices.
Smart glasses have existed for a while but have attained a whole new dimension of popularity since Meta invested in them. For those of you who might not be aware (welcome to high-tech planet, folks), smart glasses look like regular glasses but come with a number of tech add-ons, such as displays, speakers, and most notably, cameras. These smart glasses can take photos, record videos, handle phone calls, play music, let you speak to an AI assistant, figure out your way around town, get recommendations, and more.
Table of Contents
Smart glasses? Pervert glasses, more like!
Sound uber cool, cutting-edge and futuristic, don’t they? Unfortunately, this tech rose comes with a stack of thorns that would make a cactus turn even more green with envy. While the tech world and content creators may be going gaga over all these smart glasses can do, more and more people are beginning to refer to them as “pervert glasses.” There is a sound reason for this – these glasses are increasingly being used to record people (often women) without their consent and knowledge, resulting in a massive breach of a person’s privacy. There have been a number of incidents in which people have been recorded without their knowledge and the footage shared in public or private groups, causing severe trauma to those who appeared unknowingly in the footage.
What’s worse, the onus of figuring out that they are being recorded fell on the person being recorded. Being vigilant, actively looking for signs of someone wearing smart glasses, and catching up on tech cues were all part of the package – we also did a story on ways one could find out if they are being recorded as smart glasses moved from being content creators to destroyers of privacy. As incidents of “secret recordings” through these glasses increase, pressure has finally started building on the brands making these devices to make them safer not just for their users, but also for those in their vicinity.
Meta finally moves, but is it enough?
Recently, Meta finally fixed a flaw that was making it easier for users to covertly record others. In a post made on Threads (https://www.threads.com/@ahimel/post/DcjTatTGyn-), Alex Himel, Vice President of Wearables and Vice President of Augmented Reality at Meta, said that the camera on the glasses would stop working if the LED on the glasses was covered.
He was referring to a small LED indicator on the glasses that lights up when the glasses are recording. While the cameras on the glasses would not allow users to record if the LED was covered, many users found ways around this. One method was as simple as covering the LED light after starting to record the video. Following Himel’s announcement, an update will ensure that if the LED is covered at any stage (before or after starting a video recording), the glasses will automatically stop recording the video or taking photos. What’s more, if users tamper with the LED light and destroy or disable it, the glasses will now disable the camera feature permanently.
While this is definitely a step in the right direction, it does not really solve the biggest issue around these glasses. We have seen Meta’s glasses in public, and it is very difficult to spot when they are recording, especially in daylight or if the person is some distance away. The LED light is bright, but can easily be missed if one is not looking for it. What’s more, one can place a hand in front of it to stop others from seeing it, without actually covering it. We really think more needs to be done to safeguard the privacy of users in the vicinity of these devices. Brands need to come up with stronger measures that can help people spot those who may be wearing smart glasses and steer clear of their line of vision, if they so wish.
Making smart glasses safer: five more things brands can do
Given how limited the LED indicator can be, here are five measures that tech brands can take to make smart glasses safer for those in front of them:
Just make them look different…VERY different
One of the reasons why it is extremely difficult to find out if a person is wearing smart glasses is because they look exactly like usual glasses. Clear, tinted, or even running smart glasses all come with designs/frames that make them look like “normal” glasses. This makes them difficult to spot and enables users to record footage without being noticed.
We think that, given the privacy nightmares they can potentially pose, smart glasses need to look fundamentally different from everyday glasses. Visible badging, colors, even frame size or design should make them easy to spot. Who knows, this might even catch on as a style statement, but at least it will alert those in the vicinity that the person is walking around with a camera literally on their eyes!
Better, brighter (and maybe even more) LED lights
An LED light blinking while recording or taking photos is currently the only way to find out if someone is recording video or taking photographs from their smart glasses. As we have said before, a single light can be missed or even discreetly covered. The solution? Brands could perhaps use multiple LEDs of different colors, and which are of larger size, to pretty much advertise that a smart glasses’ camera is in use. Something like Nothing’s Glyph UI would be very handy!
Pump up the volume
Smart glasses should also give clear audio signals when their cameras are functioning. It should not be possible to take photographs without a loud camera shutter sound, and adding low but constant beep sounds when video is being recorded would also alert people to the presence of a camera in their vicinity.
Mandatory identifying apps
There are already apps like Zuckoff in the market that notify users if they are around someone wearing smart glasses. But these are unofficial and a little hit and miss. We think it would be wonderful if smart glass manufacturers took the initiative to come up with an app that can alert people in a small radius (say, 10 meters if based on Bluetooth), letting them know that they are in the presence of someone wearing smart glasses. Yes, it does violate the privacy of the person wearing smart glasses, as it is likely to make people in their vicinity notice them, but then that’s the price one pays for wearing such a device.
Better marketing and awareness
Brands have been pouring sackfuls of money into normalizing and promoting smart glasses. It would be great if they could allocate some of these funds to also highlight the dangers they can pose, and how they can be misused. Some might think this is counterproductive, but we feel this is the socially responsible thing to do – to make people aware that the device has its dark side too. And it is best that the brands do it themselves before they are forced to do it by Governments around the world.
The Government needs to step in as well. While new tech does make lives easier, there are always people who can find ways to misuse it. It happened with the Internet, it happened with smartphones, it is happening with AI, and it is happening with smart glasses too. To make sure that technology is not misused, there need to be strict privacy laws that are implemented effectively and come with stringent punishments. Perhaps statutory warnings on devices, advising consumers not to misuse them, might be an option worth considering. People need to realize that with great tech comes great responsibility.
Smart glasses need a Meta-morphosis, pun intended. They do not need to blend in, but to stand out and make people realize that they are present in a room. People need to know that they could be on camera. And the onus for this lies not just on those doing the recording, but on the brands who facilitate this.

Remarkable US oil deal puzzles analysts - and angers many Venezuelans
- Published
From the moment elite US troops swooped into Nicolás Maduro's compound in Caracas to forcibly remove him from power in January, President Donald Trump made clear that securing control over Venezuela's oil resources was a key goal of his administration.
The United States would "run" Venezuela, he said at the time, and manage the sale of Venezuelan oil for the foreseeable future.
The signing of a huge US-Venezuela oil deal in Caracas on Wednesday marks the fruition of that plan. The agreement grants a US-led company 100-year concessions over 17 oilfields in Venezuela, amounting to a staggering 65 billion barrels of crude. That equates to more than a fifth of the country's proven oil reserves.
Beyond the eye-watering numbers, both sides heralded the deal as good for their respective nations.
President Trump called it "the biggest oil deal in world history", while the interim Venezuelan President, Delcy Rodríguez, said the agreement was "historic", and would generate $100bn (£74bn) in investment and more than $200bn in tax revenue.
Others profoundly disagreed.
"This is a terrible deal. [Rodríguez] has given away 20% of the national patrimony for nothing," said Trump's former special representative on Venezuela and Iran, Elliott Abrams. "I think she is simply complying with the demands she's getting from Washington."
On Tuesday, the White House released a fact sheet which set out some details of the deal's framework. The US government will work alongside a private business in Venezuela called North American Blue Energy Partners (Nabep), the second largest private oil producer in Venezuela after Chevron.
One extraordinary detail of how the Trump administration will work with Nabep is that the US government will have "veto power over the appointment of any member of the board of directors, and a majority of Nabep's board of directors must be US citizens".
With the ongoing US war with Iran increasing prices at the petrol pumps, a boost in oil production outside of the Middle East could affect consumers.
Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum told Fox Business the pact was "shifting the geopolitical centre of the global energy markets" away from what he called the "choke points in the Middle East" and back to the Western Hemisphere.
There is a logic to the US-Venezuela partnership, Elliott Abrams argued, while Gulf oil supplies are currently so unreliable. But he said the terms are so one-sided they are a "kind of fever dream of what colonialism looks like".
The White House has spoken of the deal having "re-established the Monroe Doctrine", an 19th Century principle exerting US power across South America - "purging foreign malign influence from our backyard and ensuring American dominance in our hemisphere is never again questioned".
Despite the insistence from both governments that the plan will benefit both Venezuelans and Americans, it is not without pitfalls and clear unanswered questions.
The proposed timeframe alone is problematic. Trump has said the agreement will generate profit within two or three years. Energy experts, however, warn the dire state of the Venezuelan oil sector means a decade is more realistic.
Luis Pacheco, of the Baker Institute at Rice University in Houston, told BBC Mundo that Venezuela needs to invest about $100bn over eight years in order to return to its oil production levels of 30 years ago.
"It's important to know who will manage those resources and for what purpose," Pacheco said.
"Are they going to put the same people in charge of managing that money who already squandered the biggest oil boom of the century?" he asked, referring to past mismanagement of the country's oil wealth.
The Venezuelan opposition is concerned the deal deepens President Trump's relationship with Delcy Rodríguez, whom they accuse of heading the same regime as Maduro.
The Trump administration not only decried Maduro's government as a corrupt drug cartel, but surrounded Venezuela with the biggest armada of the modern era.
The ease and speed with which Washington has now pivoted to working with Maduro's former vice-president infuriates the opposition.
The Nobel Peace Prize winner and presidential hopeful, María Corina Machado, may choose not to publicly criticise President Trump, whose support she needs if she hopes to come to power. Others, though, have been more forthcoming.
"You chose to use the power of the United States not to liberate Venezuelans, but to ally yourself with our oppressors," said Venezuelan economist, Ricardo Hausmann, on social media, directing his comments at the US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
"You opted to push through an asset seizure, an unconstitutional agreement with an illegitimate and oppressive government, instead of using the leadership of the United States to first restore constitutional order and democracy," he said.
The lack of an imminent election in Venezuela – or, indeed, any clear plan towards one – strikes many opponents as a betrayal.
There is betrayal felt at the other end of the ideological spectrum, too. Although the governing socialist party, PSUV, has backed Rodríguez over the US deal, many Venezuelan socialists see it as capitulation.
After almost three decades opposing Washington's influence in the region, they feel she has gifted the country's most valuable asset to the old enemy.
The deal "hands over [the oil] and opens the doors to a new colonialism of the United States," said Rafael Ramírez, who served as the head of the state-run energy firm, PDVSA, and as the oil minister under former President Hugo Chávez.
In early 2008, Chávez presented his Sunday television programme, Aló Presidente, from former ExxonMobil oilfields in the Orinoco River Belt.
Having expropriated some of the oil company's assets in the region, he was in a defiant mood.
"We have the reins in our hands and we won't ever let them go again," he said of the state-run oil company's ownership of oilfields, and denounced how previous Washington-friendly governments had turned Venezuela into "a nation of gringos".
"It was a theft of our nation but the Bolivarian Revolution has put a stop to it," he thundered to applause from PDVSA employees.
Yet it was one of his disciples – his handpicked successor's successor – who has now signed this opaque deal with Washington and praised it as a victory for Venezuela.

New Jersey asks Supreme Court to resolve fight over Kalshi's future
The multibillion dollar battle over the future of prediction markets has reached the Supreme Court.
New Jersey on Wednesday asked the high court to weigh in on a legal battle that has pitted dozens of states against the prediction market sector, which is strongly backed by the Trump administration.
At issue is who exactly should regulate sports betting on the prediction market platform Kalshi: federal commodities regulators, as the company insists, or state gambling authorities?
While prediction market sites like Kalshi offer wagering on everything from what an executive says on an earnings call to the outcome of an election, sports bets are the most popular by far, typically representing 80% or more of the platforms' weekly trading volume.
The request from New Jersey officials follows split decisions by federal appeals courts. In April, the Third Circuit found that the Commodity Futures Trading Commission has the exclusive right to oversee the prediction market sector in a case brought by Kalshi against New Jersey. But last week, the Ninth Circuit issued the opposite opinion in a case involving Nevada, ruling that states, not the federal government, should regulate the booming industry.
In its petition to the high court, lawyers for the New Jersey Attorney General's Office argued that the law at issue, the Commodity Exchange Act, does not allow prediction market operators to ignore state law.
"States have always maintained the primary police powers for health and safety matters, including for gambling," the attorneys wrote. "Nothing in the Act gives the CFTC unprecedented authority to become the sole regulator of sports gambling in this country, much less gives companies a get-out-of-50-state-laws-free pass by self-certifying their bets on a CFTC-registered market."
In response, Kalshi said federal regulations covering financial investments apply to its markets and override state laws.
"Kalshi is an open, nationwide financial exchange. It cannot be regulated by 50 different regulators," said Kalshi spokeswoman Dani Lever. "We remain confident in the lower courts' rulings, and nothing in New Jersey's filing today changes our view."
State-regulated sports betting services, like FanDuel and DraftKings, which are subject to billions of dollars in state taxes, have been among the prediction market industry's antagonists, viewing the insurgent sites as fast-growing rivals that are cutting corners.
If the Supreme Court accepts New Jersey's petition, arguments could be scheduled this fall, with the case expected to be decided by next summer.

On June 5, at the American Diabetes Association’s Scientific Sessions in New Orleans, several attendees were removed after repeated disruptions. I apologized soon after — to the individuals directly involved and to the broader diabetes community — for the distress that day caused, and I meant it.
I also promised a full accounting by independent reviewers of what happened. That review, conducted by five independent volunteer investigators, is now complete. I believe its findings deserve to be heard directly, rather than filtered through three months of competing narratives.
Two claims have driven much of the public anger, and the review examined both directly.
The first is that ADA suppressed a viewpoint — that attendees were removed for distributing an editorial critical of federal research cuts. The review found no merit to that claim. That editorial was published in our own journal, Diabetes Care. We were not censoring content we ourselves had put into print. What led to people being asked to leave was conduct during the session — repeated disruptions, continuing after multiple requests to stop — that runs counter to our conference code of conduct, not the substance of what anyone was handing out.
The second claim is that ADA called in police to intervene against our own members. The review found that did not happen. Security personnel were on-site, as at any conference of our size, and some of them were off-duty police officers, acting in their capacity as event security, not as law enforcement. The review found no evidence that a call was placed to the New Orleans Police Department by anyone from the ADA.
I share these findings not to declare what happened June 5 a nonissue, or to suggest ADA staff and security got everything right. Let me be clear: We didn’t. The review makes clear there were missed opportunities for better communication — from our staff and from security — in the moments before and during the disruption, and we take that seriously.
But I do think it matters that established facts, once they exist, replace assumptions — including ones I did not correct quickly enough myself.
The ADA’s long-held commitment to open debate isn’t just words. Diabetes Care has published critical viewpoints of federal research policy — including the very editorial at the center of this controversy. The ADA has also made numerous public statements calling out the current and former administrations for cutting diabetes prevention programs, reducing research support, and decreasing health care coverage. We intend to keep making those comments when federal actions undercut the diabetes community.
We will also keep making room for others’ points of dissent, in our journals and in other fora. A scientific community that only tolerates agreement isn’t a healthy one. What we ask is that disagreement be expressed in ways that don’t come at the expense of everyone else’s ability to participate in the same room.
There’s another lesson from these events that I think matters more, and it’s one about us, not about that day.
This is a period of deep anxiety across the medical research community about the future of federal funding, and that anxiety is not misplaced — significant cuts to diabetes research funding have been proposed in recent budget cycles. What often goes untold is that most proposed cuts to diabetes research have thus far not materialized. Diabetes research funding has been kept largely whole against those proposals, because our community fought for it — including ADA’s role this year in the ongoing pushback against a White House Office of Management and Budget proposal that would have let political appointees, rather than career grantmaking processes, decide which research got funded. That advocacy has had impact: The Senate recently added language to the pending continuing resolution that would block the OMB rule from taking effect, and we are pressing to get the same language into House legislation.
This is the kind of work ADA does every day on behalf of this field, often without notice. But we have not always told that story well to the people most affected by it: the researchers and clinicians who show up to our meetings wondering whether anyone with influence is in their corner. That gap is at least part of why frustration that belonged elsewhere landed on us in New Orleans. We intend to close it.
Here is what I know independent of any review: This is not a moment our community can afford to spend fighting itself. Every hour spent contesting the story of one difficult day is one not spent on the fight that will determine what the next decade of diabetes research looks like. That fight has one opponent: policy that harms the health and research interests of the diabetes community.
I am not pretending that June 5 didn’t happen, and I will hold our organization accountable for where we came up short. Accountability, including the kind this review represents, is part of how trust gets rebuilt.
What I ask is that we hold two things at once: a clear-eyed accounting of what occurred, and a shared recognition that researchers, clinicians, and advocates in our community remain each other’s strongest allies against a far larger threat to work we’ve all given our careers to.
We have weathered funding fights and internal disagreements before, and come through them by choosing, eventually, to face outward together. I know we can do that again.
Charles “Chuck” Henderson is the CEO of the American Diabetes Association.

Ecuador intelligence chief and five Americans killed in Kenya helicopter crash
- Published
Ecuador's intelligence chief and his wife have been killed in a helicopter that crashed at Mount Ololokwe in central Kenya.
Michele Sensi-Contugi, 44, and his wife, fashion designer Stephany Hollihan, 42, were among the group of seven people - six tourists and the pilot - killed in Samburu county at approximately 09:13 (06:13 GMT) on Wednesday.
Five of victims were Americans, a US State Department spokesperson said. The Reuters news agency reports that Hollihan also held US citizenship.
The Kenya Civil Aviation Authority (KCAA) said the helicopter was on a scenic flight from a wildlife conservancy in Loisaba to Ewaso Nyiro, a river that flows along several national reserves.
Samburu county is a popular tourist destination with many private wildlife conservancies and is renowned for its stunning landscape.
Images from the scene show smoke at the wooded crash site on Mount Ololokwe, as members of the Kenya Red Cross approach the still-burning wreckage.
Ecuador's President Daniel Noboa named Sensi-Contugo director of the country's Centre of Strategic Intelligence (CIES) in January 2024.
The office of the president and Ecuador's National Assembly expressed their condolences over his death and that of Hollihan.
The Italian-Ecuadorean businessman had had close links to Noboa even before he was chosen to lead the intelligence service and was considered a close ally of the president.
Shortly before being named head of the CIES, he had served for four months as a minister in his cabinet.
Noboa has declared three days of national mourning starting on Thursday.
Newspapers in Ecuador have also run obituaries of Hollihan. The Guayaquil-based designer founded Sensi Studio, a brand praised for incorporating traditional Ecuadorean elements and materials in its designs.
Lady Lori Helicopters, which operated the Eurocopter EC130 B4 aircraft, said it was "deeply saddened" by the accident.
"Our deepest sympathies are with the guests, crew, their families and loved ones, and all those affected by this tragic accident," a statement read.
According to a memo seen by the BBC's US partner CBS News, external one of the Americans killed in the crash was NBCUniversal journalist José Alberto Suárez.
In the memo, NBCUniversal called Suárez "a deeply respected leader and beloved friend and colleague.
"José was an exceptional colleague and mentor to many," the memo read.
Miami restaurateur Roger Duarte was among the Americans killed in the crash, according to local and US media.
Commenting on his death on X, US Rep Carlos Antonio Gimenez wrote: "Our prayers are with their loved ones during this incredibly difficult time. May their memories be a blessing."
The other victims have not yet been identified.
Helicopter crashes are not uncommon in Kenya.
In February, a helicopter crash in the Rift Valley county of Nandi killed six people, including a member of parliament.
In 2024, the military chief, Gen Francis Omondi Ogolla, died after an army helicopter that was carrying 11 people crashed in the west of the country, with only two survivors.
In June 2021 at least 10 soldiers were killed when their helicopter crashed while landing near the capital, Nairobi.

The US energy secretary, Chris Wright, has denied Washington is seeking to commandeer huge quantities of Venezuelan oil, amid growing criticism of Donald Trump’s energy deal with the country’s interim leaders.
“Absolutely not,” Wright replied when asked by a CNBC journalist if the US was engaged in a “heavy-handed” attempt to “take” Venezuelan oil in violation of the South American country’s constitution.
Wright landed in Venezuela’s capital, Caracas, on Tuesday night, four days after Trump announced what he called “the biggest oil deal in world history”.
“I think we are seeing an absolutely historic transformation of both Venezuela and the relations between Venezuela and the US,” Wright said of the deal, which Trump has claimed will give the US control of 65bn barrels of Venezuelan oil. “This is President Trump’s grand plan to replace conflict with commerce,” Wright said.
The White House says the deal will help secure US “energy dominance for the next century” as well as “purging foreign malign influence from our back yard” by excluding China and Russia from oilfields in the country with the world’s largest proven oil reserves. But there has been criticism from across the political spectrum.
The Wall Street Journal’s editorial board said Trump’s deal with Venezuela’s unelected interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, “looks less like a normal commercial transaction than it does the famous scene of US businessmen meeting with the Cuban strongman in The Godfather Part II”.
“The US government is essentially getting in bed with a foreign dictator and her favored capitalist,” the newspaper complained, in reference to Alejandro Betancourt, the Venezuelan tycoon at the centre of the deal.
The economist Francisco Rodríguez told Democracy Now: “It’s clear that this is not a deal that any Venezuelan government would have entered into unless this country had been subject to an invasion, and unless its authorities had been held at gunpoint. So I think we’ve replaced gunboat diplomacy now for gunpoint diplomacy.”
Delcy Rodríguez was installed as interim president on 5 January, two days after the president, Nicolás Maduro, was abducted by US special forces during a predawn raid on Caracas. Trump warned Rodríguez, who was Maduro’s vice-president, she would face an even worse fate if she did not toe the US line.
Since Maduro’s capture, Rodríguez has made a series of once unthinkable concessions to US officials who their nominally socialist political movement, Chavismo, had spent years denouncing as predatory imperialists bent on stealing Venezuela’s natural resources.
On Saturday, Rodríguez claimed the oil deal had “endless” benefits and would help produce more than $209bn in revenues that could be used to improve healthcare and education. “We are thinking of Venezuela’s future,” she said during a televised broadcast to the nation.
The deal has dealt a body blow to Venezuela’s political opposition who fear Trump is unlikely to push for a democratic transition or fresh presidential elections given his lucrative arrangement with Rodríguez.
“This is a game between the Trump administration and Delcy and her people,” one opposition figure lamented after the deal was unveiled.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Dean Chou, a 53-year-old US citizen who moved back to Taiwan to be closer to his aging parents. It's been edited for length and clarity.
I was born in Taiwan, and moved to Los Angeles in 1999 for college.
After graduation, I got hired as a product coordinator for a lighting fixture company. I worked between the American office and the factories in China, and that's how I learned about procurement.
Around 2009, when the economy crashed, I was laid off. My next job was selling frozen seafood, and I continued to build the sourcing business I had started a few years earlier. I was helping American companies find factories and products in Asia.
Within two years, I got my green card. After that, I quit so I could focus on my own business. In 2018, I became a US citizen. I still do sourcing work today, along with running a roofing business in Los Angeles.
Building a life in the US
America worked out perfectly for me.
In 2010, my wife and I bought a three-bedroom house for about $450,000. It was built back in the '50s and located on a cul-de-sac, with a huge yard and a detached garage. It was a pretty good starting home.
In October 2019, we discovered that my wife had lung cancer, and she passed away in April 2021.
After she passed, I continued living in the house with our dogs. I'd planned to hold onto it until I retired because we had restored it together. But eventually, I realized I needed to look forward, and letting go of the house became part of that grieving process.
As I started thinking about what came next, my parents were a big part of the decision.
They're both 78 now, and they're still capable and happy, but I've missed out on over 25 years with them. I always felt guilty about the distance. I'm an only child; if they ever needed help, there was no one else.
Before, I was married, and moving back wasn't something I was seriously considering. But by 2025, I felt it was time. More than anything, I wanted to be closer to my parents and friends. I can still travel back to LA anytime I want.
The cost of living in Los Angeles was also getting expensive, and because I could manage my businesses remotely, moving back to Taipei made sense.
In April 2025, I sold the house in California for $1.05 million. It was really emotional when I had to hand my keys to the new owner, but all the past was past, and now it was done.
Deciding to go home
I left Los Angeles in October, with my dogs and five pieces of luggage. I rented a car to take me from the airport to my parents' apartment.
They met me downstairs when I arrived, and I remember thinking, "Oh, I'm finally home."
I stayed with my parents before getting my own place at the end of November. I now live in a 780-square-foot apartment about a 15-minute walk from Taipei 101. My rent is 40,000 Taiwan dollars, or about $1,200.
My living costs are usually around $2,500. Food is much cheaper than in LA, and I don't have a car.
I'm also still managing my LA-based company remotely with a business partner. Because Taiwan is 15 to 16 hours ahead of Los Angeles, I go to bed around 10 p.m. and wake up around 3 or 4 in the morning to go over my messages, texts, and emails. Technology really helps.
But moving back hasn't been perfect. The living spaces are much smaller. Even though I speak the language, sometimes people use terms or refer to things in ways I'm no longer familiar with.
I still think about moving back to the US sometimes. If you've lived in LA, worked there, and have friends there, it's a little hard to leave.
But I'm glad I'm right here with my parents now. They are still capable and don't need my help physically yet, but I'm ready.
When I was living in LA, we talked once or twice a week, mostly on Fridays or Saturdays. They also followed me on Instagram, so they could keep up with my life from afar.
Whenever I came back to Taiwan, my schedule was usually pretty full. My parents would tell me I needed to spend more time with them.
Now, we can see each other whenever we want. If they want me to come home, I'll come home. We'll meet for lunch or dinner and talk about everything. Sometimes we go to markets or trade shows together.
We get to share those normal, everyday moments that distance once made difficult.

Four federal agencies have been sued amid calls to release information about the secret framework that the Trump administration uses to conduct safety reviews of frontier AI models prior to release.
In a Wednesday press release announcing the lawsuit, a nonpartisan nonprofit called Protect Democracy alleged that “almost no details” have been released to the public or Congress. To everyone except a few vague “trusted partners,” it remains unclear what the government’s review process looks like, which companies are involved in constructing the framework, or what legal authority Trump officials have to conduct the reviews.
“Neither the identities of those entities nor the criteria by which they were selected have been made public,” Protect Democracy said.
That’s a problem, Protect Democracy alleged in a statement to Ars, since decisions about “which AI models are approved and released may be the most important policy question of this White House.” And it appears that at least one AI firm, OpenAI, has “negotiated a private agreement with the Federal Government to limit distribution of its cutting-edge AI models to government-vetted partners.”
The group’s lawsuit is seeking an order requiring officials to produce all information sought by September 30. That includes “unclassified procedural and contractual architecture: the framework’s text, the terms of participation, the identity of participants, and the process and criteria by which access to frontier models is granted or withheld,” the complaint said. They also want an injunction restraining officials from improperly withholding records that aren’t classified.
“The executive branch is now choosing which companies can release their products and which customers get access to a technology that could shape the future of not only American industry and national security, but economies and governments abroad as well,” Protect Democracy’s release said. “All with no oversight from Congress, the public, or tech experts outside of the executive branch.”
Secret rules allegedly hide corruption
According to Protect Democracy, the framework could potentially be “corrupt,” with officials from the Office of the National Cyber Director, the Office of Science and Technology Policy, the Treasury Department, and the Commerce Department potentially favoring rapid deployments for AI firms that Trump likes. And on the flip side, the public has already seen Trump retaliate against an AI firm for being too woke, Protect Democracy noted, pointing to a judge’s recent ruling that it was illegal for Trump to blacklist Anthropic.
As AI technology advances and cybersecurity risks escalate—OpenAI’s model hacking Hugging Face is the most obvious recent example—the public can’t afford to blindly trust Trump to act in good faith when choosing which frontier models should be rigorously tested, Protect Democracy said. And perhaps even worse, the public cannot know if new vulnerabilities discovered in the real world are due to agencies failing to complete a proper review, running outdated or ineffective tests, missing important checks, or missing steps that align with the latest mitigation strategies advanced by leading AI safety experts.
“We deserve to know what’s in the framework,” the group said, joining other calls for the agencies to be more transparent about AI model deployments.
In a post on X last month, US Representative Greg Casar (D-Va.) accused Trump of “completely failing to keep us safe from the dangers of AI” while taking “millions from AI billionaires.”
“Now, in the wake of extremely dangerous AI cybersecurity problems, he says he’s set up ‘voluntary’ review that no one has seen,” Casar said. “Asleep at the wheel. Too busy cashing in to protect our jobs or national security.”
More recently, another Democrat, California state Senator Josh Becker, urged the court to grant Protect Democracy’s request. In a declaration supporting their complaint, Becker noted that California is mulling a bill, SB 813, that would establish a process where independent organizations would set baselines for AI safety standards. If passed—unlike Trump’s approach—California’s plan would make the latest benchmarks, standards, and methodologies used to evaluate risks posed by AI systems transparent to the public, Becker said. Already, public input has shaped the bill, he noted, with one provision withdrawn following public backlash.
“In contrast to the Administration’s approach, every step of SB 813’s development has been public,” Becker wrote, emphasizing that “we are accountable for the framework we have set.”
In July, the White House launched a clearinghouse, GOLD EAGLE, that relies on industry partners to help agencies flag cybersecurity vulnerabilities across many sectors and industries. Again, Protect Democracy noted that the “White House did not identify any company participating in GOLD EAGLE, the terms on which they are participating, or any legal authority for the program.”
Then, on August 3, the White House announced that it had completed the voluntary framework for reviewing AI models before their public release. Both the framework and GOLD EAGLE are actively being used to review frontier models as the technology advances, the White House has confirmed.
Some parts of the government’s review process are classified. The executive order explained that Trump planned to develop “a classified benchmarking process” that would assess advanced capabilities of AI models and determine when models should be designated as frontier AI.
However, Protect Democracy’s complaint said the framework itself is notably not designated as classified. Despite that, the White House has refused to share details with the public. Instead, a spokesperson told reporters that “just because things are unclassified, that doesn’t mean we are going to broadcast them to everyone.”
Additionally concerning, the term “covered frontier model” is not defined, Protect Democracy said. If the definition is too narrow, some dangerous AI models could slip through the cracks, and if it’s too broad, agencies recently gutted by DOGE cuts may be spread too thin to assess too many models at once. Without more clarity, the public “can only hope this powerful technology is being governed safely and in the public interest,” Protect Democracy alleged.
So far, the framework has only been shared with “a select set of AI companies,” which excludes meaningful stakeholders, such as AI safety groups currently warning of emerging societal risks, as well as smaller or emerging AI firms whose input or model reviews may be just as critical.
Protect Democracy regularly relies on making FOIA requests in its mission to “prevent American democracy from declining into a more authoritarian form of government,” the complaint said. Fearing that Trump was seizing too much power over AI, the group sent identical FOIA requests to four US agencies, urgently seeking only non-classified information and requesting that their request be expedited. So far, no agency has produced any records, the complaint said. Only the National Cyber Director’s office responded, but it denied the group’s request to expedite the process, which Protect Democracy is now challenging as improper.
Congress is in the dark, too
On top of leaving the public in the dark—and independent researchers, advocacy groups, AI investors, and businesses in many industries with a stake in AI—lawmakers have been blocked from assessing the executive branch’s AI safety framework.
That matters, Protect Democracy alleged, because Trump’s AI safety operation may be destabilized if Congress is not on the same page. Right now, Congress is mulling whether to renew the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act (CISA) of 2015, which seemingly is the sole legal basis allowing AI firms to share information with the government through GOLD EAGLE, the complaint said.
Those protections are part of a CISA provision that lapsed once, and Congress must soon decide if the provision should be extended. There’s discord between the House of Representatives and the Senate on the deadline to vote on the extension, but the earliest that could happen is September 30 and the latest is December 11.
“In either event, Congress will soon need to decide whether to extend CISA’s liability protections that, by the administration’s own account, sustain the GOLD EAGLE program that the administration has announced but has yet to explain,” Protect Democracy’s complaint said. “Indeed, a senior administration official publicly acknowledged at GOLD EAGLE’s launch that, absent that reauthorization, ‘this effort is fundamentally challenged.’”
Deana El-Mallawany, director of Impact Programs & Counsel at Protect Democracy, told Ars that “neither Protect Democracy nor Congress has enough information about the GOLD EAGLE program to make a fully informed decision on extending CISA. Our concern is that the White House is putting Congress in the position of voting on a CISA extension without knowing how the GOLD EAGLE program is operating, who’s involved, or what statutory authority is being invoked. That’s why we’re seeking these records.”
Protect Democracy alleged that without these records, the Trump administration could escape accountability for AI safety review.
“Congress cannot meaningfully oversee programs whose terms and asserted authority it has not been shown” and “courts cannot review action they cannot identify,” the complaint said.
El-Mallawany told Ars that if Protect Democracy gets access to the framework, all documents will be posted publicly. Without more transparency, the list of concerns that Protect Democracy has about Trump’s potential ability to leverage the voluntary framework over the AI industry is long, El-Mallawany said, adding:
The risks are abundant, including the risk that the White House could use the secret process to coerce AI companies over decisions like whether to deploy AI for lethal autonomous weapons and mass surveillance (as we saw with the clash between the Pentagon and Anthropic), to extort certain investors and employees for political and financial support or punish others for perceived political opposition, or to force AI companies to incorporate politicized viewpoints into their models—not to mention the risk that the review framework is simply ineffective, creating a false sense of security.
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

- In August 2026, investigative outlet 404 Media (and later The Wall Street Journal) used location trackers to follow large shipments of books, some of which were rare, to an Amazon facility in Las Vegas. 404 Media claimed Amazon was cutting off book spines to more efficiently scan their contents for artificial intelligence data training purposes — destroying the books in the process.
- The facility, called LAS8, was home to the VGT3 operation. Publicly available Google Maps images show the entrance of the facility emblazoned with the image of a dinosaur baring its jaws, holding a book in its claws.
- According to online posts predating 404 Media's reporting by more than a year, people claiming to be Amazon employees at the site described "cutting and scanning books for up to 12 hours at a time."
- 404 Media also pointed to authentic 2024 messages from booksellers in Amazon vendor support channels raising concerns about unusually large orders for books coming from Las Vegas.
- In an email to Snopes, an Amazon spokesperson said: "Amazon purchases books through commercial channels to help develop and improve the products and services our customers use."
- It remains unclear whether Amazon specifically seeks out rare books — or whether some of the books it acquires happen to be rare. It's also unclear, as of this writing, whether the books are used purely for training AI or for some other purpose.
In August 2026, a claim circulated online that tech giant Amazon was acquiring large quantities of books, some of them rare, and cutting off the spines to more efficiently scan the pages for artificial intelligence training data — destroying the books in the process.
The rumor emerged amid news that AI companies such as Anthropic were scanning — and destroying — millions of books to train their AI models.
Social media users across multiple platforms claimed Amazon was similarly destroying books, and dozens of Snopes readers contacted us seeking answers.
"Amazon is buying massive quantities of books, scanning them for AI training data, and destroying them in the process," one Instagram user posted (archived) on Aug. 18, gaining more than 2.2 million views, as of this writing.
(Instagram user @aaronparnas)
The rumor stemmed from an Aug. 17, 2026, story by digital investigative outlet 404 Media. Reporter Emanuel Maiberg collaborated with a bookseller who suspected a large order of books was linked to Amazon's book scanning project, planting an Apple AirTag in the shipment that eventually appeared at an Amazon facility in Las Vegas called LAS8.
Maiberg pointed to posts from booksellers raising concerns about unusually large shipments as well as online forum posts by people claiming to be Amazon employees writing in about the work at VGT3, the name for the operation, which Snopes tracked down and verified below.
In a follow-up story Aug. 26, Maiberg reportedly spoke with an employee who worked at Amazon's VGT3 warehouse. The employee, who was quoted anonymously, reportedly described how machines cut the spines off books before 20 to 25 scanners flipped through the loose pages "like machines that count cash."
Asked for a response to 404 Media's reporting, an Amazon spokesperson wrote in an email to Snopes: "Amazon purchases books through commercial channels to help develop and improve the products and services our customers use."
We also reached out to Maiberg regarding whether Amazon specifically sought "rare" books and whether he came across any evidence that Amazon was scanning books for e-books, but did not immediately hear back. We will update this story if we do.
Although we verified the location of the VGT3 operation and identified the online messages referred to in 404 Media's reporting, and Amazon confirmed it purchases books for the purposes of developing its products, we left this claim unrated because it remains undetermined whether Amazon specifically seeks out "rare" books and whether it uses the books exclusively for AI training data, as well as whether the online posts truly came from Amazon employees who worked at the Las Vegas facility.
Evidence of Amazon's book-scanning operation
In July 2026, a bookseller reportedly told Maiberg they received an order of around 1,000 books on Biblio, an online bookselling marketplace. In cooperation with 404 Media they placed an AirTag in the shipment, which eventually turned up at an Amazon warehouse at 5801 Nicco Way, Las Vegas.
(Google Maps)
The entrance to the facility, where a window bears a large illustration of a dinosaur with its jaws bared holding an open book, is currently publicly viewable on Google Maps. A reporter for a local Las Vegas news outlet also captured another angle of the facility's entrance.
Google Street View imagery from February 2026 shows the same building entrance — though it did not have the dinosaur emblem at that time.
We asked Amazon whether there were similar operations in other cities or countries, which the spokesperson did not address in their response.
The Wall Street Journal also reportedly spoke with a bookseller in the Pacific Northwest who similarly followed a shipment using location trackers inside the book covers. Reporter Melissa Korn wrote:
The other book went first to a warehouse in Kenosha, Wis., then to a spot in northern Las Vegas at an intersection with at least two Amazon facilities. It eventually moved to a position in Mexicali, Mexico. While the seller couldn't determine the exact address, a Google map of the location shows a sprawling recycled-paper manufacturing facility.
404 Media also pointed to messages in Amazon support channels in which booksellers raised concerns about large orders. "This is the first order I've seen like this in over 10 years of selling here," one bookseller wrote in September 2024, reporting that the buyer's address matched an "Amazon Fulfillment Center" in Las Vegas.
An Amazon support representative responded that they were investigating the concerns, before eventually confirming the orders were legitimate.
What have purported Amazon employees said?
Both The Wall Street Journal and 404 Media referenced posts on online forums by purported Amazon employees from more than a year prior to the 2026 stories in which they described work at the Las Vegas facility, reportedly involving cutting and scanning books for up to 12 hours at a time.
"Some are assigned to cut books, and others go to receive where they get books and scan the bar codes," one comment reportedly read.
Snopes verified that this post was real (archived), as were other posts dating back to at least July 2025 (archived, archived), although we were unable to verify they were truly made by Amazon employees.

How did 404 Media define 'rare' books?
According to 404 Media, the books in the shipment it tracked were rare, meaning "there are not many copies of them in circulation." Though many people online appeared to believe Amazon and other AI companies were specifically seeking out rare books, perhaps with the intention of gatekeeping or monetizing their contents by converting them into exclusive digital copies, we did not find evidence of this, as of this writing.
