Uber shuts operations in Nigeria and Uganda with immediate effect
- Published
Uber has announced it is closing its operations in Nigeria - Africa's most populous country - and the East African nation of Uganda with immediate effect
The global ride-hailing giant said it had come to the "difficult decision" after a thorough review of its business. It began operating in Nigeria in 2014 and in Uganda two years later.
Uber taxi drivers in Nigeria have long complained that prices on the app are too low, given the rising cost of fuel, and that commission charges are too high. The company has also faced pressure from rival platforms.
The announcement came as Uber's chief executive, Dara Khosrowshahi, said the company was cutting its global workforce by 10%.
- Uber to cut over 3,000 jobs in major global restructuring 
  - Published7 hours ago
Over the last year, Uber has also pulled out of Ivory Coast and Tanzania. The latest announcement means Egypt, Ghana, Kenya and South Africa are the only African countries in which the firm now operates.
"This decision is limited strictly to these two markets and does not impact our operations across the rest of the continent," Uber's statement to the BBC said.
"We remain committed to sub-Saharan Africa, where we continue to see strong growth and opportunity."
Over its 12 years operating in Nigeria, Uber had expanded its services. In the commercial hub of Lagos, it launched a boat service in 2019 in an effort to help commuters bypass the city's notorious congestion.
Lagos, one of Africa's largest and busiest cities, is infamous for its long traffic jams that cause gridlock and hamper business activity.
Other ride-hailing taxi apps have launched in the West African nation over the last decade, including international competitors such as Bolt and inDrive, as well as a number of local operators.
But the Nigerian market has become increasingly challenging for them all, with drivers staging protests and industrial action in recent years over rising operating costs, low fares and working conditions.
The removal of Nigeria's fuel subsidy after President Bola Tinubu's election in 2023 saw the cost of living rise. The subsidy had kept down the price of petroleum products low for decades.
This year, motorists have been hit again by the rise in petrol prices following the US's war with Iran.
Uganda's Daily Monitor newspaper said Uber's departure would mean a major change for commuters in the capital, Kampala. But it said the void was likely to be filled by other taxi apps such as Faras, Bolt and SafeBoda.
Uber pledged to support employees and drivers affected by the decision and said its help centre would remain open for those in Nigeria and Uganda until 23 September to deal with outstanding issues.

'I have fired 40 of my agents for being corrupt', says Nigeria's anti-corruption chief
- Published
Nigeria's anti-corruption agency has dismissed more than 40 employees for alleged corruption and financial misconduct over the past three years.
The disclosure was made by Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) chairman Ola Olukoyede at an event assessing the agency's achievements since he took the helm in October 2023.
He said more than five of the dismissed officials were already facing prosecution, while case files are being prepared against others.
The EFCC investigates financial crimes, including fraud, money laundering and corruption - regularly pursuing cases against politicians, public officials, business figures and others accused of misusing public funds.
"In the past two-and-a-half years or three years of my service, I've asked them to dismiss over 40 staff on account of corruption and financial malpractice," Olukoyede told journalists at the briefing in the capital, Abuja.
He went on to explain that as part of the reforms he had overseen at the agency, the EFCC's Department of Internal Affairs had been renamed "the Department of Ethics and Integrity".
To fight against conflicts of interest, a policy on gifts and hospitality had also been introduced.
It requires officers to declare gifts above a certain threshold - which he did not specify - including gifts received from relatives abroad.
"You must be sure that your hands are clean. You can't be fighting corruption when your hands are soiled with corrupt practices," Olukoyede said.
The BBC asked the EFCC for more details about the alleged corruption involving its former staff members, but the agency said this information was not available.
It was keen to point to its other achievements over the last three years - highlighted at Monday's briefing, external.
Olukoyede, 56, said he had overseen a record-breaking time for the EFCC, recovering 1.23 trillion naira ($925m, £683m), with a conviction rate of more than 75%.
"The commission received 49,673 petitions, investigated 39,615 cases, filed 14,476 cases in court and secured 10,872 convictions between October 2023 and July 2026," he said.
In the first half of 2026 alone, it had recorded 1,370 convictions from 1,889 filings, the EFCC chairman added.
"These results reflect diligence, resilience and a prosecutorial approach anchored on evidence and courtroom outcomes."
Other figures disclosed at the event show that the EFCC's caseload is increasingly focused on cybercrime and fraud rather than just corruption cases against high-profile officials.

Let’s be frank: Some of Google’s recent Android feature Drops have been duds, offering little more than an expansion of Gemini summaries and chat functions. The new September Drop does have some Gemini flavor, but there are non-AI goodies, too. Your messaging threads are getting prettier and more useful, and those nifty Motion Assist dots that began appearing last week are rolling out widely. And even the Gemini expansion is not without utility.
Since this is an Android Drop rather than a Pixel Drop, these features are coming to a wider range of devices. The OS version does matter, though. If you’re on Android 16 or higher, you can now tell Gemini to log the location of items that don’t have a tracker tag attached. Just tell the AI where you put something, and include a photo if you like.
This information will be logged in Find Hub, which has thus far been used for locating phones, earbuds, and tracker tags. You can ask Gemini to recall that information or simply check Find Hub yourself the next time you forget where you put that item.
Gemini Live is also getting a new feature called Guided Vision that could be a boon for accessibility. Guided Vision can help you locate objects in the camera frame or extract information that you can’t make out, like the text on a menu in a dimly lit restaurant. Gemini interprets the camera feed to help you find things, and it can even tell you how far away your hand is from whatever you’re trying to find.
Guided Vision will be available in the system Accessibility shortcuts and can also be activated from the TalkBack menu. This feature will work on virtually all Android phones, from Android 9 Pie onward.

A devastating flash flood on Wednesday, August 26, near the Nepal-Tibet border, resulted in massive destruction in several districts of Nepal, including Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, and Gorkha, with over 700 dead and over 2,500 people still missing. Reportedly, a glacial landslide of ice and rock caused the flash floods, which destroyed homes roads, bridges and power plants.
In the days following the catastrophe, social media was rife with video clips showing the extent of devastation — from gigantic waves of floodwater gushing through entire villages, to buildings collapsing, and people being swept away under the debris.
However, Alt News found that a large number of these videos circulating on social media were not authentic. Several of these videos were not from Nepal at all, but drawn from various other calamities which occurred across the world in the last few years.
Clip From 2025 Uttarakhand Floods
An X user, Said Ercan (@saidercan), posted a compilation clip on August 27 showing the havoc wreaked by large flood waves. The first clip shows a torrential river flowing through a mountainous area, and eventually sweeping through the houses on the banks, destroying them in an instant. The post has garnered over 5.8 million views and been reshared over 5,000 times at the time of publishing. (Archive)
To verify whether the video is of the Nepal floods, we broke it down into keyframes and ran a reverse image search. This led us to an Instagram post uploaded by The Times of India, on August 5, 2025, featuring the same footage.
View this post on Instagram
The caption states that the footage is of the Uttarakhand cloudburst havoc. “At least four people have died and many are feared missing after a devastating flash flood triggered by a cloudburst in the upper catchment area of the Kheer Ganga river caused large-scale destruction in Dharali village in Uttarkashi district…,” read the caption.
A Dainik Bhaskar report also features the same video to show the scale of damage caused by the cloudburst in Uttarkashi. We ran relevant keyword searches, and found news reports from sources like Reuters, BBC, Al Jazeera, The Hindu, and others, that corroborated this finding. Thus, the video footage shared by the X user is actually of the 2025 Uttarakhand flash floods, and not of the recent Nepal havoc.
AI-generated Clip
In another instance, X user Ayesha Khan (@Ayesha0Khaan) posted a video clip, of huge waves sweeping away cars, building structures, and people. The clip received over 1 million views. (Archive)
X user Ravi Shankar Singh (@Ravishanka34381) also posted the clip with the same claim. However, we noticed some discrepancies in the video — for instance, around the 0:05 timestamp, a tree log appears out of nowhere in the debris flowing through the floodwater, indicating that the clip could be AI-generated.
We ran the video through Hive’s AI detection tool, which confirmed our suspicion, showing a 99.9% possibility of the video containing AI-generated content.
Clip From 2024 China Incident
News outlet Medya Post (@medya_post) uploaded a clip on X, which showed around 15 people getting swept away by powerful flood waves. The caption stated: “Tourists who wanted to take videos and photos during the flood disaster that occurred in Nepal were swept away by the current and disappeared.” The post had seen massive traction on social media, with over 1.5 million views. (Archive)
Two other X users with the handles (@JMNewsNetwork_) and (@redpillmd) had uploaded the same video, with the former having deleted it after it had been viewed over 45,000 times.
To verify the clip’s authencity, we ran a reverse image search, which led us to an X post, originally uploaded by an user with the handle (@Arab_Storms) on September 8, 2024.
التصوير اصبح اهم من الحياة #شاهد ❗️#الصين جرف المد القوي لنهر تشيانتانج العديد من الزوار الذين كانوا يحاولون التقاط صورة ،،،#Yagi pic.twitter.com/bdiEj7fk9b
— طقس_العالم ⚡️ (@Arab_Storms) September 8, 2024
According to the caption, the video had been taken in China, showing the powerful waves of the Qiantang River overpowering tourists on the shore who were clicking photos. The incident, which occured in the days following Asia’s most powerful storm in 2024, the Super Typhoon Yagi, had also been reported on by The Indian Express, and Newsflare.
Video From West Bengal Landslide
A news outlet TNT Media (@TNT_Media1) posted a clip which showed a mudslide from a vantage point. It also features the narrow escape of some vehicles and people gathered at the spot. The caption, written in Arabic, claims that horrifying scenes correspond to the recent Nepal flash floods. (Archive)
مشاهد مروعة من نيبال.. 😯😯 pic.twitter.com/N7f5jBl4i6
— 𝐓𝐍𝐓 (@TNT_Media1) August 26, 2026
We noticed that the car, visible in parts of the video, bears a number plate whose state code (WB) corresponds with that of West Bengal. Moreover, the recorder of the video, while shooting the clip, speaks in Bengali to warn people to get away from the waves.
A reverse image search on several keyframes of the video led us to this X post, uploaded by The Daily Jagran on August 17.
A biker had a narrow escape after a massive landslide struck the Bindu area of West Bengal’s Kalimpong district. Huge rocks, soil and debris suddenly came crashing onto the road as vehicles passed through.#Kalimpong #Landslide #WestBengal #Biker #ViralVideo #Monsoon pic.twitter.com/HgFLY7Dhjy
— The Daily Jagran (@TheDailyJagran) August 17, 2026
The caption states that the video shows a landslide in the Bindu area of West Bengal’s Kalimpong district, thereby proving that this video clip is not related to the Nepal flash floods.
Compilation Clip From Various Calamities
An X user named “Leonard Sardua $TOR” (@lsardua) posted a compilation of clips showing structures collapsing under the deluge, claiming they showed the devastation caused by the flash flood in Nepal. The clip garnered over 3.3 million views and 3,700 reshares. (Archive)
Two more users, “HadY Azmy” (@HadYAzmy1) and Ahmad Ansari (@Ahmadansari2233), amplified the same clip on August 27. The former video, which has now been deleted, had garnered over than 2.5 million views and over 3,000 reshares.
On running a reverse image search on one keyframe from the viral clip, we were led to an article published by The Times of India on July 21. The report shows the same building structure collapse under the force of floodwater, and states that the video was from the Budgam district of Jammu and Kashmir.
Another segment of the compilation shows a red building being engulfed by the gushing floodwater, sweeping away cars and other structures amid the debris.
Running a reverse image search on this keyframe, we found that the clip could be traced back to a mudslide in Japan’s Atami city from July 2021. An X user with the handle @d_t_dcg_sdh had uploaded several clips showing the mudslide sweeping away houses and vehicles. We also found news reports from Al Jazeera and Spanish news outlet La Nacion, corroborating that the clip was recorded during a mudslide in Japan in 2021.
The same compilation video also included a segment which showed a bridge being torn down by the raging floodwater.
This, we found, was in fact from an incident in Indonesia, showing the collapse of the wooden Molintogupo Bridge, owing to the overflowing of the Bone River. A video uploaded by Newsflare on Dailymotion, notes that the incident occurred on June 11, 2020. It was also reported on by VGTV.
Another segment of the same clip shows two men watching a bridge being dismantled and swept away by floodwater.
We found that this video was from Argentina. A reverse image search on a keyframe led us to this X post by AccuWeather on December 25, 2023, which shows a bridge in Argentina’s Catamarca being blown away by the turbulent floodwater.
A bridge was swept away in Catamarca, Argentina, on Christmas Day, leaving a city completely isolated.  pic.twitter.com/hVdwxmQ7QU
— AccuWeather (@accuweather) December 27, 2023
Another video, showing a white car being dragged along by the torrential flow of mud water, was also part of this compilation.
This, Alt News found, was originally from Islamabad, in Pakistan, dating back to a devastating flood that took place in July 2025.
Similarly, a segment showing a woman overlooking a building structure being swept away by flood water, was also part of this compilation, alleging that it was from Nepal.
A reverse image search proved that the image has existed on X since at least September 2024. On further investigation, we found that it showed the damage caused by Hurricane Helene in North Carolina, United States.
Don’t worry guys, weather modification isn’t real! It’s just a coincidence that Hurricane Helene is one of the most devastating “inland damage storms” in history and that hundreds of pro-Trump counties are being massively impacted during the most important election of our… pic.twitter.com/lyi8YZXB8A
— Matt Wallace (@MattWallace888) September 28, 2024
Another clip showing a submerged bus making its way through the floodwater was also featured in the compilation.
We found that this video was shot during a downpour in Pakistan’s Karachi, which left the city flooded and resulted in at least 16 deaths. Pakistani news media outlet 24 News HD, in their report on the flood dated March 19, used the same clip of the submerged bus.
Thus, the compilation clip uploaded by users “Leonard Sardua $TOR”, “HadY Azmy”, and Ahmad Ansari, with the claim that the footage depicts the havoc in Nepal is fake and misleading. The entire compilation stitches together footage from real calamities, occuring in various other parts of the world in the past few years, to wrongly claim that they are visuals from the Nepal flash floods on August 26.

Birds stop play but Medvedev flies into third round

An interruption from a pair of birds ruffled Daniil Medvedev's feathers but could not disrupt the seventh seed as he eased into the US Open third round with a dominant victory over Sebastian Gorzny.
The two birds settled down on the net for a closer look at the action midway through a second-set rally, with play continuing around them for several strokes before the chair umpire called for the point to be replayed.
Medvedev, who placed the incident in his "top five" most unusual experiences at the New York major, was visibly stunned by the decision which came just after he thought he had won the point with a cross-court forehand.
"This is very bad," the 2021 champion said as he remonstrated at the umpire on court.
Russia's Medvedev is no stranger to losing his composure on court, notably receiving a fine of almost £31,500 at last year's US Open for an extraordinary meltdown during his first-round defeat to Benjamin Bonzi.
As recently as last month's Winston-Salem Open, where he again lost in the opening round, he spent a disconsolate change of ends questioning his future in the sport, musing "maybe I should start a career in pickleball".
However, the 30-year-old, who had already flown through the first set in just 21 minutes, quickly brushed aside the avian interruption to complete a straightforward 6-1 6-3 7-5 win over American wildcard Gorzny, the world number 731.
"I saw [the birds] straight away," Medvedev - who will play Frenchman Arthur Rinderknech in the third round - said in his on-court interview.
"I thought the point would stop straight away but it didn't.
"Then we play for 45 seconds and the moment I hit the winner we say stop. I'm like, 'Why? We played for 45 seconds!'.
"But it's okay. I was not happy with the decision but it is was it is. You can't do anything with it.
"The situation was pretty crazy but I love this court, I'm happy to win, to stay in the US Open, to stay in New York for longer."
Gorzny was making his Grand Slam debut at the US Open, seven years after being given a 5% chance to live after being taken ill at the USTA Boys' 16s National Championships in Michigan.
Then aged 15, Gorzny suffered a seizure in the night and was placed in an induced coma for four days.
"The doctors aren't really sure what it was actually, but they're guessing a mosquito bite that led to some type of brain infection: meningitis, encephalitis," Gorzny told the ATP before the US Open.
A former Wimbledon boys' doubles champion, Gorzny, the world number 731, earned his place in the main draw at Flushing Meadows by winning the USTA American Collegiate Player Wildcard Playoff in June.

Wrexham got their first win of the Championship season in style as Millwall were swept aside 3-0 at the New Den.
Alex Neil's home side were coming off the back of a chastening 5-1 thrashing by Southampton on Saturday and their formerly steadfast defence suffered another horror show as their hopes of repeating last season's promotion push were dealt a blow.
After starting with two clean sheets in victories over Bristol City and Norwich, it is now eight goals conceded in two games after Wrexham put them to the sword with some clinical finishing.
Defender Zak Sturge was unfortunate in turning Issa Kabore's effort past his own goalkeeper in the first half, but there was nothing lucky about the goals scored by Phil Parkinson's side after the break as Kieffer Moore and Jacques Ekomie provided excellent finishes to hoist the visitors into the top half of the table.

It means the Welsh side finally got their campaign going after drawing with Cardiff and Watford before losing at home to Birmingham.

At the other end, Max Cleworth's header from a deep Matty James free-kick sailed harmlessly wide, as neither side offered much in the opening 25 minutes.

Robinson's rhythmical action reminiscent of McGrath - Agnew
- Published
After Ollie Robinson's England debut five years ago I said he was the most natural bowler I have seen.
A lot has gone under the bridge since – he was dropped, recalled, dropped again and is now back - but nothing has changed my mind on that.
Using the word robotic to describe him may give the wrong impression. It is a compliment.
Australia's great bowler Glenn McGrath was like that. Everything was utterly rhythmical, repetitive and perfectly grooved.
Robinson is the same.
As a former bowler I watch and see he has inherent rhythm and such a beautiful action. His wrist is just perfect.
Yes, the conditions this summer, in which he has now taken 23 wickets in three matches after England's win in the second Test at Lord's, have been perfect. Robinson would carry them around in his cricket bag if he could.
But the 32-year-old has performed magnificently in them.
Whatever he has wanted the ball to do – to swing in or out or to wobble off the seam – it has done.
He has not needed to go searching for wickets, instead just letting the ball flow naturally from his fingertips.
He will feel like he could take wickets running in blindfolded. There is no better feeling.

  - Published10 hours ago
Another thing I admire in Robinson is that he is a really good reader of the game.
Tactically, he is extremely sharp. He can spot a batsman's weakness and interpret that into what it means for his own plans very quickly.
A coach told me when he first came into the side that he was a bowler who would give talks to his team-mates about how to get batsmen out even then.
It all adds to what makes him such a good bowler.
Many people will say Robinson's performances this summer show Ben Stokes, Brendon McCullum and managing director Rob Key were wrong to leave him out of their Ashes squad last winter.
Amid talk of a breakdown in trust between Robinson and the Stokes-McCullum regime, they prioritised bowlers with greater pace.
He probably has lost his way with his fitness at different times but I also think back to bowling coach Jon Lewis calling out his fitness in 2022.
There are times Robinson has not been handled as kindly as he might have been.
Perhaps last winter's omission focused his mind, allowing Joe Root to now reap the rewards.
Robinson can also thank Australia for bringing back into the fashion the age-old tactic of the wicketkeeper standing up to the stumps to pace bowlers.
Alex Carey did it so effectively during the Ashes and England are now copying with Robinson.
It may seem obvious but that tweak is really playing into Robinson's strengths.
If the wicketkeeper was stood back the modern batsman would be walking down the pitch to Robinson. With Jamie Smith up they can't because of the risk of being stumped.
It means Robinson can bowl a yard fuller, giving his deliveries more time to swing through the air and means more of Robinson's deliveries would hit the stumps rather than bouncing over from a shorter length.
Of course, you cannot do any of this without a good wicketkeeper. Praise must also go to Jamie Smith.
After we saw Smith struggle badly through the Ashes, he has clearly improved his glovework. Wicketkeeping coach Sarah Taylor has been working him hard before play with a drill where she whacks tennis balls towards him with a racket.
The ball skids through and, with a batsman stood in front edging, missing and hitting the ball, Smith has to stay low and take them.
The results speaks for themselves.
Now the next question for Robinson is whether he can repeat this success on harder, flatter pitches, or in hot conditions which will test those fitness levels. England will face them in their three-Test series in South Africa this winter.
They have often left Robinson out for Test on more batter-friendly pitches but it is time for them to throw him in. He has earned that right.
England are working behind the scenes to get Robinson into the position where he maintains his pace around 82mph, rather than his current place of starting there before dropping to 77 or 78mph.
If he does that, the extra bounce he will get as a result should negate the loss of movement.
And before then I desperately hope England do not rest Robinson, Jofra Archer, Gus Atkinson or Josh Tongue for the third Test in Edgbaston.
England's new quartet has shown real promise. They may not have a frontline spinner but Robinson, who conceded runs at just 1.29 per over across the Lord's Test, can effectively do the holding job of a slow bowler if needed.
Do not break things up now.
After their poor run England just need to keep on winning matches and, just as importantly, this group needs to get used to bowling together as an attack.
Joe Root must also learn how to use each of them best.
This, with Robinson as the leader, is England's best attack. Stick with it in Birmingham and beyond.
Jonathan Agnew was speaking to BBC Sport's Matthew Henry

A NY hospital tried to close its birthing center. This city united to fight back
TROY, N.Y. — Like many residents of this aging industrial city on the Hudson River, Starletta Washington was stunned when she heard Troy's last remaining hospital planned to close its birthing center.
"It was devastating," said Washington, who heads the local YWCA. Washington was born at the hospital and had her children there. She couldn't believe families would now have to get to a hospital half an hour away or face the prospect of an emergency delivery.
"Nobody else was going to be born in the city of Troy unless they were born on a city bus, in the back of a cab, or, disgustingly, on the side of the street?" Washington said. "Blew my mind."
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Troy wasn't the first community to face this prospect. Since 2010, hospitals have closed hundreds of maternity units as cities and towns shrink and hospitals consolidate into larger systems.
Troy found a more hopeful ending.
Elected officials from both major parties joined patient advocates, mothers, midwives, doulas and community leaders like Washington to challenge Trinity Health, the large Catholic health system that owns Troy's hospital and birthing center. The campaign even united Planned Parenthood and the Catholic diocese.
"Whether you were Republican or Democrat, or if you didn't vote, it literally brought everyone together," said Carmella Mantello, the city's Republican mayor. "Everyone just said, 'We can't let this happen.'"
Throughout the country, healthcare remains a flash point as politicians square off ahead of November's elections. But in many places, Americans are also quietly finding common ground.
In this small city, citizens were brought together by frustration over large, corporate health systems that can seem to put profits over patients. And they resolved to work together to keep critical medical services in their community.
A community institution
Babies have been delivered at Samaritan Hospital on a hill above Troy since this city's once bustling factories produced most of America's shirt collars a century ago.
More recently, Samaritan's Burdett Birth Center had become a model for patient-focused care. Midwives and doulas work alongside OB-GYNs and support mothers who want to avoid a delivery by cesarean section unless necessary.
Patient safety advocates have pushed for years to reduce surgical deliveries, which can lead to complications. At Burdett, only about a quarter of newborns are delivered by C-section, compared with about a third statewide, according to 2025 hospital data. Burdett also had fewer preterm births and fewer babies with low birth weights.
"I wouldn't go anywhere else," said Lidia Zambrano-Madera, who gave birth to both her children at Burdett with the help of a midwife.
For Zambrano-Madera, who recently opened a children's play center in Troy, Burdett offered another advantage: It was just five minutes from home.
But three years ago, Trinity Health, a multibillion-dollar Michigan-based hospital system, said the birth center was losing money and would close.
Families from Troy and surrounding Rensselaer County would have to deliver at another Trinity hospital in Albany, up to a half-hour's drive away. The hospitals are branded under St. Peter's Health Partners in the Albany region.
"We've been frantic about trying not to cut the care at the bedside," said Steven Hanks, a physician who oversees Trinity hospitals in New York and New England. "But, you know, you get to a point where you can only consolidate so much. You can only spread people so thin, and then you have to start taking harder looks at your actual services."
Corporate backlash
Trinity's plans — news of which broke in a local newspaper — came without warning, surprising the obstetrical staff and community leaders. They set off a firestorm.
Within days, midwives, mothers, community leaders and politicians held a rally at the YWCA in downtown Troy. Others would follow. Volunteers led by doulas and midwives made T-shirts and handed out pink "Save Burdett" signs at the local farmers market.
Activists were outraged that the hospital hadn't adequately assessed the impact of the closure, particularly on low-income families. They conducted a community survey that found 1 in 4 Troy residents didn't have access to a car and would have trouble getting to Albany.
The campaign drew on deep connections that many residents had to Burdett. "They realized what a gem Burdett is, and what a great community service they provide," said Jessica Hayek, a doula and birth educator who helped lead the campaign.
Hayek and others also tapped into deep-seated frustration with Trinity, a healthcare behemoth that operates 91 hospitals and last year recorded more than $25 billion in revenue and a healthy operating margin that topped 5%.
"Trinity Health is in the Midwest, and they are not in the community," Hayek said. "So when you're looking at just the numbers from an office in the Midwest somewhere, they're not looking at the benefit that this place has on the community."
Hayek describes herself as a liberal Democrat. But Trinity's focus on its bottom line also irked many Republicans, including Mantello, who was the City Council president at the time.
"The whole hospital scene has changed," Mantello said. "It was very personable. You had nurses and doctors who were able to give more care and spend more time with patients." Now, by contrast, many hospitals have what she described as a "more corporate type of atmosphere."
Even the Catholic bishop decried the planned closure of the birthing center as out of step with the values of his faith and the hospital system's.
"Nothing is more central to the Catholic healthcare mission than supporting life and all those who bring it into the world," Bishop Edward Scharfenberger said after Trinity announced the closure plan. Scharfenberger has since retired.
A bipartisan solution
Despite the backlash, Trinity Health executives for months insisted they had no choice. The system even sued the state to push through the closure.
Ultimately, though, powerful state officials, including New York Attorney General Letitia James, a Democrat, joined the fight to save the birthing center, launching an investigation into the proposed closure and hosting a daylong hearing in Troy.
State Assemblyman John T. McDonald III, a Democrat who represents Troy, worked with Republican elected officials, including the county executive and the state senator representing Troy, to secure $5 million in state funding to help keep Burdett open.
"You had a Democrat and a bunch of Republicans all working together on the same issue," McDonald said, "because, at the end of the day, our job is to listen to what the public has to say."
Nearly a year after announcing the closure, Trinity reversed itself and said Burdett would remain open.
Lois Uttley, a New York City-based researcher and activist who has worked with communities facing hospital consolidation, said Troy's success reflects a growing bipartisan suspicion of big corporate healthcare organizations.
"The executives of these health systems will tell the community that joining a big health system will be good, that the quality of care will improve, that efficiencies will mean they can keep the costs low," Uttley said. "But what I have seen over the last 30 years of work is that those promises often are broken."
As hospitals close or downsize, she said, communities are catching on. "They're becoming more skeptical."
There's another, more hopeful lesson in Troy's success, said McDonald, the state assemblyman.
"If we take down our swords," he said, "and put out our arms, maybe we can get something done."
KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

In Summary
- A decade ago, Indian brands commanded a large chunk of the Indian smartphone market. In Q2 2016, three of the top five smartphone brands were Indian ones.
- The arrival of Chinese brands and changes in the market led to the decline and exit of many Indian phone brands. Today, while brands like Lava and AI+ exist, their market shares are nothing compared to Indian brands of the past.
- Rising smartphone prices and memory costs seem to have opened the door for Indian smartphone brands, with new brands emerging and old ones looking to make a comeback, with encouragement and support from the Government. But is this just a temporary phase, or will Indian brands win back the market dominance they lost almost a decade ago?
When I first started covering technology, the Indian smartphone market looked extremely different from what it does today. Today, there are barely any Indian brands among the major smartphone brands in the Indian market – Counterpoint’s report on Q2 2026 showed not a single Indian brand among the top eight smartphone brands in the Indian market. Yes, some Indian smartphone brands do exist, such as the persistent Lava and the newcomer AI+, but they do not command significant market shares.
The story was extremely different a decade ago.
It may be hard to believe, especially for those who have started following smartphone trends in India since 2017, but in mid-2016, Indian tech brands were not just surviving but ruling the smartphone charts. IDC’s report for Q2 2016 placed three Indian brands in the top five smartphone brands in the country – Micromax, Intex and Reliance Jio (this was around the time of the 4G revolution).
And this was not because of a lack of competition. The Indian market was home to a number of high-profile foreign smartphone players like Apple, Samsung, HTC, BlackBerry, LG, Sony, and Motorola were very much present in the Indian market, and the likes of OnePlus, Xiaomi, Vivo, and Oppo had also arrived in the market. Still, Indian brands like Micromax, Intex, Spice, and Karbonn dominated sales charts for multiple and sometimes even consecutive quarters. In fact, in Q2 2014, Micromax even overtook Samsung to be the number one smartphone brand in the country in terms of shipments. It was a time when we carried a story on how Micromax deserved to be shown more respect.
Ghosts of the Indian smartphone market past: Why Indian brands ruled, and how the Chinese brands beat them
There was a reason for this dominance. At that point of time, Indian smartphone brands mainly catered to the budget segment, mostly under Rs. 15,000 (or even Rs 10,000), which comprised a large chunk of the smartphone market. While international brands had tried to enter this segment, they had very limited success, as they could not match the price-to-spec ratio that the Indian brands were offering. Big displays, big batteries, and decent processors (often from the more affordable MediaTek) and a small price tag made phones from the likes of Micromax, Intex, and Karbonn the perfect pick for anyone looking to pick up an entry-level smartphone. The likes of Apple, Samsung, HTC, Sony, and BlackBerry were largely operating in the mid/ upper mid and premium segment.
The tech climate changed as Chinese brands began to make their presence felt. Xiaomi, OnePlus, Vivo, and Oppo all stepped into the Indian market in 2014. Oppo and Vivo seemed to be playing in the premium segment, while brands like Xiaomi and OnePlus initially seemed to focus on flagship killers (a term OnePlus popularised). However, given India’s demography, it did not take a long time for these brands to realize that real numbers were actually in the budget and mid segment.
Even as Indian brands struggled with inventory issues as the 4G revolution hit India, the Chinese brands shifted focus and brought in smartphones with prices and spec combinations that matched and, in many cases, even eclipsed what Indian brands were offering. That was not all.
With the mobile Internet becoming more accessible thanks to extremely affordable 4G rates (pioneered mainly by Reliance Jio), these brands also opted for a very unconventional plan of action, going for flash sales, online only sales, often with little to no advertising in mainstream media, and building communities online. These not only cut expenses, but built greater brand loyalty (something Indian brands had been unable to do, as they had focused mainly on price). This combination of pricing and communications affected all the other brands in the market, but hit the Indian brands particularly hard, as it took away their biggest USP – a low price tag. The years that followed saw not just Indian brands fade, but even the likes of LG, Sony and HTC bid farewell to the Indian market.
The Indian Smartphone Market Today: Rocked by a steep price rise
In the last ten years, the Indian smartphone market has changed completely. Many Indian brands that had seemed almost invincible have packed their bags and left, although some like Lava have managed to stick around, in spite of not being the force they once were. But the tech stars in the tech universe move in different ways, and the way in which they have been aligning in recent times makes me think that the time is ripe for Indian smartphone brands to make a comeback in their own market.
Hear me out before you think I am talking through my hat. We have seen a very steady shift happening in the tech world in 2026. Many brands that earlier ruled the budget, mid, and lower-mid segments have been climbing up the price ladder for a while now, seeking larger profit margins. Indeed, the number of phones available in the sub-Rs 15,000 segment has been shrinking in recent times, with many brands seemingly inching towards vacating it altogether.
The likes of Motorola, OnePlus and Xiaomi are also no longer organizations with lean portfolios and small, focused teams but have become tech behemoths with large-scale operations, huge marketing budgets, multiple sub-brands and extensive product portfolios. This has, of course, affected their ability to offer the extremely competitive price-spec combo that made them popular in the first place.
The dramatic increase in the price of memory has now made it even more difficult for existing brands to offer good devices at lower price points. Devices with specs that used to be seen in the sub-Rs 15,000 segment are now being seen at prices in the range of Rs 25,000 or more. Options at lower price points are either vanishing or are coming with relatively modest specs.
And Indian brands are suddenly appearing on the horizon again.
Guess who’s back, back again… Indian smartphone brands
White Lava had never left; it seems to have got a new lease of life. AI+ is increasingly aggressive, and Fire-Boltt, a brand known more for its wearables and hearables, has entered the smartphone market. Even as this is being written, Mivi, a mainly audio brand, has announced plans for a smartphone with a Qualcomm Snapdragon processor for under Rs 15,000, and there is also talk of Micromax returning to the market, and Boat (which, like Fire-Boltt, is known mainly for audio and wearable products) is also planning to sail in smartphone waters. And from what we know, all these brands are targeting the sub-Rs 15,000 market, from which many brands have moved products to higher price points and/ or releasing new devices with much more modest specs in the past.
The Indian Government is also making efforts to build a smartphone brand that it can call its own. On August 21, it officially sent out a notification, as per which the Union Cabinet approved a budget of Rs. 62,500 crore for a Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme (MPMS) to build globally competitive, native smartphone brands. The scheme offers a number of incentives and rewards for Indian brands. To qualify, a company must be registered in India, keep its ownership and trademarks in India, have more than 51 percent Indian shareholding, be controlled in India, and have its products designed locally without outsourcing. This is a massive push and is likely to encourage more Indian entrepreneurs to enter the smartphone market.
Welcome back, Indian brands, but this time, please stay!
But making a comeback will not be enough. The smartphone world has changed a fair bit since the time Indian brands ruled the charts. And the new ones or those making a comeback would need to adopt a fundamentally different approach to ensure that the second innings of Indian brands in the smartphone market is a long one, and does not end as abruptly as the first. Being an ‘Indian brand’ has to have a different connotation than it did in the past.
Indian brands have struggled with offering good after-sales service and good software, and have tended to compete mainly on price and specs. That needs to change. The new and not-so-new native brands have to ensure they not just deliver a smartphone at a competitive price, but follow through on the whole process that comes after. Easy access to repairs and spare parts, timely OS updates, and improved, new-age marketing strategies are all necessities for these brands to actually establish themselves in this competitive market for the long run.
Native brands also need to shed their image of merely assembling and/or importing devices from outside and rebranding them for the Indian market. Authentic and good quality products backed up with a solid sales and service system are both needed to make consumers associate Indian brands not just with low prices, but also with high quality.
As of now, Indian brands are knocking on the door of their nation’s smartphone market once again. Just how well they will do, only time will tell. While I am hoping their second coming will be a successful one and they will win back lost ground (more local brands are always welcome in any market, and the big five out there need competition), there is no way of knowing how things will actually work out. Who knows, if I am still here, covering tech a decade later, I might be telling you a completely different story altogether.
A decade is a VERY long time in tech. Stay tuned.

Marshals is back with more explosions, missing children and rural romances.
CBS has unveiled the first trailer for Season 2 of the CBS procedural, which stars Luke Grimes as Kayce Dutton, who ends the clip climbing a moving train with a big gun, obviously.
The clip answered a number of questions that arose from the Season 1 finale of the Yellowstone spinoff.
Firstly, it seems that two of Dutton’s fellow Marshals – Supervisory Deputy U.S. Marshal Pete “Cal” Calvin, played by Logan Marshall-Green and Deputy U.S. Marshal Isabel “Belle” Skinner-Turek, played by Arielle Kebbel are safe after ending the season in a shoot-out.
In fact, it appears they are more than safe, they are getting cozy together.
Watch on Deadline
Secondly, Deputy U.S. Marshal Andrea Cruz, played by Ash Santos, hasn’t gone anywhere, despite considering a job in Washington, D.C., and having said her goodbyes to her colleagues. “I never had teammates who fight for each other the way that you do,” she says in the trailer. She also calls Kayce trouble. “You really are a chaos magnet, cowboy,” she adds.
Thirdly, Dutton’s son Tate, played by Brecken Merrill, is still in trouble after being taken bass fishing in Texas by Tom Weaver, played by Chris Mulkley, a Wall Street trader turned rancher who has been trying to buy East Camp.
“It hurts my heart thinking of all you’ve been through,” Dutton tells his child. “I’m strong, like how you raised me to be. It’s the Dutton way,” replies Tate.
On the love interest front, Kayce is seemingly still getting close with Dolly Weaver, played by Ellyn Jameson. “Do you think I’m a good man?,” he asks her. “The best,” she replies. Still, she is also the daughter of the man who is threatening his child.
As with many Taylor Sheridan-produced shows, it’s about the land, man. “That Dutton family legacy… it was never about land,” Kayce says. “It’s about always having to fight. Seems like no matter where I live, someone’s willing to kill for it.”
Marshals returns to CBS on October 4 and the show has some new cast members. Deadline revealed last month that Marque Richardson is joining the show and Morgan Lindholm’s role is expanding. Richardson recurs as Assistant U.S. Attorney Patrick Burns, while Lindholm is Maddie, the bartender at the local watering hole, Bullet ’N Barrel, and daughter of Cal.
Marshals is produced by Paramount Television Studios and 101 Studios and executive produced by Grimes, Sheridan, David Glasser, John Linson, Art Linson, showrunner Spencer Hudnut, Ron Burkle, David Hutkin, Bob Yari, Michael Freidman, and Keith Cox.

Star Wars Zero Company is a great game that's busted and may never be fixed
It's hard to be confident about the game's future after the studio that made it furloughed most of its staff.
If you're on the fence about Star Wars Zero Company, you should know what you might be getting into. The game currently has an aggregate critic score of 85 on Metacritic, making it one of the best reviewed Star Wars games in recent memory. When it comes to story and gameplay, it's a masterfully executed tactics game in the style of X-COM with memorable characters. What none of the reviews I read or watched mentioned is that Zero Company is also something of a technical mess.
On PC, the game has all the trademarks of a janky Unreal Engine 5 release. I'm running a system with a Ryzen 7 5800X3D, RTX 5060 Ti and 16GB of RAM, and I'm getting constant traversal stutter and input lag when I try to play the game with a mouse and keyboard. I've also encountered a bug that forced me to restart the same mission twice. Yes, you might say I'm running the game on a glorified RTX 3070, but even those with more powerful GPUs like the RTX 5090 are complaining of poor performance. On Steam, the game has a "mostly positive" rating across nearly 9,000 reviews, and yet almost every one of those reviews mentions stuttering, game-breaking bugs and crashes.
"Started off having a great time," one negative review starts. "Then came the crashes. Crashed almost every hour, so needed to save every few minutes. On the times I forgot to save, I had to replay the entire section again. Of course it only ever crashed as I was about to complete a mission." Over on Reddit, console players are complaining of their own set of issues. YouTuber Daniel Owen has also made a video about the game's PC issues. While I haven't played the Xbox Series or PlayStation 5 ports, there are similar reports of crashes and stutters floating around the internet for each.
The experience of playing Zero Company is frustratingly similar to that of another recent UE5 Star Wars game, Jedi: Survivor. As I wrote about in 2023, that game was broken on release. It suffered from constant traversal and shader compilation stutter on PC, meaning the game would constantly hitch even on high-end systems. For NVIDIA users, the game also shipped without DLSS support. Even after nearly a dozen major patches, Jedi: Survivor still stutters on PC. At this point, I've given up hope that the game will ever play smoothly; Respawn Entertainment, Jedi: Survivor's developer, hasn't released a new patch in nearly two years.
Unfortunately, I can't confidently say Zero Company will receive even a fraction of the post-release support that Jedi: Survivor got from Respawn. That's because while Electronic Arts published both games, the new one was made by an independent studio named Bit Reactor, not a direct subsidiary, and its future depends on whether Zero Company sells enough copies.
On Monday, Game File's Stephen Totilo reported that Bit Reactor had furloughed the majority of its staff just weeks before Zero Company's release on August 27. One source told Totilo that as much as 80 percent of the studio's employees aren't being paid right now. Another source told him that only a skeleton crew remains, "ready to address any of Zero Company's post-launch bugs." A spokesperson for Bit Reactor told Totilo that the studio hopes to bring the furloughed workers back with restored pay, a promise the employees he spoke to said they weren't confident it would be able to deliver on, even if the game is a commercial success. The studio is also embroiled in a legal dispute between its co-founders that won't go to trial until early 2027.
If what remains of Bit Reactor is working to address Zero Company's many bugs and performance issues, the one public statement the studio has made on the subject isn't reassuring. On the day of the game's release, it simply said on Steam's Community forums it was aware of "emerging issues (crashes and CPU threading)," and that it was working on implementing fixes. "We'll let you know when we're able to provide an update," it added.
On the face of it, that's a fine enough statement, but it was issued before the news about its staffing levels came out, and it hasn't said anything since. EA and Bit Reactor did not immediately respond to Engadget's comment request, asking what, if any, post-release support the game will receive.
If you're thinking about buying Zero Company, just know that it might not get to a better state than it is right now. You might think I'm being overly pessimistic, but I'll point out it took Respawn, a studio with the full financial backing of EA, a year-and-a-half to get Jedi: Survivor to its current state. Another comparison here is just as illustrative. Cold Symmetry, the indie studio behind Mortal Shell II this past Saturday announced a hefty "Week One" update for its new game, which it released just seven days before Zero Company. Those two comparisons give a sense of the potential difficult road ahead for Bit Reactor, but also what an indie studio can do when it's fully staffed. Right now, Zero Company doesn't that have going for it.

India has offered to help Nepal get its hydropower plants, roads and bridges back on their feet after devastating floods and landslides ravaged critical infrastructure across the Himalayan country, according to three officials aware of the developments. They said state-run hydropower majors NHPC Ltd and SJVN Ltd have offered technical assistance towards the effort, deepening New Delhi’s role in rebuilding infrastructure in the country, where it is already a major energy partner.
Around 700 megMW of hydropower capacity have been knocked out, while key roads and bridges have been washed away by the floods on 26 August. Over 1,100 people have been reported killed by the floods, while over 4,800 people are still missing.
"The Centre and the hydro PSUs have assured that they can provide technical assistance to restore the damaged hydro power projects in Nepal. It would, however, depend upon the Nepalese authorities' decision on the matter," said an official in the know of the development.
Queries emailed to the ministries of power, road transport & highways and external affairs, the hydropower firms, as well as the Embassy of Nepal in New Delhi remained unanswered until press time.
To be sure, Indian companies already have a presence in several large hydropower projects of Nepal, including SJVN’s 900MW Arun-III and 679MW Lower Arun projects, and NHPC’s 1,200MW West Seti and Seti River-6 joint project and 480MW Phukot Karnali project. The GMR Group is also developing the 900MW Upper Karnali project.
India is also a major market for Nepal’s surplus electricity, with cross-border power trade becoming an increasingly important component of bilateral economic ties.
"The ministry of external affairs is in constant touch with the Nepalese government. As collaborative efforts are already on for relief measures, support for infrastructure redevelopment and restoration of power projects has also been assured. The immediate focus is on relief and rescue," said another official in the know.
Hitendra Dev Shakya, former managing director of the Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) told Mint that the focus is now on relief and rescue of the affected and displaced people, and in due course studies would be done to get details of the damage to power projects.
“Studies will have to be done to know where sludge has accumulated, or where turbines have been displaced. Only after that will restoration work start,” Shakya said. He identified the 24MW Trishuli and 14.1MW Devighat hydropower plants, both built with Indian assistance, as potential candidates for Indian support.
Power availability itself is not an immediate crisis, he said. Of Nepal’s installed capacity of about 4,300MW, around 3,600MW remains operational, against a peak domestic requirement of roughly 2,600MW.
Sustainable safety
Some experts called for regional cooperation to bring sustainable security in the Himalayan region, which is highly vulnerable to natural disasters due to climate change.
Abhay Kumar Singh, president of the Indian National Hydropower Association, called for a mechanism involving Nepal, India and China to assess risks from developments in upstream areas and formulate long-term safety measures for downstream regions.
India’s experience in responding to infrastructure disasters in its own Himalayan states could also provide a basis for cooperation. “NHPC is well equipped to assist in restoration in such cases with efficiency," said Raj Kumar Chaudhary, former chairman and managing director of NHPC Ltd. "A similar incident had happened in Sikkim in October 2023, which damaged the Teesta-V project of NHPC that the company has partially restored."
“The unfortunate incident (in Nepal) happened after a moraine burst happened at the Nepal-Tibet border and there was probably no adequate information with Nepal, and they could not take the required safety measures in terms of shifting people to safer places or releasing water from the dams to hold this heavier flow of war out of the glacial burst,” Chaudhary said. "However, on the Indian side, due to timely information, water was released from the Gandak and Kosi barrages in a controlled manner to curb major impact here."
Neighbour ties
India’s infrastructure partnership with Nepal extends beyond hydropower to roads and bridges, with New Delhi increasingly combining project development with support for reconstruction after natural disasters. It was also involved in restoration work for infrastructure projects damaged in natural calamities earlier.
In April, the two countries jointly inaugurated a 70-metre high-capacity modular bridge in Nepal. It is one of the 10 similar pre-fabricated bridges provided by the government of India to Nepal, to help in the restoration of connectivity following the devastating rains of October 2025 in eastern and central Nepal, as per a statement by the Indian embassy in Kathmandu.
These 10 bailey bridges, worth more than 73 crore Nepalese rupees (around ₹45.35 crore), along with technical assistance for their installation, are being provided on a grant basis.
Earlier, in the aftermath of Nepal's floods and landslides in September 2024, India had supplied 10 pre-fabricated steel bridges, worth 41 crore Nepalese rupees.
India’s involvement spans the entire infrastructure cycle: from financing and constructing hydropower, roads and bridges, to providing technical expertise and emergency reconstruction support when these assets are damaged.
Roads and bridges are critical in Nepal, where difficult terrain and limited alternative routes mean damage to a single bridge or road stretch can isolate entire communities.
“We are ready to repair and reconstruct damaged roads and bridges in Nepal, but would be guided by directions from the ministry of external affairs to undertake such work," said a senior official from the roads ministry on the condition of anonymity. "The current focus is relief and humanitarian measures, for which Nepal has already accepted Indian assistance.”

Anantnag, Sep 03: The Ministry of Railways has approved an experimental stoppage of the Jammu Tawi-Srinagar Vande Bharat Express at Anantnag railway station, officials said.
In a communication issued by the Railway Board, the Board said the stoppage will be provided for Jammu Tawi-Srinagar Vande Bharat Express, at Anantnag.
The Railway Board has directed that the stoppage be introduced from an “early convenient date”, subject to requisite security clearance. The Board has also directed the concerned authorities to closely monitor ticket sales at Anantnag station to assess the performance of the stoppage.
“Give wide publicity, ensure compliance and confirm,” the communication states.
The move is expected to improve rail connectivity for residents of Anantnag and adjoining areas and benefit tourists, traders, students and other passengers travelling between Jammu and Kashmir.
The stoppage will initially be experimental, with passenger response and ticket sales to be monitored before a decision is taken on its continuation.
Railway sources told KNO that the stoppage is likely to become operational by the end of September. The exact date of commencement, along with the arrival and departure timings at Anantnag, is yet to be notified.—(KNO)

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Teri Williams, president and chief operating officer of OneUnited Bank. It has been edited for length and clarity.
Growing up in Indiantown, Florida, I used to follow my great-grandmother around, whom I called Ma Honey. Ma Honey owned a penny candy store, a barbecue place, and a juke joint, where I learned how to play pool. She also owned rental properties, and I'd go with her to collect the rents.
Ma Honey's businesses shielded her family from the dangers of a segregated southern town. Her money also gave our family opportunities: she paid for my grandparents to move so that my father could attend high school, since there wasn't a Black high school in their town. She also built houses, one of which my parents and I still lived in when I was growing up.
But they say wealth lasts for three generations, and I was the fourth. By the time I went to college at Brown University, I was on a scholarship, and I felt embarrassed about Ma Honey and my small-town Southern roots.
I started running a bank while raising kids
I didn't think about Ma Honey as a businesswoman until I was in my 50s. But looking back, I can see that her spirit shaped my success. I went to Brown, then Harvard Business School, before working for major national banks.
In the mid-90s, my husband Kevin and I consolidated four banks in Boston, Los Angeles, and Miami to form OneUnited Bank. The banks we consolidated were serving the Black community, and that's what we've done since.
Kevin and I were growing the bank — he as chairman and CEO, me as president and chief operating officer — while we were raising our kids, who are now 30 and 32.
I taught my kids to prioritize savings
I'm curious if my kids thought about us as bankers or just accepted the environment they were raised in without questioning too much, as I did with Ma Honey.
The lifestyle of bankers isn't what people might think. In our house, being bankers meant prioritizing savings. One of the most important things we've taught our kids is to save, save, save.
I explain it like this: savings allows you to take risks. And to succeed, you need to take those risks — even more mainstream ones, like owning a home. The higher the risk, the higher the reward, and having a healthy savings account gives you a cushion for when mistakes and pitfalls inevitably happen.
Financial literacy is hard, even in my family
Building financial literacy was also very important — not just for my kids, but for the wider Black community. I wrote a children's book that addressed some of the issues in the Black community, such as check cashers and payday loans. At OneUnited, we've integrated these terms into our financial literacy programs in schools.
All the financial terms can still be overwhelming. One of my children called me when she was a young adult. She was confused about the balance on her credit card. In talking, I realized that she thought her balance was what she had available. I had to tell her it was what she owed.
I almost fell off my chair, thinking, "Where did I go wrong?" Then I reminded myself that financial terms can be complicated. There's no embarrassment or shame in not understanding terms that aren't easy to comprehend at first glance.
My kids use money differently from me
I tried to remember that as my children transitioned into adulthood. We had talked with them about money a lot. And yet, when you're suddenly dealing with your own paycheck, taxes, bills, and credit cards — well, that's a road that's different once you're actually traveling it.
My kids handle money differently from the way I did. I invested mostly in mutual funds, whereas they often chose individual stocks. They invested in crypto, which I wouldn't do. It's natural for financial decisions to change over time, so this doesn't worry me too much.
I hope this next generation thinks bigger. Ma Honey was able to serve her town, and through OneUnited, my husband and I now serve all 50 states. I hope my children, or my children's children, might be able to serve the world.

The effect of political and religious indoctrination on young minds resembles a slow-release poison. Unfolding in observational vignettes, Pankaj Johar and Sunaina Kapoor’s thought-provoking documentary centres on Vidya Mutth, a prestigious Hindu school in the holy city of Varanasi, India, where sectarian beliefs are drilled into its students, all in the name of cultural preservation.
The film opens with controversial speeches made by the school’s spiritual leader, Guru Avimuktesh, who advocates the abolition of religious freedom, and for Indian Muslims to either convert to Hinduism or leave for Pakistan. A prominent Hindu figure with a large following, he personally oversees the entrance exam, a sequence captured in dynamic handheld shots. While boys take the test, their parents look on with apprehension and anxiety; to be accepted would be an honour, not only for their child but for the whole family.
For those who do get in to Vidya Mutth, what follows is far from a glorious, enlightening experience. Focusing on two new entrants called Satyarth and Hari, the film documents their daily routines, which largely revolve around Sanskrit classes. The learning of this ancient script, supposedly to maintain a linguistic tradition, is actually in service of religious dogmatism; in between classes, Guru Avimuktesh continues to preach Islamophobic and casteist ideas, packaged as fact.
Moreover, though fanatically strict on its Hindu teachings, the school pays little attention to the mental and physical wellbeing of the pupils. Scenes of the school’s lavish celebration of its leader’s birthday are intercut with the students’ ramshackle living quarters. Even more shocking than this are the changes we observe in the boys over the course of mere months. Once a fresh-faced youth with a gentle demeanour, Hari soon starts to parrot the guru’s intolerant ideology with terrifying conviction. Laying bare the mechanism of indoctrination, Johar and Kapoor’s film sounds an urgent alarm for a new generation growing up under the spell of extremism.

Madagascar ex-Senate chief sentenced to hard labour over deadly Gen Z protest crackdown
- Published
Madagascar's former Senate president has been sentenced to 10 years of hard labour over his alleged role in the violent crackdown on youth-led protests that helped bring down the previous government last year.
Richard Ravalomanana, a retired general and close ally of former President Andry Rajoelina, was found guilty of complicity in murder by a court in the capital, Antananarivo, on Tuesday.
Prosecutors accused him of giving instructions to security forces to use violence against demonstrators during the so-called Gen Z protests in September and October 2025.
Ravalomanana denied the allegations and said he would appeal against the judgement.
- From prison to presidential palace: Who is Madagascar's new military ruler? 
  - Published17 October 2025
The protests began a year ago, initially sparked by anger over persistent power and water shortages, before developing into a broader movement against Rajoelina's government.
At least 22 people were killed and more than 100 injured during the unrest, according to UN figures cited by local media.
The protests eventually triggered a political crisis that led to Rajoelina's removal from power and the installation of a new administration led by Col Michael Randrianirina.
The crackdown was led by the gendarmerie, where Ravalomanana retained considerable influence at the time.
He "directed violent actions to suppress the demonstrations", a state prosecutor said in December 2025.
Ravalomanana was removed as Senate president in October, shortly after the protests, and was arrested at his home in December after failing to respond to a summons from the gendarmerie.
He was later placed in pre-trial detention at the high-security Imerintsiatosika prison outside Antananarivo, where he has spent the past seven months.
He is among several senior figures associated with Rajoelina's former government who have faced legal proceedings since the change of power. Ravalomanana is also facing a separate corruption investigation.
A former national police chief who testified at the trial backed his account, saying Ravalomanana was not part of the operational chain of command and had issued no orders to police, gendarmes or soldiers deployed during the unrest.
His lawyer questioned the evidence linking him directly to the violence.
"Is there confirmed written or verbal evidence... to accuse him?" he asked the court, arguing that prosecutors had failed to produce proof that security officers had received orders from his client.
Ravalomanana's defence team said it would challenge the verdict in a higher court.
The court dropped a separate allegation of making a death threat after ruling that the case was too old to prosecute.
Known for wearing a cowboy hat and displaying his military medals, Ravalomanana was viewed by protesters as a symbol of authoritarian power.
